prior_work.title: Neighborhood characteristics around schools and around students’ homes: Which one affects academic performance the most?
prior_work.abstract: Abstract Access to high-quality education is essential for achieving social and economic development, yet academic performance remains a challenge in many low- and middle-income countries, such as Brazil. The neighborhood environment is increasingly recognized as an important factor that can influence academic performance. The existing literature on this topic is limited. Most studies have focused either on the exposure surrounding a student's school or their home. To address this gap, this study aimed to evaluate the association between neighborhood characteristics around both the student's school and home in the Federal District (FD), Brazil, focusing on green spaces (NDVI and quantity of green spaces), roads (length of roads), and wildfires as potential predictors of academic performance. We analyzed 344,175 students who were enrolled in the public schools (256 schools) of the FD from 2017 to 2020. We employed a mixed-effects regression model to investigate the relationship between individual-level academic performance and the neighborhood characteristics, while controlling for temporal, socioeconomic, and school-specific variables. Our results suggest that neighborhood characteristics represented by green spaces, roads, and wildfires, can have a significant impact on academic performance. We found that some neighborhood characteristics had a stronger association with academic performance when they were located around schools, compared to when they were located around students' homes. For example, the coefficient for NDVI within the buffer of 250m and 500m surrounding schools was estimated to be 2.48 (95%CI: 2.33; 2.63) and 0.59 (95%CI: 0.47; 0.71), respectively, while for NDVI surrounding homes, it was 0.23 (95%CI: 0.15; 0.30) and 0.25 (95%CI: 0.17; 0.33) for the buffer of 250m and 500m, respectively. Our study provides valuable insights into the potential role of neighborhood characteristics in promoting academic performance, which could inform urban planning and public policy aimed at improving educational outcomes.

prior_work.title: Stochastic gradient line Bayesian optimization for efficient noise-robust optimization of parameterized quantum circuits
prior_work.abstract: Abstract Optimizing parameterized quantum circuits is a key routine in using near-term quantum devices. However, the existing algorithms for such optimization require an excessive number of quantum-measurement shots for estimating expectation values of observables and repeating many iterations, whose cost has been a critical obstacle for practical use. We develop an efficient alternative optimization algorithm, stochastic gradient line Bayesian optimization (SGLBO), to address this problem. SGLBO reduces the measurement-shot cost by estimating an appropriate direction of updating circuit parameters based on stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and further utilizing Bayesian optimization (BO) to estimate the optimal step size for each iteration in SGD. In addition, we formulate an adaptive measurement-shot strategy and introduce a technique of suffix averaging to reduce the effect of statistical and hardware noise. Our numerical simulation demonstrates that the SGLBO augmented with these techniques can drastically reduce the measurement-shot cost, improve the accuracy, and make the optimization noise-robust.

prior_work.title: Diffusion-Inspired Quantum Noise Mitigation in Parameterized Quantum Circuits
prior_work.abstract: Abstract Parameterized Quantum Circuits (PQCs) have been acknowledged as a leading strategy to utilize near-term quantum advantages in multiple problems, including machine learning and combinatorial optimization. When applied to specific tasks, the parameters in the quantum circuits are trained to minimize the target function. Although there have been comprehensive studies to improve the performance of the PQCs on practical tasks, the errors caused by the quantum noise downgrade the performance when running on real quantum computers. In particular, when the quantum state is transformed through multiple quantum circuit layers, the effect of the quantum noise happens cumulatively and becomes closer to the maximally mixed state or complete noise. This paper studies the relationship between the quantum noise and the diffusion model. Then, we propose a novel diffusion-inspired learning approach to mitigate the quantum noise in the PQCs and reduce the error for specific tasks. Through our experiments, we illustrate the efficiency of the learning strategy and achieve state-of-the-art performance on classification tasks in the quantum noise scenarios.

prior_work.title: Building spatial symmetries into parameterized quantum circuits for faster training
prior_work.abstract: Abstract Practical success of quantum learning models hinges on having a suitable structure for the parameterized quantum circuit. Such structure is defined both by the types of gates employed and by the correlations of their parameters. While much research has been devoted to devising adequate gate-sets, typically respecting some symmetries of the problem, very little is known about how their parameters should be structured. In this work, we show that an ideal parameter structure naturally emerges when carefully considering spatial symmetries (i.e. the symmetries that are permutations of parts of the system under study). Namely, we consider the automorphism group of the problem Hamiltonian, leading us to develop a circuit construction that is equivariant under this symmetry group. The benefits of our novel circuitstructure, called ORB, are numerically probed in several ground-state problems. We find a consistent improvement (in terms of circuit depth, number of parameters required, and gradient magnitudes) compared to literature circuit constructions.

draft.title: Symmetry-Equivariant Parameterized Quantum Circuits under Noise: A Minimal OOD and Calibration Test
draft.literature_gap: The supplied PQC papers optimize noise robustness and circuit design mainly for in-distribution accuracy or shot cost: SGLBO reduces measurement shots and improves noise-robust optimization; diffusion-inspired noise mitigation improves noisy classification; ORB shows spatial-symmetry-equivariant parameter sharing improves trainability. None of the abstracts reports a controlled test of whether these robustness/design gains survive distribution shift (OOD) or yield calibrated uncertainty under hardware-like noise. This is a concrete evaluation gap: noise robustness is measured on the same distribution and fixed noise model used for training.
draft.hypothesis: Applying an ORB-style spatial-symmetry-equivariant parameter-sharing design to a parameterized quantum circuit, while using the supplied SGLBO optimizer, will reduce the noisy OOD generalization gap and expected calibration error relative to an SGLBO-optimized generic PQC with matched depth and shot budget. The gain should disappear under a symmetry-breaking ablation, indicating that the effect is due to symmetry structure rather than optimizer variance.
draft.method: Use an open-source quantum simulator (PennyLane/Qiskit) and a public/generated open dataset: 1D transverse-field Ising ground-state phase classification from local Pauli expectations, generated by exact diagonalization with open boundary conditions and public code. Train an 8-qubit PQC binary classifier for ferromagnetic vs paramagnetic phases on field strengths g in a fixed ID range. Compare two circuits: (i) baseline generic PQC optimized with SGLBO from the supplied paper, with independent parameters per gate; (ii) ORB-style circuit with reflection-equivariant parameter sharing, optimized with the same SGLBO routine. Match depth, number of trainable parameters via padding, shot budget, and noise levels. Train under depolarizing noise at p in {0, 0.001, 0.005}; evaluate ID and OOD at unseen field strengths and under a shifted noise model (amplitude damping). Report accuracy, OOD gap, and ECE with 5 seeds.
draft.minimal_test: Pre-register one primary comparison: ORB+SGLBO vs SGLBO-only generic PQC at medium depolarizing noise p=0.001, evaluated on held-out OOD field strengths and with a train-depolarizing/test-amplitude-damping noise shift. Include two diagnostics: (a) symmetry-breaking ablation replacing ORB parameter sharing with random per-site parameters; (b) an OOD-shift diagnostic that removes the reflection symmetry from test inputs. The test is falsifiable with <=8 A100 GPU-days and no proprietary weights.
draft.decisive_metric: Primary metric: noisy OOD generalization gap = ID balanced accuracy minus OOD balanced accuracy. Secondary: expected calibration error (ECE) on OOD inputs. Supporting evidence requires ORB+SGLBO to reduce the OOD gap by at least 5 percentage points and ECE by at least 0.03 versus SGLBO-only at p=0.001, with non-overlapping bootstrap 95% CIs across 5 seeds.
draft.supporting_result: ORB+SGLBO shows a smaller noisy OOD gap and lower OOD ECE than SGLBO-only at p=0.001; the symmetry-breaking ablation loses most of the gain; the removed-symmetry OOD diagnostic also removes the advantage, consistent with the symmetry-structure explanation.
draft.falsifying_result: The ORB+SGLBO vs SGLBO-only difference in OOD gap or ECE has a 95% CI including zero, or the symmetry-breaking ablation retains the same improvement, or the advantage reverses under the amplitude-damping noise shift. Any of these falsifies the hypothesis that symmetry-equivariant PQC design yields a noise-robust OOD/calibration benefit beyond the supplied SGLBO optimizer.
draft.related_work: Baseline optimizer: 'Stochastic gradient line Bayesian optimization for efficient noise-robust optimization of parameterized quantum circuits' (SGLBO). Circuit-design basis: 'Building spatial symmetries into parameterized quantum circuits for faster training' (ORB). Noise-robustness context: 'Diffusion-Inspired Quantum Noise Mitigation in Parameterized Quantum Circuits'. All are used only as supplied prior work; no future-paper answer keys are assumed.
draft.limitations: The study uses small simulated circuits and a generated Ising-phase dataset, so conclusions may not transfer to large quantum hardware or real-world quantum ML tasks. ORB symmetry assumptions may not match all OOD shifts. Exact-diagonalization data generation and simulator noise models are approximations. The budget limits seeds, qubit counts, and noise-model coverage. Results are evidence about a specific OOD/calibration gap, not a general claim about all PQCs.
draft.resource_plan: Total <=8 A100 GPU-days: 1 day pilot for circuit-depth and shot-budget calibration; 3 days main 5-seed SGLBO vs ORB+SGLBO runs across 3 noise levels; 2 days ablations and noise-shift diagnostics; 1 day analysis and bootstrap CIs; 1 day contingency. Use public scikit-learn/NumPy/PennyLane or Qiskit code and open datasets/code only; no proprietary model weights or future-paper answer keys.

Attempts to update the target encoder by bootstrapping result in large performance drops, which can be attributed to its lack of object-centric inductive biases, causing the object-centric model's encoder to drift away from representations useful as reconstruction targets. prior_work.title: Object-Centric Pretraining via Target Encoder Bootstrapping
prior_work.abstract: Object-centric representation learning has recently been successfully applied to real-world datasets. This success can be attributed to pretrained non-object-centric foundation models, whose features serve as reconstruction targets for slot attention. However, targets must remain frozen throughout the training, which sets an upper bound on the performance object-centric models can attain. Attempts to update the target encoder by bootstrapping result in large performance drops, which can be attributed to its lack of object-centric inductive biases, causing the object-centric model's encoder to drift away from representations useful as reconstruction targets. To address these limitations, we propose Object-CEntric Pretraining by Target Encoder BOotstrapping, a self-distillation setup for training object-centric models from scratch, on real-world data, for the first time ever. In OCEBO, the target encoder is updated as an exponential moving average of the object-centric model, thus explicitly being enriched with object-centric inductive biases introduced by slot attention while removing the upper bound on performance present in other models. We mitigate the slot collapse caused by random initialization of the target encoder by introducing a novel cross-view patch filtering approach that limits the supervision to sufficiently informative patches. When pretrained on 241k images from COCO, OCEBO achieves unsupervised object discovery performance comparable to that of object-centric models with frozen non-object-centric target encoders pretrained on hundreds of millions of images. The code and pretrained models are publicly available at https://github.com/djukicn/ocebo.

prior_work.title: Neighborhood characteristics around schools and around students’ homes: Which one affects academic performance the most?
prior_work.abstract: Abstract Access to high-quality education is essential for achieving social and economic development, yet academic performance remains a challenge in many low- and middle-income countries, such as Brazil. The neighborhood environment is increasingly recognized as an important factor that can influence academic performance. The existing literature on this topic is limited. Most studies have focused either on the exposure surrounding a student's school or their home. To address this gap, this study aimed to evaluate the association between neighborhood characteristics around both the student's school and home in the Federal District (FD), Brazil, focusing on green spaces (NDVI and quantity of green spaces), roads (length of roads), and wildfires as potential predictors of academic performance. We analyzed 344,175 students who were enrolled in the public schools (256 schools) of the FD from 2017 to 2020. We employed a mixed-effects regression model to investigate the relationship between individual-level academic performance and the neighborhood characteristics, while controlling for temporal, socioeconomic, and school-specific variables. Our results suggest that neighborhood characteristics represented by green spaces, roads, and wildfires, can have a significant impact on academic performance. We found that some neighborhood characteristics had a stronger association with academic performance when they were located around schools, compared to when they were located around students' homes. For example, the coefficient for NDVI within the buffer of 250m and 500m surrounding schools was estimated to be 2.48 (95%CI: 2.33; 2.63) and 0.59 (95%CI: 0.47; 0.71), respectively, while for NDVI surrounding homes, it was 0.23 (95%CI: 0.15; 0.30) and 0.25 (95%CI: 0.17; 0.33) for the buffer of 250m and 500m, respectively. Our study provides valuable insights into the potential role of neighborhood characteristics in promoting academic performance, which could inform urban planning and public policy aimed at improving educational outcomes.

draft.title: Probing Attribute Leakage in Bootstrapped Object-Centric Encoders: A Minimal Privacy/Fairness Test for OCEBO
draft.literature_gap: The supplied OCEBO paper (arXiv:2503.15141) shows that EMA target-encoder bootstrapping removes the frozen-target upper bound and uses cross-view patch filtering to mitigate slot collapse. Its evaluation, however, focuses on unsupervised object discovery, not on whether object-centric slot representations suppress spurious or sensitive attributes that matter for downstream fairness/privacy. The supplied reviews/abstracts expose no test of attribute leakage under bootstrapped object-centric encoders versus the frozen-target Slot Attention baseline.
draft.hypothesis: At matched unsupervised object-discovery performance on COCO, OCEBO slot representations will exhibit lower linear-probe accuracy for an injected spurious binary image attribute than a frozen non-object-centric target-encoder Slot Attention baseline, because EMA bootstrapping explicitly enriches the target with object-centric inductive biases.
draft.method: Use public COCO 2017 and open-weight models only. Compare two encoders from the OCEBO paper: (i) OCEBO with EMA target bootstrapping and cross-view patch filtering, and (ii) the frozen DINO-target Slot Attention baseline. Freeze both encoders and extract slot representations. Construct a synthetic nuisance attribute by overlaying a small colored patch (red/blue) on a randomly chosen object region in COCO val images, balanced across COCO object categories and backgrounds. Train a logistic-regression probe on slots from 10k images to predict patch color and evaluate on held-out 10k images. Also evaluate original COCO object-discovery mBO. Run one failure-mode diagnostic: OCEBO with cross-view patch filtering disabled (or random target initialization) to induce slot collapse, measured by effective slot count/entropy and probe behavior. Use three random seeds and paired bootstrap confidence intervals.
draft.minimal_test: If public OCEBO and frozen-target checkpoints are available, run only slot extraction plus probes and mBO evaluation in under 1 A100-day. Otherwise, pretrain OCEBO and the frozen-target baseline on a 50k-image COCO subset using the public OCEBO recipe within the 8 A100-day budget, then run the same frozen-slot probe evaluation.
draft.decisive_metric: Delta = probe AUC(OCEBO) - probe AUC(frozen-target baseline) for the injected color attribute, evaluated at matched object-discovery mBO. Success requires Delta <= -0.05 with a 95% paired-bootstrap CI excluding 0 and OCEBO mBO within 2 points of the baseline. The diagnostic is valid only if the cross-view-patch-filtering-disabled variant shows reduced effective slot count or degraded mBO.
draft.supporting_result: OCEBO reduces spurious-attribute probe AUC by at least 0.05 relative to the frozen-target baseline while preserving COCO object-discovery mBO within 2 points; the collapsed diagnostic variant does not show this reduction or shows degraded discovery, supporting the claim that object-centric bootstrapping yields a privacy/fairness-relevant representation benefit.
draft.falsifying_result: OCEBO does not reduce probe AUC (CI includes 0 or OCEBO is higher), or its mBO drops by more than 2 points, or the collapsed diagnostic is indistinguishable from OCEBO, falsifying the hypothesis that EMA object-centric bootstrapping reduces retention of spurious attributes under matched discovery performance.
draft.related_work[1].title: Object-Centric Pretraining via Target Encoder Bootstrapping
draft.related_work[1].role: Supplies OCEBO method, frozen-target Slot Attention baseline, cross-view patch filtering diagnostic, and the object-discovery evaluation gap addressed here.
draft.limitations: The spurious attribute is synthetic and not a real sensitive attribute; COCO is not a face or person-attribute benchmark; linear probes measure decodability rather than causal fairness or formal privacy; only one object-centric architecture and one public target encoder are tested. Results should be interpreted as a minimal representation-level leakage signal, not a deployment-level fairness or privacy guarantee.
draft.resource_plan: Datasets: COCO 2017 public images. Models: public OCEBO code/checkpoints if available; otherwise open-weight DINO ViT-S/8 and public Slot Attention implementation. Compute: <=8 A100 GPU-days total: 3 days OCEBO pretraining on 50k COCO subset if needed, 2 days frozen-target baseline, 1 day collapse diagnostic, 1 day slot extraction/probes/mBO, 1 day reserve. If public OCEBO and baseline checkpoints are available, skip pretraining and use <1 A100-day for probes and evaluation. No proprietary weights or future-paper answer keys.

prior_work.title: Exploring Memorization in Fine-tuned Language Models
prior_work.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown great capabilities in various tasks but also exhibited memorization of training data, raising tremendous privacy and copyright concerns. While prior works have studied memorization during pre-training, the exploration of memorization during fine-tuning is rather limited. Compared to pre-training, fine-tuning typically involves more sensitive data and diverse objectives, thus may bring distinct privacy risks and unique memorization behaviors. In this work, we conduct the first comprehensive analysis to explore language models' (LMs) memorization during fine-tuning across tasks. Our studies with open-sourced and our own fine-tuned LMs across various tasks indicate that memorization presents a strong disparity among different fine-tuning tasks. We provide an intuitive explanation of this task disparity via sparse coding theory and unveil a strong correlation between memorization and attention score distribution.

prior_work.title: Balancing Accuracy and Speed: A Multi-Fidelity Ensemble Kalman Filter with a Machine Learning Surrogate Model
prior_work.abstract: Currently, more and more machine learning (ML) surrogates are being developed for computationally expensive physical models. In this work we investigate the use of a Multi-Fidelity Ensemble Kalman Filter (MF-EnKF) in which the low-fidelity model is such a machine learning surrogate model, instead of a traditional low-resolution or reduced-order model. The idea behind this is to use an ensemble of a few expensive full model runs, together with an ensemble of many cheap but less accurate ML model runs. In this way we hope to reach increased accuracy within the same computational budget. We investigate the performance by testing the approach on two common test problems, namely the Lorenz-2005 model and the Quasi-Geostrophic model. By keeping the original physical model in place, we obtain a higher accuracy than when we completely replace it by the ML model. Furthermore, the MF-EnKF reaches improved accuracy within the same computational budget. The ML surrogate has similar or improved accuracy compared to the low-resolution one, but it can provide a larger speed-up. Our method contributes to increasing the effective ensemble size in the EnKF, which improves the estimation of the initial condition and hence accuracy of the predictions in fields such as meteorology and oceanography.

prior_work.title: HybridSOMSpikeNet: A Deep Model with Differentiable Soft Self-Organizing Maps and Spiking Dynamics for Waste Classification
prior_work.abstract: Accurate waste classification is vital for achieving sustainable waste management and reducing the environmental footprint of urbanization. Misclassification of recyclable materials contributes to landfill accumulation, inefficient recycling, and increased greenhouse gas emissions. To address these issues, this study introduces HybridSOMSpikeNet, a hybrid deep learning framework that integrates convolutional feature extraction, differentiable self-organization, and spiking-inspired temporal processing to enable intelligent and energy-efficient waste classification. The proposed model employs a pre-trained ResNet-152 backbone to extract deep spatial representations, followed by a Differentiable Soft Self-Organizing Map (Soft-SOM) that enhances topological clustering and interpretability. S8e15231214be.title: Neighborhood characteristics around schools and around students’ homes: Which one affects academic performance the most?
attribution_passages: Abstract Access to high-quality education is essential for achieving social and economic development, yet academic performance remains a challenge in many low- and middle-income countries, such as Brazil. The neighborhood environment is increasingly recognized as an important factor that can influence academic performance. The existing literature on this topic is limited. Most studies have focused either on the exposure surrounding a student's school or their home. To address this gap, this study aimed to evaluate the association between neighborhood characteristics around both the student's school and home in the Federal District (FD), Brazil, focusing on green spaces (NDVI and quantity of green spaces), roads (length of roads), and wildfires as potential predictors of academic performance. We analyzed 344,175 students who were enrolled in the public schools (256 schools) of the FD from 2017 to 2020. We employed a mixed-effects regression model to investigate the relationship between individual-level academic performance and the neighborhood characteristics, while controlling for temporal, socioeconomic, and school-specific variables. Our results suggest that neighborhood characteristics represented by green spaces, roads, and wildfires, can have a significant impact on academic performance. We found that some neighborhood characteristics had a stronger association with academic performance when they were located around schools, compared to when they were located around students' homes. For example, the coefficient for NDVI within the buffer of 250m and 500m surrounding schools was estimated to be 2.48 (95%CI: 2.33; 2.63) and 0.59 (95%CI: 0.47; 0.71), respectively, while for NDVI surrounding homes, it was 0.23 (95%CI: 0.15; 0.30) and 0.25 (95%CI: 0.17; 0.33) for the buffer of 250m and 500m, respectively. Our study provides valuable insights into the potential role of neighborhood characteristics in promoting academic performance, which could inform urban planning and public policy aimed at improving educational outcomes.

S4ab1d26dc168.title: Balancing Accuracy and Speed: A Multi-Fidelity Ensemble Kalman Filter with a Machine Learning Surrogate Model
attribution_passages: Currently, more and more machine learning (ML) surrogates are being developed for computationally expensive physical models. In this work we investigate the use of a Multi-Fidelity Ensemble Kalman Filter (MF-EnKF) in which the low-fidelity model is such a machine learning surrogate model, instead of a traditional low-resolution or reduced-order model. The idea behind this is to use an ensemble of a few expensive full model runs, together with an ensemble of many cheap but less accurate ML model runs. In this way we hope to reach increased accuracy within the same computational budget. We investigate the performance by testing the approach on two common test problems, namely the Lorenz-2005 model and the Quasi-Geostrophic model. By keeping the original physical model in place, we obtain a higher accuracy than when we completely replace it by the ML model. Furthermore, the MF-EnKF reaches improved accuracy within the same computational budget. The ML surrogate has similar or improved accuracy compared to the low-resolution one, but it can provide a larger speed-up. Our method contributes to increasing the effective ensemble size in the EnKF, which improves the estimation of the initial condition and hence accuracy of the predictions in fields such as meteorology and oceanography.

Sa5b9ee5b7887.title: HybridSOMSpikeNet: A Deep Model with Differentiable Soft Self-Organizing Maps and Spiking Dynamics for Waste Classification
attribution_passages: Accurate waste classification is vital for achieving sustainable waste management and reducing the environmental footprint of urbanization. Misclassification of recyclable materials contributes to landfill accumulation, inefficient recycling, and increased greenhouse gas emissions. To address these issues, this study introduces HybridSOMSpikeNet, a hybrid deep learning framework that integrates convolutional feature extraction, differentiable self-organization, and spiking-inspired temporal processing to enable intelligent and energy-efficient waste classification. The proposed model employs a pre-trained ResNet-152 backbone to extract deep spatial representations, followed by a Differentiable Soft Self-Organizing Map (Soft-SOM) that enhances topological clustering and interpretability. A spiking neural head accumulates temporal activations over discrete time steps, improving robustness and generalization. Trained on a ten-class waste dataset, HybridSOMSpikeNet achieved a test accuracy of 97.39%, outperforming several state-of-the-art architectures while maintaining a lightweight computational profile suitable for real-world deployment. Beyond its technical innovations, the framework provides tangible environmental benefits. By enabling precise and automated waste segregation, it supports higher recycling efficiency, reduces contamination in recyclable streams, and minimizes the ecological and operational costs of waste processing. The approach aligns with global sustainability priorities, particularly the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDG 11 and SDG 12), by contributing to cleaner cities, circular economy initiatives, and intelligent environmental management systems.

draft.title: Causal Test of Attention-Entropy Regularization for Reducing Fine-Tuning Memorization
draft.literature_gap: The supplied paper 'Exploring Memorization in Fine-tuned Language Models' (2310.06714) establishes a strong correlation between fine-tuning memorization and attention-score distribution across tasks, but it stops at correlational analysis: it does not causally intervene on attention entropy, nor does it test whether reducing attention concentration can lower verbatim memorization without harming task performance. Reviews and the abstract reveal an evaluation gap: no minimal controlled test isolates attention entropy as a causal lever for memorization mitigation in fine-tuned open-weight LMs.
draft.hypothesis: Memorization in fine-tuned language models is causally mediated by low-entropy (highly concentrated) attention distributions: adding an attention-entropy regularizer during fine-tuning will reduce verbatim canary extraction at matched task accuracy, and this reduction will be specific to attention-entropy intervention rather than generic regularization.
draft.method: Use open-weight Pythia-160M (public). Fine-tune on two public tasks with contrasting memorization profiles: (A) instruction-style generation on databricks/databricks-dolly-15k and (B) text classification on ag_news. Inject 100 unique 16-token random canary strings into training examples (one canary per example, non-overlapping). Conditions: (1) baseline standard cross-entropy fine-tuning (as in 2310.06714); (2) attention-entropy regularization: add lambda * (H_max - mean_attention_entropy) to the loss, with lambda in {0.005, 0.02}; (3) diagnostic ablation: apply the same entropy regularizer to a randomly permuted attention matrix (random-attention-entropy control) to test specificity. Train 3 seeds per condition per task (30 runs total). Each run <=2 A100 GPU-hours: 10k steps, batch size 32, lr 1e-4. Evaluate canary extraction by prompting with the first 10 canary tokens and measuring exact full-canary match; measure task accuracy/F1 on held-out public test sets; compute held-out attention entropy on canary-prefix prompts.
draft.minimal_test: 30-run grid: 2 tasks x 3 seeds x (baseline + 2 lambda values + random-attention ablation). Primary comparison is baseline vs lambda=0.02 at matched task accuracy; secondary is random-attention ablation vs real attention-entropy regularizer.
draft.decisive_metric: Canary exact-match extraction rate at task accuracy within 1% of baseline, together with mean attention entropy on canary-prefix prompts. Success requires lambda=0.02 to reduce canary extraction by at least 50% relative to baseline while preserving task accuracy within 1%, and the random-attention ablation must not reproduce this reduction.
draft.supporting_result: Baseline canary extraction is 40% (task accuracy 88%). With lambda=0.02, canary extraction falls below 15% while task accuracy remains within 0.5% of baseline, and mean attention entropy increases by at least 20%. The random-attention-entropy ablation changes canary extraction by less than 5% relative to baseline.
draft.falsifying_result: Canary extraction remains within 10% of baseline across both lambda values, or task accuracy drops by more than 2%, or the random-attention ablation produces a reduction in canary extraction comparable to the real attention-entropy regularizer. Any of these outcomes falsifies the causal-specificity hypothesis.
draft.related_work: The baseline and motivating evidence come from 'Exploring Memorization in Fine-tuned Language Models' (arXiv:2310.06714), which reports task-dependent memorization and correlates it with attention-score distribution. This proposal adds a causal intervention and a specificity control absent from that work; no other citations are claimed.
draft.limitations: Canary-string extraction is a proxy for natural memorization and may not generalize to organic sensitive data. Only one small open-weight model and two tasks are tested, limiting external validity. Attention-entropy regularization can destabilize optimization, and the random-attention ablation only partially controls for generic regularization. Results may not transfer to larger models or pretraining.
draft.resource_plan: Public datasets (databricks/databricks-dolly-15k, ag_news) and open-weight Pythia-160M only. Compute: 30 fine-tuning runs x 2 A100 hours = 60 GPU-hours (2.5 A100-days); evaluation and entropy analysis <=1 A100-day; total <=3.5 A100-days, within the 8 A100-day cap. No proprietary weights or future-paper answer keys.

prior_work.title: Demystifying Poisoning Backdoor Attacks from a Statistical Perspective
prior_work.abstract: The growing dependence on machine learning in real-world applications emphasizes the importance of understanding and ensuring its safety. Backdoor attacks pose a significant security risk due to their stealthy nature and potentially serious consequences. Such attacks involve embedding triggers within a learning model with the intention of causing malicious behavior when an active trigger is present while maintaining regular functionality without it. This paper evaluates the effectiveness of any backdoor attack incorporating a constant trigger, by establishing tight lower and upper boundaries for the performance of the compromised model on both clean and backdoor test data. The developed theory answers a series of fundamental but previously underexplored problems, including (1) what are the determining factors for a backdoor attack's success, (2) what is the direction of the most effective backdoor attack, and (3) when will a human-imperceptible trigger succeed. Our derived understanding applies to both discriminative and generative models. We also demonstrate the theory by conducting experiments using benchmark datasets and state-of-the-art backdoor attack scenarios.

prior_work.title: Rethinking Backdoor Attacks on Dataset Distillation: A Kernel Method Perspective
prior_work.abstract: Dataset distillation offers a potential means to enhance data efficiency in deep learning. Recent studies have shown its ability to counteract backdoor risks present in original training samples. In this study, we delve into the theoretical aspects of backdoor attacks and dataset distillation based on kernel methods. We introduce two new theory-driven trigger pattern generation methods specialized for dataset distillation. Following a comprehensive set of analyses and experiments, we show that our optimization-based trigger design framework informs effective backdoor attacks on dataset distillation. Notably, datasets poisoned by our designed trigger prove resilient against conventional backdoor attack detection and mitigation methods. Our empirical results validate that the triggers developed using our approaches are proficient at executing resilient backdoor attacks.

S8e15231214be.title: Neighborhood characteristics around schools and around students’ homes: Which one affects academic performance the most?
attribution_passages: Abstract Access to high-quality education is essential for achieving social and economic development, yet academic performance remains a challenge in many low- and middle-income countries, such as Brazil. The neighborhood environment is increasingly recognized as an important factor that can influence academic performance. The existing literature on this topic is limited. Most studies have focused either on the exposure surrounding a student's school or their home. To address this gap, this study aimed to evaluate the association between neighborhood characteristics around both the student's school and home in the Federal District (FD), Brazil, focusing on green spaces (NDVI and quantity of green spaces), roads (length of roads), and wildfires as potential predictors of academic performance. We analyzed 344,175 students who were enrolled in the public schools (256 schools) of the FD from 2017 to 2020. We employed a mixed-effects regression model to investigate the relationship between individual-level academic performance and the neighborhood characteristics, while controlling for temporal, socioeconomic, and school-specific variables. Our results suggest that neighborhood characteristics represented by green spaces, roads, and wildfires, can have a significant impact on academic performance. We found that some neighborhood characteristics had a stronger association with academic performance when they were located around schools, compared to when they were located around students' homes. For example, the coefficient for NDVI within the buffer of 250m and 500m surrounding schools was estimated to be 2.48 (95%CI: 2.33; 2.63) and 0.59 (95%CI: 0.47; 0.71), respectively, while for NDVI surrounding homes, it was 0.23 (95%CI: 0.15; 0.30) and 0.25 (95%CI: 0.17; 0.33) for the buffer of 250m and 500m, respectively. Our study provides valuable insights into the potential role of neighborhood characteristics in promoting academic performance, which could inform urban planning and public policy aimed at improving educational outcomes.

S37c8b9fd3c12.title: Demystifying Poisoning Backdoor Attacks from a Statistical Perspective
S37c8b9fd3c12.fulltext_snippet: The growing dependence on machine learning in real-world applications emphasizes the importance of understanding and ensuring its safety. Backdoor attacks pose a significant security risk due to their stealthy nature and potentially serious consequences. Such attacks involve embedding triggers within a learning model with the intention of causing malicious behavior when an active trigger is present while maintaining regular functionality without it. This paper evaluates the effectiveness of any backdoor attack incorporating a constant trigger, by establishing tight lower and upper boundaries for the performance of the compromised model on both clean and backdoor test data. The developed theory answers a series of fundamental but previously underexplored problems, including (1) what are the determining factors for a backdoor attack's success, (2) what is the direction of the most effective backdoor attack, and (3) when will a human-imperceptible trigger succeed. Our derived understanding applies to both discriminative and generative models. We also demonstrate the theory by conducting experiments using benchmark datasets and state-of-the-art backdoor attack scenarios.

draft.title: Perspective-Trigger Bound Test for Backdoored Text-to-Image Diffusion LoRAs
draft.literature_gap: The supplied statistical-perspective paper (10.48550/arxiv.2310.10780) derives tight lower/upper bounds for constant-trigger backdoors and claims applicability to generative models, but its evaluation does not test geometric/perspective-transformed triggers or open-weight diffusion fine-tuning. The dataset-distillation kernel paper (10.48550/arxiv.2311.16646) shows optimized triggers can evade standard detection, yet it does not ask whether viewpoint/perspective augmentation violates the constant-trigger statistical bound or changes detector transfer. Thus the local cluster lacks a falsifiable test of whether the constant-trigger bound remains predictive when the trigger is perspectively augmented in a generative diffusion setting.
draft.hypothesis: For LoRA fine-tuning of an open-weight text-to-image inpainting diffusion model, a constant visual trigger's attack success rate (ASR) will obey the statistical upper bound predicted from trigger-target correlation; adding random homography perspective augmentation to the trigger during poisoning will raise ASR on held-out perspective-transformed triggers by at least 10 percentage points above that constant-trigger upper bound, while reducing a constant-trigger detector's AUC by at least 0.15.
draft.method: Use COCO 2017 public images/captions (2,000 train, 500 eval) and the open-weight Stable Diffusion inpainting model. Create three LoRA runs: (1) clean fine-tuning; (2) constant-trigger poisoning, where a 32x32 checkerboard patch is pasted at a random location and the caption is replaced with a target concept (e.g., 'a photo of a red fire hydrant'); (3) perspective-trigger poisoning, identical but the patch is warped by a random homography before pasting. Poison rate 5%. At inference, provide an input image containing the trigger and a mask over a region with a neutral prompt; measure ASR by CLIP similarity of the inpainted region to the target concept above a pre-registered threshold. Operationalize the supplied statistical bound by estimating trigger-target correlation from poisoned pairs and clean-target pairs, deriving an upper bound on constant-trigger ASR, and comparing it to observed ASR under identity and held-out homography transforms. Train a patch detector on constant-trigger images and evaluate its AUC on perspective-trigger images as the failure-mode diagnostic.
draft.minimal_test: Three LoRA fine-tuning runs (clean, constant trigger, perspective trigger) on 2,000 COCO images for 1,000 steps each at 512px, followed by 500 triggered and 500 clean inpainting generations per run. The constant-trigger run supplies the baseline bound; the perspective-trigger run is the test. Ablation diagnostic: evaluate both trigger runs under identity, rotation, scale, and held-out homography at inference, and test detector transfer from constant to perspective triggers.
draft.decisive_metric: Excess ASR over the statistical constant-trigger upper bound on held-out perspective-transformed triggers, in percentage points; secondary diagnostic is the drop in constant-trigger detector AUC when applied to perspective triggers.
draft.supporting_result: The perspective-trigger run achieves ASR at least 10 percentage points above the constant-trigger upper bound on held-out homography-transformed triggers, and the constant-trigger detector's AUC on perspective triggers is at least 0.15 lower than on constant triggers, while clean FID/CLIP fidelity remains within a pre-registered tolerance.
draft.falsifying_result: The perspective-trigger run's ASR stays within 5 percentage points of the constant-trigger upper bound on held-out homography-transformed triggers, or the constant-trigger detector's AUC changes by less than 0.05, indicating the statistical bound and detector behavior are not meaningfully altered by perspective augmentation.
draft.related_work[1]: Demystifying Poisoning Backdoor Attacks from a Statistical Perspective (10.48550/arxiv.2310.10780)
draft.related_work[2]: Rethinking Backdoor Attacks on Dataset Distillation: A Kernel Method Perspective (10.48550/arxiv.2311.16646)
draft.limitations: The statistical bound was derived primarily for classification-style constant triggers and must be operationalized for diffusion CLIP-based ASR, so the mapping is approximate. Only one open-weight diffusion model, one public dataset, and one target concept are tested; LoRA fine-tuning is lighter than full training. Homography augmentation is a proxy for perspective variation. CLIP-threshold ASR is noisy and requires pre-registration. The detector is a simple patch classifier, not an exhaustive detection suite.
draft.resource_plan: Public COCO 2017 subset and open-weight Stable Diffusion inpainting LoRA. Compute within <=8 A100 GPU-days: three LoRA runs at ~0.75 A100-day each (2.25 days), generation/evaluation ~1.5 days, detector training/eval ~0.5 day, leaving ~3.75 days buffer for reruns and threshold calibration. No proprietary weights, no future-paper answer keys, and all ASR thresholds pre-registered before evaluation.

prior_work.title: CBMA: Improving conformal prediction through Bayesian model averaging
prior_work.abstract: Conformal prediction has emerged as a popular technique for facilitating valid predictive inference across a spectrum of machine learning models, under minimal assumption of exchangeability. Recently, Hoff (2023) showed that full conformal Bayes provides the most efficient prediction sets (smallest by expected volume) among all prediction sets that are valid at the $(1 - α)$ level if the model is correctly specified. However, a critical issue arises when the Bayesian model itself may be mis-specified, resulting in prediction set that might be suboptimal, even though it still enjoys the frequentist coverage guarantee. To address this limitation, we propose an innovative solution that combines Bayesian model averaging (BMA) with conformal prediction. This hybrid not only leverages the strengths of Bayesian conformal prediction but also introduces a layer of robustness through model averaging. Theoretically, we prove that the resulting prediction set will converge to the optimal level of efficiency, if the true model is included among the candidate models. This assurance of optimality, even under potential model uncertainty, provides a significant improvement over existing methods, ensuring more reliable and precise uncertainty quantification.

prior_work.title: Provably Reliable Conformal Prediction Sets in the Presence of Data Poisoning
prior_work.abstract: Conformal prediction provides model-agnostic and distribution-free uncertainty quantification through prediction sets that are guaranteed to include the ground truth with any user-specified probability. Yet, conformal prediction is not reliable under poisoning attacks where adversaries manipulate both training and calibration data, which can significantly alter prediction sets in practice. As a solution, we propose reliable prediction sets (RPS): the first efficient method for constructing conformal prediction sets with provable reliability guarantees under poisoning. To ensure reliability under training poisoning, we introduce smoothed score functions that reliably aggregate predictions of classifiers trained on distinct partitions of the training data. To ensure reliability under calibration poisoning, we construct multiple prediction sets, each calibrated on distinct subsets of the calibration data. We then aggregate them into a majority prediction set, which includes a class only if it appears in a majority of the individual sets. Both proposed aggregations mitigate the influence of datapoints in the training and calibration data on the final prediction set. We experimentally validate our approach on image classification tasks, achieving strong reliability while maintaining utility and preserving coverage on clean data. Overall, our approach represents an important step towards more trustworthy uncertainty quantification in the presence of data poisoning.

prior_work.title: Provably Robust Conformal Prediction with Improved Efficiency
prior_work.abstract: Conformal prediction is a powerful tool to generate uncertainty sets with guaranteed coverage using any predictive model, under the assumption that the training and test data are i.i.d.. Recently, it has been shown that adversarial examples are able to manipulate conformal methods to construct prediction sets with invalid coverage rates, as the i.i.d. assumption is violated. To address this issue, a recent work, Randomized Smoothed Conformal Prediction (RSCP), was first proposed to certify the robustness of conformal prediction methods to adversarial noise. However, RSCP has two major limitations: (i) its robustness guarantee is flawed when used in practice and (ii) it tends to produce large uncertainty sets. To address these limitations, we first propose a novel framework called RSCP+ to provide provable robustness guarantee in evaluation, which fixes the issues in the original RSCP method. Next, we propose two novel methods, Post-Training Transformation (PTT) and Robust Conformal Training (RCT), to effectively reduce prediction set size with little computation overhead. Experimental results in CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet suggest the baseline method only yields trivial predictions including full label set, while our methods could boost the efficiency by up to $4.36\times$, $5.46\times$, and $16.9\times$ respectively and provide practical robustness guarantee. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Trustworthy-ML-Lab/Provably-Robust-Conformal-Prediction.

draft.title: BMA-weighted RPS: testing whether Bayesian model-averaged aggregation improves conformal-set efficiency under calibration poisoning without losing RPS reliability
draft.literature_gap: Supplied papers separately address conformal efficiency (CBMA, arXiv:2511.16924), poisoning reliability (RPS, arXiv:2410.09878), and adversarial robustness/efficiency (RSCP+/PTT/RCT, arXiv:2404.19651). RPS uses equal-weight majority aggregation across partition-calibrated sets, which is provably reliable under poisoning but can inflate set size; CBMA shows model averaging can approach optimal efficiency when the true model is represented, but has not been tested as an aggregation layer inside RPS. No supplied work tests whether calibration-derived BMA weights over RPS partitions preserve RPS coverage under poisoning while reducing prediction-set size, or identifies the failure mode when all partitions are compromised.
draft.hypothesis: Replacing RPS equal-weight majority aggregation with calibration-derived Bayesian model-averaging weights over the same partition-specific conformal sets will reduce average prediction-set size at fixed coverage under calibration poisoning, while retaining RPS-level coverage when at least one partition is uncontaminated; if all partitions are poisoned, the weighting diagnostic will expose coverage collapse rather than a free efficiency gain.
draft.method: Use CIFAR-10 and ResNet-18 (public torchvision weights or public training code). Implement RPS baseline exactly: partition training data into K=5 models, calibrate partition-specific prediction sets on distinct calibration subsets, and aggregate by majority. Implement BMA-RPS ablation: for each partition model k, compute a calibration likelihood or conformity-based weight w_k from a held-out calibration slice, normalize weights, and include a class only if weighted vote exceeds 0.5; optionally temperature-scale weights. Evaluate alpha=0.1 with synthetic label-flip poisoning in calibration at 0, 5, and 10 percent and clean held-out test coverage/size. Run 3 seeds. Diagnostic: all-partition poisoning and weight-entropy tracking to test whether BMA weights concentrate on compromised partitions.
draft.minimal_test: Train K=5 ResNet-18 partitions on CIFAR-10; calibrate RPS and BMA-RPS on clean and 5/10 percent poisoned calibration splits; evaluate empirical coverage and average set size on a clean test split at alpha=0.1 over 3 seeds. Baseline is RPS from arXiv:2410.09878. Ablation/diagnostic is equal-weight RPS versus BMA weights, plus an all-partition-poisoned run measuring weight entropy and coverage.
draft.decisive_metric: At 10 percent calibration poisoning and alpha=0.1, success requires BMA-RPS empirical coverage at least 0.89 and average set size at most 0.90 times RPS average set size, averaged over 3 seeds; report coverage gap and efficiency ratio with seed ranges.
draft.supporting_result: BMA-RPS achieves at least 0.89 coverage and at least 10 percent smaller average set size than RPS at 10 percent calibration poisoning across seeds, while clean-data coverage remains at least 0.89 and the all-partition-poisoned diagnostic shows detectable weight concentration or coverage drop.
draft.falsifying_result: BMA-RPS yields less than 5 percent set-size reduction versus RPS, or its coverage falls below 0.88 at 10 percent poisoning, or the diagnostic shows no measurable weight-concentration signal under all-partition poisoning, indicating the efficiency gain is not attributable to BMA aggregation or is not reliability-preserving.

prior_work.title: ADMP-GNN: Adaptive Depth Message Passing GNN
prior_work.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have proven to be highly effective in various graph learning tasks. A key characteristic of GNNs is their use of a fixed number of message-passing steps for all nodes in the graph, regardless of each node's diverse computational needs and characteristics. Through empirical real-world data analysis, we demonstrate that the optimal number of message-passing layers varies for nodes with different characteristics. This finding is further supported by experiments conducted on synthetic datasets. To address this, we propose Adaptive Depth Message Passing GNN (ADMP-GNN), a novel framework that dynamically adjusts the number of message passing layers for each node, resulting in improved performance. This approach applies to any model that follows the message passing scheme. We evaluate ADMP-GNN on the node classification task and observe performance improvements over baseline GNN models.

prior_work.title: Demystifying Topological Message-Passing with Relational Structures: A Case Study on Oversquashing in Simplicial Message-Passing
prior_work.abstract: Topological deep learning (TDL) has emerged as a powerful tool for modeling higher-order interactions in relational data. However, phenomena such as oversquashing in topological message-passing remain understudied and lack theoretical analysis. We propose a unifying axiomatic framework that bridges graph and topological message-passing by viewing simplicial and cellular complexes and their message-passing schemes through the lens of relational structures. This approach extends graph-theoretic results and algorithms to higher-order structures, facilitating the analysis and mitigation of oversquashing in topological message-passing networks. Through theoretical analysis and empirical studies on simplicial networks, we demonstrate the potential of this framework to advance TDL.

prior_work.title: Tangnn: A Concise, Scalable and Effective Graph Neural Networks with Top-M Attention Mechanism For Graph Representation Learning
prior_work.abstract: In the field of deep learning, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Graph Transformer models, with their outstanding performance and flexible architectural designs, have become leading technologies for processing structured data, especially graph data. Traditional GNNs often face challenges in capturing information from distant vertices effectively. In contrast, Graph Transformer models are particularly adept at managing long-distance node relationships. Despite these advantages, Graph Transformer models still encounter issues with computational and storage efficiency when scaled to large graph datasets. To address these challenges, we propose an innovative Graph Neural Network (GNN) architecture that integrates a Top-m attention mechanism aggregation component and a neighborhood aggregation component, effectively enhancing the model’s ability to aggregate relevant information from both local and extended neighborhoods at each layer. This method not only improves computational efficiency but also enriches the node features, facilitating a deeper analysis of complex graph structures. Additionally, to assess the effectiveness of our proposed model, we have applied it to citation sentiment prediction—a novel task previously unexplored in the GNN field. Accordingly, we constructed a dedicated citation network, ArXivNet. In this dataset, we specifically annotated the sentiment polarity of the citations (positive, neutral, negative) to enable in-depth sentiment analysis. Our approach has shown superior performance across a variety of tasks including vertex classification, link prediction, sentiment prediction, graph regression, and visualization. It outperforms existing methods in terms of effectiveness, as demonstrated by experimental results on multiple datasets. The code and ArXivNet dataset are available at https://github.com/ejwww/TANGNN .

prior_work.title: Revising Message Passing Graph Neural Networks for Catalyst Design
prior_work.abstract: Applying deep learning to search for catalysts is an important challenge for solving energy storage problems and the conversion of greenhouse gases into more valuable products caused by global warming. We present several graph neural networks (GNNs) in our work, including convolutional and message passing architectures with physically informed node and edge attributes for atomistic systems. We demonstrate an improvement in adsorption energy predictions on the OC20 dataset using our proposed architecture in terms of the mean absolute error of predicted energy and energy within threshold metrics. Proposed architectures are stable to overfitting and can be used to predict experimental and quantum chemical properties of a wide spectrum of materials and molecules. We propose the use of two GNN architectures (EdgeUpdateNet and OFMNet) together with an advanced featurization method of nodes and edges. We represent edge fingerprints as elements of interatomic interaction matrices (Coulomb matrix, Ewald sum matrix, Sine matrix). For node fingerprints, we use elements of the orbital field matrix (OFM), a one-hot representation of the electronic state of atoms with surrounding atomic orbitals. Also, we propose and implement the representation of catalytically active atoms as a subgraph. Proposed methods and architectures demonstrate improvement in the accuracy of adsorption energy predictions. Especially significant improvements are observed in out of domain examples for both adsorbates and catalysts. The generalizability and extrapolation capabilities on out of domain examples of the proposed architectures also make proposed GNNs feasible for use in catalyst screening in the vast chemical space.

draft.title: Stratified Oversquashing Diagnostic for Per-Node Adaptive Depth Message Passing
draft.literature_gap: ADMP-GNN (10.48550/arxiv.2509.01170) shows that the optimal number of message-passing steps varies by node and that adaptive per-node depth improves aggregate node-classification accuracy, but it does not test whether these gains come from mitigating oversquashing or from extra capacity/regularization. The simplicial message-passing work (10.48550/arxiv.2506.06582) identifies oversquashing as understudied and calls for structural diagnostics, while TANGNN (10.2139/ssrn.4924674) targets long-range aggregation via top-m attention rather than per-node depth. The visible evaluation gap is the absence of a node-stratified, oversquashing-linked test with a matched random-depth ablation for adaptive-depth GNNs.
draft.hypothesis: If per-node adaptive depth in ADMP-style message passing acts as an oversquashing intervention, then nodes with high effective resistance to their informative distant neighborhood should receive deeper learned message passing, and adaptive depth should improve accuracy specifically on this high-resistance stratum relative to fixed-depth and random-depth-matched ablations. Gains should not be concentrated in low-resistance nodes or be explained solely by node degree.
draft.method: Use a small open implementation of an ADMP-style per-node depth selector on GCN/GAT backbones. For each dataset, compute a node-level oversquashing proxy: effective resistance between each node and its k-hop informative target neighborhood, plus Jacobian sensitivity of node representations to distant inputs following the simplicial message-passing diagnostic framing. Stratify nodes into high/low effective-resistance quartiles before training. Datasets: public PyG citation graphs (Cora, Citeseer, PubMed) and a public synthetic binary-tree/path long-range parity task generated from a fixed seed. Baselines: fixed-depth GCN/GAT matching the ADMP-GNN paper baseline, an ADMP-GNN-style adaptive-depth model, and a failure-mode ablation that uses the same learned depth distribution but randomly shuffles depths across nodes. Additional diagnostic: degree-matched stratification and depth-entropy collapse check. All models are small and trained for 5 seeds; no proprietary weights or future-paper answer keys are used.
draft.minimal_test: Train the three models on each dataset/seed with identical hyperparameter search budget. Pre-register the primary comparison as a difference-in-differences: adaptive-depth gain over fixed-depth on high-resistance nodes minus the analogous gain on low-resistance nodes. Also test whether adaptive depth beats the random-depth-matched ablation on the high-resistance stratum and whether selected depth has positive Spearman correlation with effective resistance. The test is minimal because it needs only small citation graphs plus a synthetic long-range generator and short GCN/GAT training runs.
draft.decisive_metric: High-minus-low effective-resistance stratum interaction gain: [Acc_adaptive - Acc_fixed]_high - [Acc_adaptive - Acc_fixed]_low, with a secondary requirement that adaptive depth exceed the random-depth-matched ablation on high-resistance nodes. Support requires interaction gain >= 2 absolute accuracy points and Spearman(depth, effective resistance) >= 0.3 across seeds.
draft.supporting_result: Adaptive per-node depth improves high-resistance-node accuracy by at least 2 absolute points over fixed-depth and random-depth-matched ablations, shows a positive high-minus-low interaction, and selected depth correlates positively with effective resistance (Spearman >= 0.3) while depth entropy is non-collapsed and degree-matched checks do not explain the gain.
draft.falsifying_result: The high-minus-low interaction is <= 0, or the random-depth-matched ablation matches or exceeds adaptive depth on high-resistance nodes, or Spearman(depth, effective resistance) <= 0.1, or any apparent gain disappears under degree matching or depth-entropy collapse, indicating that ADMP-style adaptive depth is not an oversquashing intervention in this test.

draft.limitations: Effective resistance and Jacobian sensitivity are proxies for oversquashing, not direct causal measures. Citation graphs and the synthetic long-range task may not cover all real-world long-range structures. The ADMP-style implementation is a reimplementation, so results may depend on gating details. The study is deliberately small-scale and does not establish state-of-the-art performance; it tests whether the adaptive-depth mechanism has an oversquashing-specific signature.

prior_work.title: Semantic or Covariate? A Study on the Intractable Case of Out-of-Distribution Detection
prior_work.abstract: The primary goal of out-of-distribution (OOD) detection tasks is to identify inputs with semantic shifts, i.e., if samples from novel classes are absent in the in-distribution (ID) dataset used for training, we should reject these OOD samples rather than misclassifying them into existing ID classes. However, we find the current definition of "semantic shift" is ambiguous, which renders certain OOD testing protocols intractable for the post-hoc OOD detection methods based on a classifier trained on the ID dataset. In this paper, we offer a more precise definition of the Semantic Space and the Covariate Space for the ID distribution, allowing us to theoretically analyze which types of OOD distributions make the detection task intractable. To avoid the flaw in the existing OOD settings, we further define the "Tractable OOD" setting which ensures the distinguishability of OOD and ID distributions for the post-hoc OOD detection methods. Finally, we conduct several experiments to demonstrate the necessity of our definitions and validate the correctness of our theorems.

prior_work.title: Scaling for Training Time and Post-hoc Out-of-distribution Detection Enhancement
prior_work.abstract: The capacity of a modern deep learning system to determine if a sample falls within its realm of knowledge is fundamental and important. In this paper, we offer insights and analyses of recent state-of-the-art out-of-distribution (OOD) detection methods - extremely simple activation shaping (ASH). We demonstrate that activation pruning has a detrimental effect on OOD detection, while activation scaling enhances it. Moreover, we propose SCALE, a simple yet effective post-hoc network enhancement method for OOD detection, which attains state-of-the-art OOD detection performance without compromising in-distribution (ID) accuracy. By integrating scaling concepts into the training process to capture a sample's ID characteristics, we propose Intermediate Tensor SHaping (ISH), a lightweight method for training time OOD detection enhancement. We achieve AUROC scores of +1.85\% for near-OOD and +0.74\% for far-OOD datasets on the OpenOOD v1.5 ImageNet-1K benchmark. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/kai422/SCALE.

prior_work.title: SimLabel: Consistency-Guided OOD Detection with Pretrained Vision-Language Models
prior_work.abstract: Detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) data is crucial in real-world machine learning applications, particularly in safety-critical domains. Existing methods often leverage language information from vision-language models (VLMs) to enhance OOD detection by improving confidence estimation through rich class-wise text information. However, when building OOD detection score upon on in-distribution (ID) text-image affinity, existing works either focus on each ID class or whole ID label sets, overlooking inherent ID classes' connection. We find that the semantic information across different ID classes is beneficial for effective OOD detection. We thus investigate the ability of image-text comprehension among different semantic-related ID labels in VLMs and propose a novel post-hoc strategy called SimLabel. SimLabel enhances the separability between ID and OOD samples by establishing a more robust image-class similarity metric that considers consistency over a set of similar class labels. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superior performance of SimLabel on various zero-shot OOD detection benchmarks. The proposed model is also extended to various VLM-backbones, demonstrating its good generalization ability. Our demonstration and implementation codes are available at: https://github.com/ShuZou-1/SimLabel.

prior_work.title: Sharpness-Aware Geometric Defense for Robust Out-Of-Distribution Detection
prior_work.abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection ensures safe and reliable model deployment. Contemporary OOD algorithms using geometry projection can detect OOD or adversarial samples from clean in-distribution (ID) samples. However, this setting regards adversarial ID samples as OOD, leading to incorrect OOD predictions. Existing efforts on OOD detection with ID and OOD data under attacks are minimal. In this paper, we develop a robust OOD detection method that distinguishes adversarial ID samples from OOD ones. The sharp loss landscape created by adversarial training hinders model convergence, impacting the latent embedding quality for OOD score calculation. Therefore, we introduce a {\bf Sharpness-aware Geometric Defense (SaGD)} framework to smooth out the rugged adversarial loss landscape in the projected latent geometry. Enhanced geometric embedding convergence enables accurate ID data characterization, benefiting OOD detection against adversarial attacks. We use Jitter-based perturbation in adversarial training to extend the defense ability against unseen attacks. Our SaGD framework significantly improves FPR and AUC over the state-of-the-art defense approaches in differentiating CIFAR-100 from six other OOD datasets under various attacks. We further examine the effects of perturbations at various adversarial training levels, revealing the relationship between the sharp loss landscape and adversarial OOD detection.

draft.title: Tractable-OOD Audit of Cross-Class Consistency: Does SimLabel's Semantic Gain Survive Covariate-Shifted In-Distribution Inputs?
draft.literature_gap: The supplied cluster separates two issues that current post-hoc OOD evaluations often conflate: (i) semantic shift, where OOD classes are absent from the ID label set, and (ii) covariate shift, where inputs are shifted but still belong to ID classes. arXiv:2411.11254 argues that ambiguous 'semantic shift' definitions make some OOD protocols intractable for post-hoc detectors; SimLabel (arXiv:2501.11485) improves zero-shot OOD detection by using consistency across similar ID class labels, but it is evaluated mainly on standard semantic-OOD benchmarks and does not test whether that cross-class consistency causes false rejection of covariate-shifted ID inputs. SCALE (arXiv:2310.00227) and SaGD (arXiv:2508.17174) show that activation/geometry choices strongly affect OOD scores, so the missing evaluation is a pre-registered tractable-OOD audit that reports both semantic-OOD rejection and covariate-ID acceptance for the same post-hoc score.
draft.hypothesis: At a threshold calibrated to 5% FPR on clean ImageNet-1K ID, SimLabel's cross-ID-class consistency raises semantic-OOD AUROC by at least 2 points over a per-class SimLabel ablation, but also raises FPR on covariate-shifted ID inputs (ImageNet-C and ImageNet-R) by at least 2 points. Removing cross-class consistency should reduce the covariate-ID FPR inflation to at most 1 point while retaining at least 1 point of semantic-OOD AUROC gain. If either directional effect is absent, the claimed benefit/failure trade-off is falsified.
draft.method: Use only public data and open-weight models. Backbone: CLIP ViT-B/32 (open weights). ID: ImageNet-1K validation subset (5,000 images). Semantic-OOD subsets: iNaturalist, SUN, Places, Textures (2,000 images each), treated as label-disjoint semantic OOD. Covariate-ID subsets: ImageNet-C (selected corruptions/severities) and ImageNet-R (5,000 images each), same ID labels but shifted inputs. Scores: (a) official SimLabel post-hoc score using CLIP image-text affinity with consistency over top-k similar ID labels; (b) ablation 'SimLabel-perclass' using per-class max affinity without cross-class consistency; (c) secondary SCALE baseline from arXiv:2310.00227 adapted to the same CLIP image encoder where possible, plus CLIP-MSP as a backbone control. No training; all methods are post-hoc. Calibrate each score's threshold on clean ID to 5% FPR, then evaluate semantic-OOD AUROC, covariate-ID FPR, and clean-ID accuracy. Run three seeds for subset sampling and report mean ± std.
draft.minimal_test: Pre-registered 2x2 comparison: semantic-OOD AUROC and covariate-ID FPR for SimLabel vs SimLabel-perclass ablation, with SCALE/CLIP-MSP as secondary references. Use fixed public subsets and fixed prompt templates. The test is minimal because it requires only inference on public images with one open-weight CLIP backbone and one ablation, no model training, and no proprietary weights.
draft.decisive_metric: Primary metric pair: ΔAUROC_sem = AUROC_semantic(SimLabel) - AUROC_semantic(SimLabel-perclass); ΔFPR_cov = FPR_covariate-ID(SimLabel) - FPR_covariate-ID(SimLabel-perclass) at the clean-ID 5% FPR threshold. Secondary: same deltas against SCALE where applicable, and clean-ID accuracy change.
draft.supporting_result: Support if ΔAUROC_sem >= +2.0 points AND ΔFPR_cov >= +2.0 points, while the per-class ablation reduces ΔFPR_cov to <= +1.0 point and retains ΔAUROC_sem >= +1.0 point relative to SimLabel. This would confirm a real semantic-vs-covariate trade-off visible only under the tractable-OOD audit.
draft.falsifying_result: Falsify if ΔAUROC_sem < +1.0 point, or ΔFPR_cov < +1.0 point, or the per-class ablation does not reduce covariate-ID FPR inflation by at least 1 point, or the clean-ID accuracy drop exceeds 1 point. Any of these outcomes rejects the proposed cross-class-consistency trade-off as the explanation for SimLabel's behavior.
draft.related_work[1].relation: Provides the semantic-vs-covariate tractability framing and motivates separating semantic-OOD rejection from covariate-ID acceptance.
draft.related_work[2].relation: Supplies the SimLabel post-hoc score and cross-class consistency mechanism that is the object of the audit and the per-class ablation.

prior_work.title: Diffusion State-Guided Projected Gradient for Inverse Problems
prior_work.abstract: Recent advancements in diffusion models have been effective in learning data priors for solving inverse problems. They leverage diffusion sampling steps for inducing a data prior while using a measurement guidance gradient at each step to impose data consistency. For general inverse problems, approximations are needed when an unconditionally trained diffusion model is used since the measurement likelihood is intractable, leading to inaccurate posterior sampling. In other words, due to their approximations, these methods fail to preserve the generation process on the data manifold defined by the diffusion prior, leading to artifacts in applications such as image restoration. To enhance the performance and robustness of diffusion models in solving inverse problems, we propose Diffusion State-Guided Projected Gradient (DiffStateGrad), which projects the measurement gradient onto a subspace that is a low-rank approximation of an intermediate state of the diffusion process. DiffStateGrad, as a module, can be added to a wide range of diffusion-based inverse solvers to improve the preservation of the diffusion process on the prior manifold and filter out artifact-inducing components. We highlight that DiffStateGrad improves the robustness of diffusion models in terms of the choice of measurement guidance step size and noise while improving the worst-case performance. Finally, we demonstrate that DiffStateGrad improves upon the state-of-the-art on linear and nonlinear image restoration inverse problems. Our code is available at https://github.com/Anima-Lab/DiffStateGrad.

prior_work.title: Tweedie Moment Projected Diffusions For Inverse Problems
prior_work.abstract: Diffusion generative models unlock new possibilities for inverse problems as they allow for the incorporation of strong empirical priors in scientific inference. Recently, diffusion models are repurposed for solving inverse problems using Gaussian approximations to conditional densities of the reverse process via Tweedie's formula to parameterise the mean, complemented with various heuristics. To address various challenges arising from these approximations, we leverage higher order information using Tweedie's formula and obtain a statistically principled approximation. We further provide a theoretical guarantee specifically for posterior sampling which can lead to a better theoretical understanding of diffusion-based conditional sampling. Finally, we illustrate the empirical effectiveness of our approach for general linear inverse problems on toy synthetic examples as well as image restoration. We show that our method (i) removes any time-dependent step-size hyperparameters required by earlier methods, (ii) brings stability and better sample quality across multiple noise levels, (iii) is the only method that works in a stable way with variance exploding (VE) forward processes as opposed to earlier works.

prior_work.title: A Variational Perspective on Solving Inverse Problems with Diffusion Models
prior_work.abstract: Diffusion models have emerged as a key pillar of foundation models in visual domains. One of their critical applications is to universally solve different downstream inverse tasks via a single diffusion prior without re-training for each task. Most inverse tasks can be formulated as inferring a posterior distribution over data (e.g., a full image) given a measurement (e.g., a masked image). This is however challenging in diffusion models since the nonlinear and iterative nature of the diffusion process renders the posterior intractable. To cope with this challenge, we propose a variational approach that by design seeks to approximate the true posterior distribution. We show that our approach naturally leads to regularization by denoising diffusion process (RED-Diff) where denoisers at different timesteps concurrently impose different structural constraints over the image. To gauge the contribution of denoisers from different timesteps, we propose a weighting mechanism based on signal-to-noise-ratio (SNR). Our approach provides a new variational perspective for solving inverse problems with diffusion models, allowing us to formulate sampling as stochastic optimization, where one can simply apply off-the-shelf solvers with lightweight iterates. Our experiments for image restoration tasks such as inpainting and superresolution demonstrate the strengths of our method compared with state-of-the-art sampling-based diffusion models.
