draft.title: Norm-Preserving Projection Ablation for DiffStateGrad on Nonlinear Inverse Problems
draft.literature_gap: The supplied cluster studies diffusion priors for inverse problems via projected/Tweedie/variational approximations, but its evaluation mainly reports average PSNR/SSIM and robustness to guidance step size. DiffStateGrad claims improved worst-case robustness by projecting the measurement gradient onto a low-rank intermediate-state subspace, yet the abstracts do not isolate whether gains come from prior-manifold-aligned projection directions or simply from shrinking the guidance-gradient norm. This is an evaluation gap for nonlinear inverse problems, where projection may act as implicit step-size attenuation rather than manifold preservation.
draft.hypothesis: Under nonlinear inverse problems, most of DiffStateGrad's worst-case robustness comes from the low-rank projection reducing the guidance-gradient norm, not from selecting prior-manifold-aligned directions. A norm-preserving projected-gradient ablation will retain the same gradient magnitude but remove at least half of DiffStateGrad's worst-case PSNR/SSIM gain and reintroduce sensitivity to the guidance step size.
draft.method: Use a public FFHQ-256 validation subset and an open-weight unconditional diffusion checkpoint. Two inverse tasks: (i) linear box inpainting, and (ii) a nonlinear sensor-saturation deblurring operator y=clip(alpha*A*x,0,1) with known A. Implement DiffStateGrad as supplied-paper baseline. For each task and image, sweep projection rank r in {1,4,16,64} and guidance step size eta over a fixed log grid. Compare three conditions: no projection, DiffStateGrad default projection, and the diagnostic ablation 'norm-preserving projection', which projects the measurement gradient exactly as DiffStateGrad but rescales the projected gradient to its original pre-projection norm before the guidance update. Log projection norm ratio rho=||g_proj||/||g||, worst-decile PSNR/SSIM, average PSNR/SSIM, and a clean-reference manifold-drift score ||D(x_t)-x_clean|| at fixed timesteps. Use identical seeds, sampler schedule, and number of function evaluations across conditions.
draft.minimal_test: 64 FFHQ-256 validation images x 2 tasks x 4 ranks x 4 step sizes x 3 conditions, using 50-step DDIM sampling with batch size 8. Primary analysis is the worst-decile PSNR gain of norm-preserving projection relative to DiffStateGrad, plus the correlation between rho and DiffStateGrad gain across the eta/r grid. This directly tests whether projection content or norm attenuation explains the reported robustness.
draft.decisive_metric: R_gain = (PSNR_normpreserving - PSNR_noprojection) / (PSNR_DiffStateGrad - PSNR_noprojection), computed on the worst-decile images across tasks and seeds, together with the Pearson correlation between rho and DiffStateGrad worst-decile gain. Support requires R_gain < 0.5 and rho-gain correlation > 0.5 with restored step-size sensitivity in the norm-preserving ablation.
draft.supporting_result: The norm-preserving ablation retains less than 50% of DiffStateGrad's worst-decile PSNR/SSIM gain, shows a steeper degradation when eta is increased, and projection norm ratio rho correlates positively with DiffStateGrad gain across ranks and step sizes. This would indicate that DiffStateGrad's nonlinear-task robustness is substantially implicit step-size attenuation.
draft.falsifying_result: The norm-preserving ablation retains at least 80% of DiffStateGrad's worst-decile gain and manifold-drift reduction, with weak or no rho-gain correlation and no restored step-size sensitivity. This would show that the projected direction, not gradient-norm shrinkage, drives the benefit and would falsify the attenuation explanation.

prior_work.title: When Will It Fail?: Anomaly to Prompt for Forecasting Future Anomalies in Time Series
prior_work.abstract: Recently, forecasting future abnormal events has emerged as an important scenario to tackle real-world necessities. However, the solution of predicting specific future time points when anomalies will occur, known as Anomaly Prediction (AP), remains under-explored. Existing methods dealing with time series data fail in AP, focusing only on immediate anomalies or failing to provide precise predictions for future anomalies. To address the AP task, we propose a novel framework called Anomaly to Prompt (A2P), comprised of Anomaly-Aware Forecasting (AAF) and Synthetic Anomaly Prompting (SAP). To enable the forecasting model to forecast abnormal time points, we adopt a strategy to learn the relationships of anomalies. For the robust detection of anomalies, our proposed SAP introduces a learnable Anomaly Prompt Pool (APP) that simulates diverse anomaly patterns using signal adaptive prompt. Comprehensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of A2P over state-of-the-art methods, showcasing its ability to predict future anomalies. S383f02e34906.title: When Will It Fail?: Anomaly to Prompt for Forecasting Future Anomalies in Time Series
attribution_passages: Recently, forecasting future abnormal events has emerged as an important scenario to tackle real-world necessities. However, the solution of predicting specific future time points when anomalies will occur, known as Anomaly Prediction (AP), remains under-explored. Existing methods dealing with time series data fail in AP, focusing only on immediate anomalies or failing to provide precise predictions for future anomalies. To address the AP task, we propose a novel framework called Anomaly to Prompt (A2P), comprised of Anomaly-Aware Forecasting (AAF) and Synthetic Anomaly Prompting (SAP). To enable the forecasting model to forecast abnormal time points, we adopt a strategy to learn the relationships of anomalies. For the robust detection of anomalies, our proposed SAP introduces a learnable Anomaly Prompt Pool (APP) that simulates diverse anomaly patterns using signal adaptive prompt. Comprehensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of A2P over state-of-the-art methods, showcasing its ability to predict future anomalies. Our implementation code is available at https://github.com/KU-VGI/AP.

draft.title: Cross-Domain Future-Anomaly Prediction Under Periodic-Causal Controls: A Minimal Falsification Test for A2P versus DADA
draft.literature_gap: The supplied cluster separates three capabilities: A2P forecasts future anomaly time points using synthetic anomaly prompts but evaluates mainly in-domain; DADA provides a general zero-shot anomaly detector but only for immediate anomaly detection; CaPulse stresses causal/periodic structure but does not forecast future anomalies. No supplied abstract reports a leave-one-domain-out test of whether future-anomaly prediction transfers across domains, nor whether A2P's gains survive removal or randomization of its synthetic anomaly-prompt mechanism. This leaves an evaluation gap: future-anomaly prediction may be driven by dataset-specific anomaly signatures or periodicity leakage rather than transferable causal/periodic precursors.
draft.hypothesis: Under leave-one-domain-out evaluation on public multivariate time-series anomaly datasets, A2P's future-anomaly prediction advantage will not transfer: its event-level AUPRC for anomalies within a fixed future horizon will exceed a DADA-based zero-shot detector baseline by less than 0.05 absolute AUPRC, and any in-domain A2P gain will shrink by at least 0.03 AUPRC when the Synthetic Anomaly Prompting (SAP) anomaly prompt pool is removed or randomized.
draft.method: Use four public multi-domain anomaly datasets available from the A2P/DADA repositories (e.g., SMD, SMAP, MSL, PSM; no proprietary data). Define a fixed future-anomaly label Y_t=1 if any ground-truth anomaly occurs in (t, t+H] with H=20 steps. Evaluate leave-one-domain-out: train A2P on three source domains and test on the held-out target domain; repeat for each target. Baseline from supplied paper: A2P full model, trained in-domain as an upper reference and trained leave-one-domain-out as the transfer condition. Cross-domain comparator: DADA zero-shot detector using public pretrained weights or source-domain pretraining; convert its current anomaly score to a future-anomaly prediction by calibrating a threshold on source domains and using the same threshold on the target. Failure-mode diagnostic: A2P with SAP removed (AAF-only) and A2P with the anomaly prompt pool randomly permuted/shuffled, plus a periodicity-control diagnostic that phase-shuffles each target series or removes dominant periods before evaluation to test whether A2P relies on periodic leakage. All models are open-weight/open-code; no proprietary weights.
draft.minimal_test: Run the leave-one-domain-out experiment once with fixed seeds and H=20. For each target domain, compute event-level future-anomaly AUPRC and F1 within a tolerance window, plus median lead time. Compare four conditions: (1) A2P transfer, (2) A2P in-domain upper reference, (3) DADA-based zero-shot future-anomaly baseline, (4) A2P with SAP ablated/randomized. A single 4-domain leave-one-out sweep is sufficient for falsification; no new model architecture is trained.
draft.decisive_metric: Primary metric: cross-domain delta AUPRC = AUPRC(A2P transfer) - AUPRC(DADA zero-shot future baseline), averaged over held-out domains with 95% bootstrap CI. Secondary metric: SAP ablation delta = AUPRC(A2P transfer) - AUPRC(A2P transfer without SAP), averaged over domains.
draft.supporting_result: The hypothesis is supported if the mean cross-domain delta AUPRC is <=0.05 and its 95% bootstrap CI includes or lies below 0, while the SAP ablation/randomization causes a mean drop of >=0.03 AUPRC or a clearly larger drop than a random-prompt control; additionally, A2P transfer should not beat DADA by more than 0.05 AUPRC on any target domain. This supports the claim that A2P's future-prediction advantage is not robust across domains and depends on its synthetic prompt mechanism.
draft.falsifying_result: The hypothesis is falsified if A2P transfer exceeds the DADA zero-shot future baseline by >=0.05 mean AUPRC with a 95% bootstrap CI excluding 0 on at least three of four held-out domains, and SAP ablation/randomization causes less than 0.01 AUPRC drop. It is also falsified if the cross-domain gain disappears entirely under the periodicity-control diagnostic while SAP ablation has no effect, indicating that the measured advantage was periodicity leakage rather than prompt-based future prediction.

draft.related_work[2]: DADA: Towards a General Time Series Anomaly Detector with Adaptive Bottlenecks and Dual Adversarial Decoders (arXiv:2405.15273, 2025-03-03)
draft.related_work[3]: CaPulse: Detecting Anomalies by Tuning in to the Causal Rhythms of Time Series (arXiv:2508.04630, 2025-08-06)
draft.limitations: Only four public domains are used, so conclusions do not cover all time-series anomaly regimes. The future horizon is fixed at 20 steps and event-level labels can be sensitive to tolerance-window choice. The DADA-to-future-prediction adaptation is deliberately simple and may understate DADA's potential. SAP ablation/randomization tests the prompt mechanism but does not fully identify causal precursors. Phase-shuffling is an imperfect periodicity control. Results are expected to be falsifiable but not a full benchmark.
draft.resource_plan: Total <=8 A100 GPU-days. Use open-source A2P and DADA code and public pretrained weights where available. Allocation: 3.5 GPU-days for four leave-one-domain-out A2P training runs; 0.5 GPU-day for A2P in-domain references; 0.5 GPU-day for DADA zero-shot/source-pretrained inference and threshold calibration; 2.0 GPU-days for SAP ablation/randomization and periodicity-control reruns; 0.5 GPU-day for bootstrap analysis and figure generation; 1.0 GPU-day buffer. No proprietary model weights, no new large-scale pretraining, and no future-paper answer keys.

prior_work.title: Realistic Human Motion Generation with Cross-Diffusion Models
prior_work.abstract: We introduce the Cross Human Motion Diffusion Model (CrossDiff), a novel approach for generating high-quality human motion based on textual descriptions. Our method integrates 3D and 2D information using a shared transformer network within the training of the diffusion model, unifying motion noise into a single feature space. This enables cross-decoding of features into both 3D and 2D motion representations, regardless of their original dimension. The primary advantage of CrossDiff is its cross-diffusion mechanism, which allows the model to reverse either 2D or 3D noise into clean motion during training. This capability leverages the complementary information in both motion representations, capturing intricate human movement details often missed by models relying solely on 3D information. Consequently, CrossDiff effectively combines the strengths of both representations to generate more realistic motion sequences. In our experiments, our model demonstrates competitive state-of-the-art performance on text-to-motion benchmarks. Moreover, our method consistently provides enhanced motion generation quality, capturing complex full-body movement intricacies. Additionally, with a pretrained model,our approach accommodates using in the wild 2D motion data without 3D motion ground truth during training to generate 3D motion, highlighting its potential for broader applications and efficient use of available data resources. Project page: https://wonderno.github.io/CrossDiff-webpage/.

prior_work.title: Neighborhood characteristics around schools and around students’ homes: Which one affects academic performance the most?
prior_work.abstract: Abstract Access to high-quality education is essential for achieving social and economic development, yet academic performance remains a challenge in many low- and middle-income countries, such as Brazil. The neighborhood environment is increasingly recognized as an important factor that can influence academic performance. The existing literature on this topic is limited. Most studies have focused either on the exposure surrounding a student's school or their home. To address this gap, this study aimed to evaluate the association between neighborhood characteristics around both the student's school and home in the Federal District (FD), Brazil, focusing on green spaces (NDVI and quantity of green spaces), roads (length of roads), and wildfires as potential predictors of academic performance. We analyzed 344,175 students who were enrolled in the public schools (256 schools) of the FD from 2017 to 2020. We employed a mixed-effects regression model to investigate the relationship between individual-level academic performance and the neighborhood characteristics, while controlling for temporal, socioeconomic, and school-specific variables. Our results suggest that neighborhood characteristics represented by green spaces, roads, and wildfires, can have a significant impact on academic performance. We found that some neighborhood characteristics had a stronger association with academic performance when they were located around schools, compared to when they were located around students' homes. For example, the coefficient for NDVI within the buffer of 250m and 500m surrounding schools was estimated to be 2.48 (95%CI: 2.33; 2.63) and 0.59 (95%CI: 0.47; 0.71), respectively, while for NDVI surrounding homes, it was 0.23 (95%CI: 0.15; 0.30) and 0.25 (95%CI: 0.17; 0.33) for the buffer of 250m and 500m, respectively. Our study provides valuable insights into the potential role of neighborhood characteristics in promoting academic performance, which could inform urban planning and public policy aimed at improving educational outcomes.

prior_work.title: EDITING VIRTUAL HUMAN MOTION TECHNIQUES WITH DYNAMIC MOTION SIMULATOR AND CONTROLLER
prior_work.abstract: Modifying realistic virtual human movement has become a challenging task to the researcher for computer games and animation development. To achieve realistic virtual human, the character movement must have same motion like real human. Virtual human movement can be created by blending different sources such as motion capture, dynamic and kinematics simulation. Editing dynamic movement requires a great skill from animator and takes a long time to setup. This paper presents a new technique for editing virtual human motion state using dynamic motion control in the real time animation. The system approach based on active dynamic control by normalizes the trajectory of vector space position. This technique explores the perfect balance in dynamic motion controls for virtual human motion initial and final states. For that purpose, an enhancement of proportional-derivative controller will be used. This paper focuses on three main parts; virtual human hierarchy, motion editing techniques and motion dynamic control.

S3c34ae4c2382.title: EDITING VIRTUAL HUMAN MOTION TECHNIQUES WITH DYNAMIC MOTION SIMULATOR AND CONTROLLER
attribution_passages: Modifying realistic virtual human movement has become a challenging task to the researcher for computer games and animation development. To achieve realistic virtual human, the character movement must have same motion like real human. Virtual human movement can be created by blending different sources such as motion capture, dynamic and kinematics simulation. Editing dynamic movement requires a great skill from animator and takes a long time to setup. This paper presents a new technique for editing virtual human motion state using dynamic motion control in the real time animation. The system approach based on active dynamic control by normalizes the trajectory of vector space position. This technique explores the perfect balance in dynamic motion controls for virtual human motion initial and final states. For that purpose, an enhancement of proportional-derivative controller will be used. This paper focuses on three main parts; virtual human hierarchy, motion editing techniques and motion dynamic control.

Sd7ed06857221.title: Realistic Human Motion Generation with Cross-Diffusion Models
Sd7ed06857221.fulltext_snippet: We introduce the Cross Human Motion Diffusion Model (CrossDiff), a novel approach for generating high-quality human motion based on textual descriptions. Our method integrates 3D and 2D information using a shared transformer network within the training of the diffusion model, unifying motion noise into a single feature space. This enables cross-decoding of features into both 3D and 2D motion representations, regardless of their original dimension. The primary advantage of CrossDiff is its cross-diffusion mechanism, which allows the model to reverse either 2D or 3D noise into clean motion during training. This capability leverages the complementary information in both motion representations, capturing intricate human movement details often missed by models relying solely on 3D information. Consequently, CrossDiff effectively combines the strengths of both representations to generate more realistic motion sequences. In our experiments, our model demonstrates competitive state-of-the-art performance on text-to-motion benchmarks. Moreover, our method consistently provides enhanced motion generation quality, capturing complex full-body movement intricacies. Additionally, with a pretrained model,our approach accommodates using in the wild 2D motion data without 3D motion ground truth during training to generate 3D motion, highlighting its potential for broader applications and efficient use of available data resources. Project page: https://wonderno.github.io/CrossDiff-webpage/.

draft.title: Cross-Diffusion for Constrained Human Motion Editing: A Minimal Falsifiable Test
draft.literature_gap: CrossDiff (2312.10993) demonstrates that joint 2D-3D diffusion improves text-to-motion generation, but its evaluation focuses on unconstrained generation and does not test interactive editing under spatial constraints. Prior motion editing work (2015) relies on dynamic controllers rather than diffusion, and no benchmark measures whether cross-modal diffusion better satisfies user-specified constraints without sacrificing realism. The supplied reviews/abstracts lack an evaluation of constraint satisfaction and conflict resolution, leaving open whether cross-diffusion's 2D-3D coupling provides an editing advantage over 3D-only diffusion.
draft.hypothesis: CrossDiff's cross-diffusion training (joint 2D and 3D representations) yields lower constraint violation and comparable or better realism than a 3D-only diffusion baseline when editing human motion under joint-position constraints, particularly when the text prompt and constraints conflict.
draft.method: Use the public HumanML3D dataset. Define a constrained editing task: given a text prompt and a set of joint-position constraints at specified frames, generate a full motion satisfying both. Adapt pretrained CrossDiff and a 3D-only ablation (same architecture but without 2D branch) using a masked inpainting scheme during denoising: at each step, replace constrained joint positions with known values (RePaint-style). Train lightweight adapters (or use zero-shot inpainting) on 20% of the training split for 1 epoch to adapt to editing. Evaluate on 100 held-out test samples and 50 conflict scenarios where the text implies motion inconsistent with the constraints. Measure constraint error (mean per-joint position error on constrained joints) and FID. Diagnostic: compare text-only generation vs. constrained generation to quantify conflict resolution.
draft.minimal_test: Train CrossDiff and a 3D-only baseline with the same masked inpainting procedure on 20% of HumanML3D for 1 epoch (or zero-shot), then evaluate on 100 held-out samples and 50 conflict samples. Use 4 A100 GPU-days for training and evaluation.
draft.decisive_metric: Constraint satisfaction error (lower is better) and FID (lower is better). Support if CrossDiff achieves at least 20% lower constraint error than 3D-only with FID within 5% of 3D-only; falsify if no significant difference or CrossDiff worse.
draft.supporting_result: CrossDiff reduces constraint error by >20% relative to 3D-only while maintaining FID within 5%, and shows better conflict resolution (e.g., lower constraint error in conflict scenarios without increased FID).
draft.falsifying_result: CrossDiff shows no significant improvement in constraint error over 3D-only (e.g., <10% reduction) or degrades FID by >10%, or fails to resolve conflicts better than 3D-only.
draft.related_work: CrossDiff (10.48550/arxiv.2312.10993) provides the cross-diffusion baseline; editing virtual human motion with dynamic controllers (10.11113/jt.v75.5063) motivates constrained editing but lacks diffusion; the neighborhood paper (10.21203/rs.3.rs-2920071/v1) is unrelated to motion generation and is excluded.
draft.limitations: Only one dataset (HumanML3D), simplified joint-position constraints, small-scale adapter training, and no full interactive user study. The 3D-only ablation may not be a perfect control, and zero-shot inpainting may underperform fine-tuned editing.
draft.resource_plan: 8 A100 GPU-days total: 1 day data preparation and adapter implementation, 2 days training adapters (CrossDiff and 3D-only) on 20% of HumanML3D, 2 days evaluation on held-out and conflict sets, 1 day analysis, and 2 days buffer. Use public HumanML3D and open-weight CrossDiff (or reimplementation from the paper). No proprietary weights or future-paper answer keys.

prior_work.title: Severing Spurious Correlations with Data Pruning
prior_work.abstract: Deep neural networks have been shown to learn and rely on spurious correlations present in the data that they are trained on. Reliance on such correlations can cause these networks to malfunction when deployed in the real world, where these correlations may no longer hold. To overcome the learning of and reliance on such correlations, recent studies propose approaches that yield promising results. These works, however, study settings where the strength of the spurious signal is significantly greater than that of the core, invariant signal, making it easier to detect the presence of spurious features in individual training samples and allow for further processing. In this paper, we identify new settings where the strength of the spurious signal is relatively weaker, making it difficult to detect any spurious information while continuing to have catastrophic consequences. We also discover that spurious correlations are learned primarily due to only a handful of all the samples containing the spurious feature and develop a novel data pruning technique that identifies and prunes small subsets of the training data that contain these samples. Our proposed technique does not require inferred domain knowledge, information regarding the sample-wise presence or nature of spurious information, or human intervention. Finally, we show that such data pruning attains state-of-the-art performance on previously studied settings where spurious information is identifiable.

prior_work.title: Does the Unemployment Invariance Hypothesis Hold for Canada?
prior_work.abstract: This article explores the long-run relationship between unemployment rate and labor force participation rate in Canada. The cointegration analysis vindicates the existence of a long-run relationship between these two variables. This finding leads us to doubt the pertinence of the unemployment invariance hypothesis for Canada. This is consistent with the empirical studies for Japan, Sweden and the United States, but contradicts the empirical studies for Australia, Romania and Turkey. There are contradictory studies for the United Kingdom.

prior_work.title: News Articles and the Invariance Hypothesis
prior_work.abstract: Using a database of news articles from Thomson Reuters for 2003-2008, we investigate how the arrival rate of news articles mentioning an individual stock varies with the level of trading activity in that stock. Defining trading activity W as the product of dollar volume and volatility, we estimate that the arrival rate of news articles is proportional to W0:68. Market microstructure invariance predicts that the stock trading process unfolds in “business time” which passes at a rate proportional to W2=3. Since the estimated exponent of '368 is close to 2/3, we conclude that information in news articles flows into the market in the same units of business time that microstructure invariance predicts to govern the trading process for stocks. The arrival of news articles is well approximated by a negative binomial process with the over-dispersion parameter of 2.11.

Most studies have focused either on the exposure surrounding a student's school or their home. To address this gap, this study aimed to evaluate the association between neighborhood characteristics around both the student's school and home in the Federal District (FD), Brazil, focusing on green spaces (NDVI and quantity of green spaces), roads (length of roads), and wildfires as potential predictors of academic performance. We analyzed 344,175 students who were enrolled in the public schools (256 schools) of the FD from 2017 to 2020. We employed a mixed-effects regression model to investigate the relationship between individual-level academic performance and the neighborhood characteristics, while controlling for temporal, socioeconomic, and school-specific variables. Our results suggest that neighborhood characteristics represented by green spaces, roads, and wildfires, can have a significant impact on academic performance. We found that some neighborhood characteristics had a stronger association with academic performance when they were located around schools, compared to when they were located around students' homes. For example, the coefficient for NDVI within the buffer of 250m and 500m surrounding schools was estimated to be 2.48 (95%CI: 2.33; 2.63) and 0.59 (95%CI: 0.47; 0.71), respectively, while for NDVI surrounding homes, it was 0.23 (95%CI: 0.15; 0.30) and 0.25 (95%CI: 0.17; 0.33) for the buffer of 250m and 500m, respectively. Our study provides valuable insights into the potential role of neighborhood characteristics in promoting academic performance, which could inform urban planning and public policy aimed at improving educational outcomes.

S6d45779d5300.title: Does the Unemployment Invariance Hypothesis Hold for Canada?
S6d45779d5300.fulltext_snippet: This article explores the long-run relationship between unemployment rate and labor force participation rate in Canada. The cointegration analysis vindicates the existence of a long-run relationship between these two variables. This finding leads us to doubt the pertinence of the unemployment invariance hypothesis for Canada. This is consistent with the empirical studies for Japan, Sweden and the United States, but contradicts the empirical studies for Australia, Romania and Turkey. There are contradictory studies for the United Kingdom.

Sdba40e1bb8d7.title: News Articles and the Invariance Hypothesis
Sdba40e1bb8d7.fulltext_snippet: Using a database of news articles from Thomson Reuters for 2003-2008, we investigate how the arrival rate of news articles mentioning an individual stock varies with the level of trading activity in that stock. Defining trading activity W as the product of dollar volume and volatility, we estimate that the arrival rate of news articles is proportional to W0:68. Market microstructure invariance predicts that the stock trading process unfolds in “business time” which passes at a rate proportional to W2=3. Since the estimated exponent of '368 is close to 2/3, we conclude that information in news articles flows into the market in the same units of business time that microstructure invariance predicts to govern the trading process for stocks. The arrival of news articles is well approximated by a negative binomial process with the over-dispersion parameter of 2.11.

draft.title: Activation-Level Core-vs-Spurious Retention Test for Weak-Signal Data Pruning
draft.literature_gap: The supplied pruning paper (10.48550/arxiv.2503.18258) shows that weak spurious correlations can be catastrophic and that pruning a handful of samples can sever them, but its evaluation is accuracy/worst-group-centric. It does not test whether the pruned model retains core invariant features at the activation level, nor whether gains come from removing spurious features rather than collateral removal of core features. This leaves an evaluation gap: a pruning method can improve worst-group accuracy while silently degrading core-feature representations. The local cluster therefore lacks a minimal activation-level audit that distinguishes spurious-feature suppression from core-feature damage under weak spurious signals.
draft.hypothesis: On public image datasets with a weakened spurious correlation, the baseline pruning procedure from 10.48550/arxiv.2503.18258 will reduce linear-probe accuracy for the spurious attribute in penultimate activations substantially more than it reduces linear-probe accuracy for the core label. Concretely: after matched training, spurious-probe accuracy drops by at least 10 points relative to no-pruning ERM, while core-probe accuracy drops by at most 2 points, and worst-group accuracy improves by at least 3 points. If core-probe accuracy drops comparably to spurious-probe accuracy, or if worst-group accuracy does not improve, the hypothesis is falsified.
draft.method: Use two public datasets: Waterbirds (core = bird type, spurious = background) and CelebA (core = Blond Hair, spurious = Male). Construct weak-spurious training splits by subsampling majority-group examples to reduce the spurious correlation to roughly 0.65-0.75 while preserving group labels. Train an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 (torchvision open weights) with three conditions per dataset: (i) no-pruning ERM baseline, (ii) the data-pruning procedure from 10.48550/arxiv.2503.18258 applied at its selected prune rate, and (iii) a random-pruning ablation at the same prune rate. For each trained model, freeze the backbone and train linear probes on penultimate activations from a held-out group-balanced split: a core-label probe and a spurious-attribute probe. Evaluate average accuracy, worst-group accuracy, core-probe accuracy, and spurious-probe accuracy on the official/held-out test split. Run 3 seeds per condition; report mean and bootstrap 95% CI. All datasets and model weights are public; no proprietary models or future-paper answer keys are used.
draft.minimal_test: A single two-dataset, three-condition ResNet-50 experiment: weak-spurious Waterbirds and CelebA, comparing no pruning vs the supplied paper's pruning vs matched random pruning, with activation probes for core and spurious attributes. The test is minimal because it requires only public data, one open-weight architecture, and linear probes; it directly asks whether pruning suppresses spurious information without erasing core information.
draft.decisive_metric: Primary metric: R = (drop in spurious-probe accuracy from no-pruning to paper-pruning) / (drop in core-probe accuracy from no-pruning to paper-pruning), paired with worst-group accuracy change. Decision rule: success if R >= 3, core-probe drop <= 2 points, and worst-group accuracy gain >= 3 points vs no-pruning; failure if R <= 1 or core-probe drop >= spurious-probe drop. Random-pruning ablation must show lower R and no comparable worst-group gain.
draft.supporting_result: Paper-pruning yields R >= 3, core-probe accuracy within 2 points of no-pruning, spurious-probe accuracy at least 10 points lower than no-pruning, and worst-group accuracy at least 3 points higher than no-pruning. Random pruning at the same rate shows no such separation, confirming that the effect is not merely from training on fewer samples.
draft.falsifying_result: Paper-pruning reduces core-probe accuracy by an amount statistically indistinguishable from or larger than its reduction in spurious-probe accuracy, or it fails to improve worst-group accuracy by 3 points over no-pruning. A secondary falsifier is that random pruning matches paper-pruning on R and worst-group accuracy, indicating the diagnostic does not isolate spurious-feature removal.
draft.related_work[1]: 10.48550/arxiv.2503.18258: Severing Spurious Correlations with Data Pruning. This is the supplied baseline paper and the source of the pruning procedure and weak-spurious-signal motivation.
draft.related_work[2]: Other supplied papers in the expansion neighborhood are not directly used because they concern education-neighborhood regression, unemployment invariance, and news-arrival invariance rather than spurious-correlation pruning in neural networks.
draft.limitations: The test is limited to two image-classification datasets and one architecture; probe accuracy is a proxy for feature retention, not a causal mechanism; the weak-spurious construction may not exactly match the baseline paper's internal weak-signal settings; reimplementation of the pruning procedure may introduce variance; and the study does not directly test safety, privacy, or alignment behaviors beyond fairness-relevant spurious correlations.

prior_work.title: Accounting for Regressor-Error Dependencies in Educational Data: A Bayesian Mixture Approach
prior_work.abstract: Because frequently random assignment is not feasible in educational studies, our understanding of causal effects of student characteristics on academic performance has made little progress over the years. Omitted variables inducing correlations between regressors and error terms in multilevel data are a major hurdle. If the independence assumption of regressors and error components is not met, standard multilevel regression models yield biased and inconsistent results. This paper focusses on within-level regressor-error dependencies, caused by omitted variables, which are difficult to diagnose and remedy when additional data in the form of instrumental variables are not available. Specifically, we develop a multilevel mixture model that can account for correlations between regressor and error terms. The proposed approach allows for different specifications such as choice- or self-selection models. We present a flexible Bayesian estimation method that can be adapted easily to researchers' specific needs. Investigating the relationship between IQ and educational performance, we find empirical support for self-selection effects that distort substantially the observed relation between these measures.

draft.title: Hierarchical Bayesian Optimization Search for Privacy–Fairness Trade-offs with Regressor-Error Correction
draft.literature_gap: The supplied neighborhood study compares school- vs home-buffer effects with mixed-effects regression, but it does not test hierarchical search over model/privacy/fairness hyperparameters, nor does it evaluate subgroup fairness under a formal privacy constraint. The supplied Bayesian mixture paper addresses regressor-error dependencies from omitted variables but does not connect that correction to a hierarchical Bayesian optimization (HBO) search space or to safety/fairness/privacy Pareto frontiers. Thus the visible gap is: no minimal falsifiable test of whether HBO over a hierarchical privacy–fairness–model search space, with explicit regressor-error correction, improves worst-group safety/fairness under differential privacy (DP) without unacceptable utility loss.
draft.hypothesis: A hierarchical Bayesian optimization search over group-level privacy budget, subgroup-level fairness penalty, and layer-level LoRA adaptation will find DP-fine-tuned open-weight model configurations with a better Pareto frontier of utility, worst-group safety/fairness gap, and privacy budget than (i) flat Bayesian optimization and (ii) a supplied-paper Bayesian mixture regressor-error correction baseline. The improvement will disappear when the regressor-error correction is ablated under synthetic label noise correlated with sensitive attributes.
draft.method: Use a public text-safety/fairness dataset with identity subgroup labels (e.g., CivilComments identity annotations) and an open-weight small language model (e.g., Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct) fine-tuned with LoRA and DP-SGD. Define a hierarchical search space: top level = DP epsilon {1,3,8}; middle level = fairness regularizer strength and group-weighting scheme; bottom level = LoRA rank/layer subset and learning rate. Run HBO for 30 trials x 3 seeds. Baselines: flat Bayesian optimization over the same hyperparameters without hierarchy, and the supplied Bayesian mixture model for regressor-error dependencies adapted as a subgroup-metric correction layer for noisy/omitted subgroup labels. Diagnostic: inject synthetic label noise correlated with identity and ablate the mixture correction; HBO should lose its advantage if the correction is necessary. Evaluate on held-out identity subgroups.
draft.minimal_test: Train/evaluate Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct LoRA adapters under DP-SGD on public CivilComments identity data for 30 HBO trials, 30 flat-BO trials, and the Bayesian-mixture-corrected baseline, each with 3 seeds. Primary comparison at epsilon=3: worst-group toxicity gap, AUROC, and Pareto hypervolume over (AUROC, -worst-group gap, -epsilon). Diagnostic run repeats the best HBO configuration with synthetic identity-correlated label noise and with the regressor-error correction ablated. Total compute target <=4 A100 GPU-days.
draft.decisive_metric: Pareto hypervolume over utility (AUROC), worst-group fairness gap, and privacy budget, plus worst-group gap at epsilon=3. Support requires HBO to improve hypervolume by >=5% over flat BO and >=3% over the supplied Bayesian-mixture baseline at matched epsilon, with worst-group gap reduced by >=2 points and AUROC drop <=1 point. The diagnostic must show >=5% hypervolume loss when error correction is ablated under correlated label noise.
draft.supporting_result: HBO selects configurations with higher Pareto hypervolume, smaller worst-group safety/fairness gap at epsilon=3, and no >1-point AUROC loss versus flat BO and the Bayesian-mixture baseline. Under synthetic identity-correlated label noise, the full HBO+correction method retains its advantage, while the ablated diagnostic loses >=5% hypervolume, confirming the correction is doing measurable work.
draft.falsifying_result: HBO fails to improve Pareto hypervolume by the stated margins over flat BO or the supplied Bayesian-mixture baseline, or worst-group gap is not reduced at epsilon=3, or the ablation diagnostic shows no meaningful degradation under correlated label noise. Any of these outcomes falsifies the claim that hierarchical search plus regressor-error correction materially improves the privacy–fairness–utility frontier in this setting.

prior_work.title: On the Role of Attention Heads in Large Language Model Safety
prior_work.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve state-of-the-art performance on multiple language tasks, yet their safety guardrails can be circumvented, leading to harmful generations. In light of this, recent research on safety mechanisms has emerged, revealing that when safety representations or component are suppressed, the safety capability of LLMs are compromised. However, existing research tends to overlook the safety impact of multi-head attention mechanisms, despite their crucial role in various model functionalities. Hence, in this paper, we aim to explore the connection between standard attention mechanisms and safety capability to fill this gap in the safety-related mechanistic interpretability. We propose a novel metric which tailored for multi-head attention, the Safety Head ImPortant Score (Ships), to assess the individual heads' contributions to model safety. Based on this, we generalize Ships to the dataset level and further introduce the Safety Attention Head AttRibution Algorithm (Sahara) to attribute the critical safety attention heads inside the model. Our findings show that the special attention head has a significant impact on safety. Ablating a single safety head allows aligned model (e.g., Llama-2-7b-chat) to respond to 16 times more harmful queries, while only modifying 0.006% of the parameters, in contrast to the ~ 5% modification required in previous studies. More importantly, we demonstrate that attention heads primarily function as feature extractors for safety and models fine-tuned from the same base model exhibit overlapping safety heads through comprehensive experiments. Together, our attribution approach and findings provide a novel perspective for unpacking the black box of safety mechanisms within large models.

prior_work.title: Multimodal Situational Safety
prior_work.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are rapidly evolving, demonstrating impressive capabilities as multimodal assistants that interact with both humans and their environments. However, this increased sophistication introduces significant safety concerns. In this paper, we present the first evaluation and analysis of a novel safety challenge termed Multimodal Situational Safety, which explores how safety considerations vary based on the specific situation in which the user or agent is engaged. We argue that for an MLLM to respond safely, whether through language or action, it often needs to assess the safety implications of a language query within its corresponding visual context. To evaluate this capability, we develop the Multimodal Situational Safety benchmark (MSSBench) to assess the situational safety performance of current MLLMs. The dataset comprises 1,820 language query-image pairs, half of which the image context is safe, and the other half is unsafe. We also develop an evaluation framework that analyzes key safety aspects, including explicit safety reasoning, visual understanding, and, crucially, situational safety reasoning. Our findings reveal that current MLLMs struggle with this nuanced safety problem in the instruction-following setting and struggle to tackle these situational safety challenges all at once, highlighting a key area for future research. Furthermore, we develop multi-agent pipelines to coordinately solve safety challenges, which shows consistent improvement in safety over the original MLLM response. Code and data: mssbench.github.io.

prior_work.title: How Does Vision-Language Adaptation Impact the Safety of Vision Language Models?
prior_work.abstract: Vision-Language adaptation (VL adaptation) transforms Large Language Models (LLMs) into Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) for multimodal tasks, but this process often compromises the inherent safety capabilities embedded in the original LLMs. Despite potential harmfulness due to weakened safety measures, in-depth analysis on the effects of VL adaptation on safety remains under-explored. This study examines how VL adaptation influences safety and evaluates the impact of safety fine-tuning methods. Our analysis reveals that safety degradation occurs during VL adaptation, even when the training data is safe. While safety tuning techniques like supervised fine-tuning with safety datasets or reinforcement learning from human feedback mitigate some risks, they still lead to safety degradation and a reduction in helpfulness due to over-rejection issues. Further analysis of internal model weights suggests that VL adaptation may impact certain safety-related layers, potentially lowering overall safety levels. Additionally, our findings demonstrate that the objectives of VL adaptation and safety tuning are divergent, which often results in their simultaneous application being suboptimal. To address this, we suggest the weight merging approach as an optimal solution effectively reducing safety degradation while maintaining helpfulness. These insights help guide the development of more reliable and secure LVLMs for real-world applications.

draft.title: Do Safety-Critical Attention Heads Survive Vision-Language Adaptation? A Minimal Head-Ablation Test on Multimodal Situational Safety
draft.literature_gap: The supplied papers reveal three disconnected findings: (1) text-only LLM safety is concentrated in a small set of attention heads identified by Ships/Sahara, where ablating one head can massively increase harmful responses (arXiv:2410.13708); (2) MLLMs struggle with multimodal situational safety, where the safety of a query depends on visual context (arXiv:2410.06172); and (3) vision-language adaptation degrades safety even with safe training data, and safety tuning can cause over-rejection (arXiv:2410.07571). No supplied work tests whether the safety-critical attention heads found in a text-only LLM remain the same heads that govern safety when that LLM is used as the language backbone of an LVLM, nor whether ablating those heads disproportionately breaks multimodal situational safety. This is a concrete mechanistic evaluation gap: head-level safety attribution has not been connected to the multimodal situational safety benchmark.
draft.hypothesis: Attention heads identified as safety-critical by Ships/Sahara in the text-only language backbone of an open-weight LVLM remain safety-critical in the vision-language setting: ablating the top-k Ships heads will increase unsafe responses on the unsafe subset of MSSBench significantly more than ablating k random heads, without a comparably larger increase in over-rejection on the safe subset.
draft.method: Use the open-weight LLaVA-1.5-7b model (Vicuna-7b language backbone) and the public MSSBench dataset (1,820 query-image pairs, half safe and half unsafe image contexts). Step 1: replicate Ships at the head level on the language backbone using a public text safety prompt set (e.g., 500 harmful prompts from AdvBench or Safety Prompts). For each attention head, ablate it and measure the change in a safety score (e.g., refusal rate or Llama Guard 2 judged harmfulness) relative to the unablated model; rank heads by Ships and select top-k (k=1,5,10). Step 2: evaluate on MSSBench under three conditions: no ablation (baseline), top-k Ships head ablation, and random-k head ablation. Generate responses with greedy decoding and judge each response as safe/unsafe with an open-weight judge (Llama Guard 2) plus a rule-based refusal detector as a cross-check. Step 3: compute unsafe response rate on the MSSBench unsafe subset and over-rejection rate on the safe subset for each condition. The baseline from a supplied paper is the Sahara/Ships top-head attribution and ablation procedure from arXiv:2410.13708; the failure-mode/ablation diagnostic is random-k head ablation, plus a safe-subset over-rejection check to detect global refusal degradation rather than situational safety-specific breakage.
draft.minimal_test: A single controlled ablation study on LLaVA-1.5-7b with MSSBench: compare unsafe response rates on the 910 unsafe MSSBench pairs after ablating the top-1, top-5, and top-10 Ships heads versus ablating the same numbers of random heads, with unablated MSSBench performance as the reference. All models, datasets, and judges are public or open-weight.
draft.decisive_metric: Absolute difference in unsafe response rate on the MSSBench unsafe subset between top-k Ships-head ablation and random-k head ablation, with a paired bootstrap 95% confidence interval; supporting evidence requires top-k ablation to increase unsafe rate by at least 10 percentage points more than random-k ablation (p<0.05) while increasing over-rejection on the safe subset by no more than 5 percentage points more than random-k ablation.
draft.supporting_result: Top-k Ships-head ablation produces a significantly larger increase in unsafe responses on MSSBench unsafe pairs than random-k ablation (e.g., +15 percentage points for top-5 vs random-5), while over-rejection on safe MSSBench pairs remains comparable between the two ablation conditions. This would indicate that text-derived safety heads remain functionally important for multimodal situational safety and that head-level attribution transfers across modality adaptation.
draft.falsifying_result: Top-k Ships-head ablation does not increase unsafe responses on MSSBench unsafe pairs significantly more than random-k ablation, or it increases over-rejection on safe pairs substantially more than random-k ablation. Either outcome would falsify the claim that Ships-identified safety heads remain the dominant safety-relevant heads after vision-language adaptation and would suggest that VL adaptation redistributes safety mechanisms away from the text-only head set.
draft.related_work: This test directly connects three supplied papers: arXiv:2410.13708 introduces Ships and Sahara for attention-head safety attribution in text-only LLMs; arXiv:2410.06172 introduces MSSBench and shows MLLMs struggle with multimodal situational safety; arXiv:2410.07571 shows vision-language adaptation can degrade safety and that safety tuning may cause over-rejection. The proposal uses Ships/Sahara as the head-selection baseline from a supplied paper and MSSBench as the multimodal evaluation target, testing whether the mechanistic safety-head finding transfers to the multimodal situational safety setting.
draft.limitations: The study uses one open-weight LVLM (LLaVA-1.5-7b) and one multimodal safety benchmark (MSSBench), so conclusions may not generalize to other LVLM architectures or safety benchmarks. The open-weight judge (Llama Guard 2) and refusal detector are imperfect proxies for human safety judgments. Head ablation can have confounds beyond safety, and random-k ablation is only one diagnostic; future work should test additional control heads and larger k. The method does not prove causality at the level of individual head function, only functional necessity under ablation.
draft.resource_plan: Total budget <=8 A100 GPU-days. Day 1: compute Ships for all attention heads on 500 public safety prompts using LLaVA-1.5-7b's language backbone (forward passes only, no training). Days 2-3: run MSSBench inference (1,820 pairs) under no-ablation, top-k ablation (k=1,5,10), and random-k ablation (k=1,5,10), using greedy decoding; approximately 8 conditions over 1,820 pairs is well within inference budget. Day 4: run Llama Guard 2 and rule-based refusal judging on all generated responses. Days 5-6: analysis, bootstrap confidence intervals, and ablation diagnostic checks. Days 7-8: buffer for failed runs, hyperparameter checks, and write-up. All models (LLaVA-1.5-7b, Llama Guard 2), datasets (MSSBench, AdvBench/Safety Prompts), and code are public or open-weight; no proprietary model weights or future-paper answer keys are used.

prior_work.title: FFB: A Fair Fairness Benchmark for In-Processing Group Fairness Methods
prior_work.abstract: This paper introduces the Fair Fairness Benchmark (\textsf{FFB}), a benchmarking framework for in-processing group fairness methods. Ensuring fairness in machine learning is important for ethical compliance. However, there exist challenges in comparing and developing fairness methods due to inconsistencies in experimental settings, lack of accessible algorithmic implementations, and limited extensibility of current fairness packages and tools. draft.title: Testing Individual-Fairness Degradation and a Light Consistency Repair for FFB In-Processing Group-Fairness Baselines
draft.literature_gap: The supplied cluster has a clear evaluation gap: FFB standardizes in-processing group-fairness benchmarking but its abstract emphasizes group notions and does not report individual fairness; FairGI argues that group and individual fairness are rarely handled together and is GNN-specific; Aranyani addresses online group fairness but not individual consistency. No minimal controlled test isolates whether standard FFB in-processing group-fairness methods degrade individual fairness on tabular data, nor whether a low-cost consistency regularizer can repair that degradation without erasing group-fairness gains. This is an evaluation-gap test, not a new broad framework.
draft.hypothesis: In FFB's tabular in-processing group-fairness pipelines, enforcing group fairness (demographic parity or equal opportunity) reduces individual fairness measured as prediction consistency under small input perturbations relative to unconstrained ERM. Adding a light consistency regularizer to one FFB group-fairness baseline will recover at least half of the lost individual consistency while increasing the group-fairness gap by no more than 0.02 and decreasing accuracy by no more than 0.01 absolute.
draft.method: Use the open-source FFB benchmarking pipeline and public tabular datasets Adult and COMPAS. Train logistic-regression and small MLP classifiers with FFB's unconstrained ERM baseline and at least one FFB in-processing group-fairness baseline (e.g., adversarial debiasing or fairness constraints). For each trained model, compute: (i) group fairness: demographic-parity gap and equal-opportunity gap; (ii) accuracy; (iii) individual fairness as consistency error: mean absolute change in predicted probability under Gaussian feature noise (sigma matched to each feature's training standard deviation) and under 10% feature dropout, averaged over 5 seeds. Then add a consistency regularizer to the selected FFB group-fairness baseline: for each minibatch, draw perturbed copies x' = x + epsilon, epsilon ~ N(0, sigma^2 I), and add lambda * mean((f(x)-f(x'))^2) to the original fairness+task loss. Sweep lambda in {0, 0.01, 0.1, 1.0} on a validation split. Diagnostic arms: (a) group-only baseline, (b) group+consistency, (c) failure-mode ablation using random-pair regularization (penalize prediction differences between random unrelated examples) to test whether any repair is specific to local consistency rather than generic smoothness. All models use public code and open-weight scikit-learn/PyTorch implementations; no proprietary weights.
draft.minimal_test: A 5-seed paired experiment on Adult and COMPAS with logistic regression and a small MLP: compare ERM, one FFB group-fairness baseline, the same baseline plus consistency regularizer, and the random-pair ablation. Primary comparison is within-seed paired differences in consistency error and group-fairness gaps. Total runs: 2 datasets x 2 model classes x 4 arms x 5 seeds = 80 short tabular training runs, well within <=8 A100 GPU-days (expected <2 A100-days).
draft.decisive_metric: Primary metric: relative change in consistency error, Delta_IF = (IF_group_only - IF_ERM) / IF_ERM, where IF is mean prediction change under perturbation (lower is better). Repair metric: recovery fraction R = (IF_group_only - IF_group_plus_consistency) / (IF_group_only - IF_ERM). Success requires: (1) Delta_IF >= +5% relative (group-only worse than ERM) with a paired bootstrap 95% CI excluding 0 on at least one dataset/model; (2) R >= 0.5; (3) group-fairness gap increase <=0.02 and accuracy drop <=0.01 absolute versus group-only. The random-pair ablation must show R_ablation < 0.25, otherwise the effect is attributed to generic smoothing.
draft.supporting_result: Group-only FFB in-processing methods improve the targeted group-fairness gap but increase consistency error by at least 5% relative to ERM on Adult or COMPAS. The consistency regularizer recovers at least half of that increase, with <=0.02 group-gap worsening and <=0.01 accuracy loss, while the random-pair ablation recovers less than a quarter, supporting a specific local-consistency mechanism.
draft.falsifying_result: The hypothesis is falsified if group-only FFB baselines show no meaningful individual-fairness degradation (Delta_IF < 2% relative with CI including 0) on both datasets/model classes, or if the consistency regularizer fails to recover at least 50% of any observed degradation, or if it recovers consistency only by increasing the group-fairness gap by more than 0.05 or dropping accuracy by more than 0.03 absolute. It is also falsified if the random-pair ablation matches the consistency regularizer's recovery, indicating no specific individual-consistency effect.
draft.related_work: FFB (arXiv:2306.09468) supplies the open in-processing group-fairness benchmark and baselines used here, but its reported evaluation is group-fairness-centric. FairGI (arXiv:2404.17511) motivates combining group and individual fairness and introduces individual fairness within groups for GNNs; our test transfers that concern to FFB-style tabular in-processing and adds a controlled degradation/repair diagnostic. Aranyani (arXiv:2310.11401) studies online group fairness with oblique decision forests but does not measure individual consistency; our experiment is offline and tabular, isolating the group-only training side effect. No other prior citations are claimed.
draft.limitations: The test is limited to tabular Adult/COMPAS data, logistic regression and small MLPs, one FFB group-fairness baseline family, and a perturbation-based proxy for individual fairness rather than the full FairGI similarity-matrix notion. It does not cover graph data, online learning, privacy, or safety alignment directly. The consistency regularizer is intentionally simple; negative results would not rule out other individual-fairness repairs. The random-pair ablation is a diagnostic, not a complete alternative method.
draft.resource_plan: Datasets: public Adult and COMPAS via FFB or OpenML/UCI; no proprietary data. Models: scikit-learn logistic regression and a small PyTorch MLP; open-weight only. Code: FFB open-source repository plus a small consistency-regularizer wrapper. Compute: 80 short tabular runs, 5 seeds, expected <=2 A100 GPU-days and <=1 CPU-day for preprocessing/evaluation, within the <=8 A100 GPU-day envelope. Personnel: one researcher for implementation and analysis. No future-paper answer keys or proprietary model weights are used.

prior_work.title: BLSP: Bootstrapping Language-Speech Pre-training via Behavior Alignment of Continuation Writing
prior_work.abstract: The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has sparked significant interest in extending their remarkable language capabilities to speech. However, modality alignment between speech and text still remains an open problem. Current solutions can be categorized into two strategies. One is a cascaded approach where outputs (tokens or states) of a separately trained speech recognition system are used as inputs for LLMs, which limits their potential in modeling alignment between speech and text. The other is an end-to-end approach that relies on speech instruction data, which is very difficult to collect in large quantities. In this paper, we address these issues and propose the BLSP approach that Bootstraps Language-Speech Pre-training via behavior alignment of continuation writing. We achieve this by learning a lightweight modality adapter between a frozen speech encoder and an LLM, ensuring that the LLM exhibits the same generation behavior regardless of the modality of input: a speech segment or its transcript. The training process can be divided into two steps. The first step prompts an LLM to generate texts with speech transcripts as prefixes, obtaining text continuations. In the second step, these continuations are used as supervised signals to train the modality adapter in an end-to-end manner. We demonstrate that this straightforward process can extend the capabilities of LLMs to speech, enabling speech recognition, speech translation, spoken language understanding, and speech conversation, even in zero-shot cross-lingual scenarios.

prior_work.title: Spoken Question Answering and Speech Continuation Using Spectrogram-Powered LLM
prior_work.abstract: We present Spectron, a novel approach to adapting pre-trained large language models (LLMs) to perform spoken question answering (QA) and speech continuation. By endowing the LLM with a pre-trained speech encoder, our model becomes able to take speech inputs and generate speech outputs. The entire system is trained end-to-end and operates directly on spectrograms, simplifying our architecture. Key to our approach is a training objective that jointly supervises speech recognition, text continuation, and speech synthesis using only paired speech-text pairs, enabling a `cross-modal' chain-of-thought within a single decoding pass. Our method surpasses existing spoken language models in speaker preservation and semantic coherence. Furthermore, the proposed model improves upon direct initialization in retaining the knowledge of the original LLM as demonstrated through spoken QA datasets. We release our audio samples (https://michelleramanovich.github.io/spectron/spectron) and spoken QA dataset (https://github.com/google-research-datasets/LLAMA1-Test-Set).

prior_work.title: Unlocking Speech Instruction Data Potential with Query Rewriting
prior_work.abstract: End-to-end Large Speech Language Models~(\textbf{LSLMs}) demonstrate strong potential in response latency and speech comprehension capabilities, showcasing general intelligence across speech understanding tasks. However, the ability to follow speech instructions has not been fully realized due to the lack of datasets and heavily biased training tasks. Leveraging the rich ASR datasets, previous approaches have used Large Language Models~(\textbf{LLMs}) to continue the linguistic information of speech to construct speech instruction datasets. Yet, due to the gap between LLM-generated results and real human responses, the continuation methods further amplify these shortcomings. Given the high costs of collecting and annotating speech instruction datasets by humans, using speech synthesis to construct large-scale speech instruction datasets has become a balanced and robust alternative. Although modern Text-To-Speech~(\textbf{TTS}) models have achieved near-human-level synthesis quality, it is challenging to appropriately convert out-of-distribution text instruction to speech due to the limitations of the training data distribution in TTS models. To address this issue, we propose a query rewriting framework with multi-LLM knowledge fusion, employing multiple agents to annotate and validate the synthesized speech, making it possible to construct high-quality speech instruction datasets without relying on human annotation. Experiments show that this method can transform text instructions into distributions more suitable for TTS models for speech synthesis through zero-shot rewriting, increasing data usability from 72\% to 93\%. It also demonstrates unique advantages in rewriting tasks that require complex knowledge and context-related abilities.

prior_work.title: LLaMA-Omni: Seamless Speech Interaction with Large Language Models
prior_work.abstract: Models like GPT-4o enable real-time interaction with large language models (LLMs) through speech, significantly enhancing user experience compared to traditional text-based interaction. However, there is still a lack of exploration on how to build speech interaction models based on open-source LLMs. To address this, we propose LLaMA-Omni, a novel model architecture designed for low-latency and high-quality speech interaction with LLMs. LLaMA-Omni integrates a pretrained speech encoder, a speech adaptor, an LLM, and a streaming speech decoder. It eliminates the need for speech transcription, and can simultaneously generate text and speech responses directly from speech instructions with extremely low latency. We build our model based on the latest Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model. To align the model with speech interaction scenarios, we construct a dataset named InstructS2S-200K, which includes 200K speech instructions and corresponding speech responses. Experimental results show that compared to previous speech-language models, LLaMA-Omni provides better responses in both content and style, with a response latency as low as 226ms. Additionally, training LLaMA-Omni takes less than 3 days on just 4 GPUs, paving the way for the efficient development of speech-language models in the future.

S95d14fa8fa13.title: Spoken Question Answering and Speech Continuation Using Spectrogram-Powered LLM
attribution_passages: We present Spectron, a novel approach to adapting pre-trained large language models (LLMs) to perform spoken question answering (QA) and speech continuation. By endowing the LLM with a pre-trained speech encoder, our model becomes able to take speech inputs and generate speech outputs. The entire system is trained end-to-end and operates directly on spectrograms, simplifying our architecture. Key to our approach is a training objective that jointly supervises speech recognition, text continuation, and speech synthesis using only paired speech-text pairs, enabling a `cross-modal' chain-of-thought within a single decoding pass. Our method surpasses existing spoken language models in speaker preservation and semantic coherence. Furthermore, the proposed model improves upon direct initialization in retaining the knowledge of the original LLM as demonstrated through spoken QA datasets. We release our audio samples (https://michelleramanovich.github.io/spectron/spectron) and spoken QA dataset (https://github.com/google-research-datasets/LLAMA1-Test-Set).

Sed9ab4c2d973.title: Unlocking Speech Instruction Data Potential with Query Rewriting
attribution_passages: End-to-end Large Speech Language Models~(\textbf{LSLMs}) demonstrate strong potential in response latency and speech comprehension capabilities, showcasing general intelligence across speech understanding tasks. However, the ability to follow speech instructions has not been fully realized due to the lack of datasets and heavily biased training tasks. Leveraging the rich ASR datasets, previous approaches have used Large Language Models~(\textbf{LLMs}) to continue the linguistic information of speech to construct speech instruction datasets. Yet, due to the gap between LLM-generated results and real human responses, the continuation methods further amplify these shortcomings. Given the high costs of collecting and annotating speech instruction datasets by humans, using speech synthesis to construct large-scale speech instruction datasets has become a balanced and robust alternative. Although modern Text-To-Speech~(\textbf{TTS}) models have achieved near-human-level synthesis quality, it is challenging to appropriately convert out-of-distribution text instruction to speech due to the limitations of the training data distribution in TTS models. To address this issue, we propose a query rewriting framework with multi-LLM knowledge fusion, employing multiple agents to annotate and validate the synthesized speech, making it possible to construct high-quality speech instruction datasets without relying on human annotation. Experiments show that this method can transform text instructions into distributions more suitable for TTS models for speech synthesis through zero-shot rewriting, increasing data usability from 72\% to 93\%. It also demonstrates unique advantages in rewriting tasks that require complex knowledge and context-related abilities.

S1ebe84e74f3b.title: LLaMA-Omni: Seamless Speech Interaction with Large Language Models
attribution_passages: Models like GPT-4o enable real-time interaction with large language models (LLMs) through speech, significantly enhancing user experience compared to traditional text-based interaction. However, there is still a lack of exploration on how to build speech interaction models based on open-source LLMs. To address this, we propose LLaMA-Omni, a novel model architecture designed for low-latency and high-quality speech interaction with LLMs. LLaMA-Omni integrates a pretrained speech encoder, a speech adaptor, an LLM, and a streaming speech decoder. It eliminates the need for speech transcription, and can simultaneously generate text and speech responses directly from speech instructions with extremely low latency. We build our model based on the latest Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model. To align the model with speech interaction scenarios, we construct a dataset named InstructS2S-200K, which includes 200K speech instructions and corresponding speech responses. Experimental results show that compared to previous speech-language models, LLaMA-Omni provides better responses in both content and style, with a response latency as low as 226ms. Additionally, training LLaMA-Omni takes less than 3 days on just 4 GPUs, paving the way for the efficient development of speech-language models in the future.

draft.title: Continuation-Safety Transfer Test: Does BLSP-Style Speech-LLM Alignment Preserve Refusal Behavior Under Speech Inputs?
draft.literature_gap: The supplied cluster advances open speech-LLM alignment via continuation behavior alignment (BLSP), spectrogram-powered speech continuation/QA (Spectron), synthetic speech-instruction construction with query rewriting, and low-latency speech interaction (LLaMA-Omni). However, the abstracts expose an evaluation gap: BLSP and Spectron evaluate recognition, translation, spoken QA, continuation, and speaker preservation; Query Rewriting explicitly warns that LLM-generated continuations can amplify LLM shortcomings and that TTS distribution limits data usability; LLaMA-Omni evaluates content/style/latency. None isolates whether safety refusal behavior from a text LLM survives a lightweight speech-to-LLM adapter, nor whether continuation curation is a sufficient safety intervention. This is a concrete alignment/safety gap visible in the supplied papers, not a broad proposal.
draft.hypothesis: A BLSP-style frozen-encoder + frozen-LLM adapter trained with standard unfiltered text continuations will show a speech-vs-text refusal gap of at least 10 percentage points on public safety prompts, and replacing those continuations with safety-filtered/rewritten continuations will reduce the gap to at most 5 percentage points without degrading public spoken-QA/ASR utility by more than 2 percentage points.
draft.method: Use open-weight Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as the frozen LLM and an open Whisper encoder as the frozen speech encoder. Train only a BLSP-style lightweight modality adapter on public speech-text pairs (LibriSpeech train-clean-100/360 plus a small public Common Voice subset) using the BLSP continuation objective: prompt the LLM with transcripts as prefixes, collect text continuations, and supervise the adapter to reproduce the same continuation behavior from speech. Two adapters are trained identically except for continuation curation: (A) standard BLSP unfiltered continuations, the supplied-paper baseline; (B) safety-filtered/rewritten continuations using an open-weight safety classifier plus an open-weight LLM rewrite step inspired by the Query Rewriting paper's data-curation idea. Evaluate the same public safety prompts (e.g., AdvBench/HarmBench subsets) in text and in speech synthesized by an open-weight TTS system, plus benign prompts as controls. Use a fixed open-weight judge plus a 100-item human spot-check for refusal labels. Utility checks: LibriSpeech test-clean WER for the adapter and spoken QA accuracy on the public Spectron-released spoken QA dataset. Diagnostic ablations: (i) cascaded frozen-ASR + frozen text LLM as a modality-gap reference; (ii) continuation-leakage probe measuring whether standard BLSP reproduces unsafe text continuations from speech prefixes; (iii) benign-refusal control to detect over-refusal.
draft.minimal_test: Train two adapters (standard BLSP baseline and safety-filtered continuation variant) under identical compute, then evaluate 200 unsafe and 200 benign public prompts in text and synthesized speech. Primary comparison is the speech-minus-text refusal-rate gap for standard BLSP versus the filtered variant. Secondary diagnostics are harmful-continuation rate, continuation-leakage rate, benign over-refusal rate, LibriSpeech WER, and spoken-QA accuracy. The cascaded ASR+text-LLM system is evaluated only as a failure-mode reference.
draft.decisive_metric: Primary metric: absolute speech-vs-text refusal gap Δ = |Refusal_speech - Refusal_text| on unsafe prompts. Supporting threshold: standard BLSP Δ >= 10 percentage points and filtered Δ <= 5 percentage points, with harmful-continuation gap reduced by at least half and utility drop <= 2 percentage points (WER increase or spoken-QA accuracy decrease). Falsification threshold: standard BLSP Δ <= 5 percentage points, or filtered variant fails to reduce Δ below 10 percentage points, or utility drop > 5 percentage points.
draft.supporting_result: Standard BLSP shows Δ >= 10 percentage points (e.g., text refusal 85%, speech refusal 70% or lower) and a speech harmful-continuation rate at least 5 points above text. Safety-filtered continuation adapter reduces Δ to <= 5 percentage points and halves the harmful-continuation gap, while ASR WER and spoken-QA accuracy remain within 2 percentage points of the standard BLSP adapter. Cascaded ASR+text LLM shows a smaller modality gap, indicating the gap is adapter/continuation-specific rather than only acoustic.
draft.falsifying_result: Standard BLSP already has Δ <= 5 percentage points, or the safety-filtered continuation adapter still has Δ >= 10 percentage points, or safety filtering reduces spoken-QA accuracy by more than 5 percentage points / increases WER by more than 5 relative percent, or the continuation-leakage probe shows no association between unfiltered continuations and speech refusal failures. Any of these would reject the hypothesis that continuation curation is the decisive safety-transfer lever in this setting.
draft.related_work[1]: BLSP (arXiv:2309.00916): supplies the baseline BLSP behavior-alignment method and continuation-writing objective used for the standard adapter.
draft.related_work[2]: Spectron (arXiv:2305.15255): supplies the speech-continuation/spoken-QA framing and a public spoken QA dataset for utility evaluation.
draft.related_work[3]: Query Rewriting (arXiv:2507.08603): motivates the concern that LLM continuations amplify flaws and supplies the query-rewriting/data-curation intervention idea adapted here as safety-filtered continuations.
draft.related_work[4]: LLaMA-Omni (arXiv:2409.06666): supplies an open speech-interaction architecture reference and justifies using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with a frozen speech encoder under modest GPU budgets.
draft.limitations: This test uses synthesized speech from an open-weight TTS system, so conclusions may not transfer to all acoustic conditions or real user speech. It covers public safety prompts, not the full space of privacy or fairness harms; privacy leakage is only probed indirectly via harmful-continuation and refusal behavior. The adapter is lightweight, so negative results may reflect adapter capacity rather than a fundamental limitation of speech-LLM alignment. The judge is an open-weight model with a small human spot-check, not a large human safety study. No proprietary model weights or future-paper answer keys are used.
draft.resource_plan: Total <=8 A100 GPU-days: 1 day for public data preparation, TTS synthesis of text/speech safety and benign prompts, and utility-set setup; 2 days to train the standard BLSP adapter baseline; 2 days to train the safety-filtered continuation adapter; 2 days for inference/evaluation across text, speech, cascaded ASR reference, and open-weight judging; 1 day for continuation-leakage/over-refusal diagnostics, human spot-check, and analysis. All models and datasets are public or open-weight; no proprietary API is used.
