prior_work.title: Endowing Protein Language Models with Structural Knowledge
prior_work.abstract: Understanding the relationships between protein sequence, structure and function is a long-standing biological challenge with manifold implications from drug design to our understanding of evolution. Recently, protein language models have emerged as the preferred method for this challenge, thanks to their ability to harness large sequence databases. Yet, their reliance on expansive sequence data and parameter sets limits their flexibility and practicality in real-world scenarios. Concurrently, the recent surge in computationally predicted protein structures unlocks new opportunities in protein representation learning. While promising, the computational burden carried by such complex data still hinders widely-adopted practical applications. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel framework that enhances protein language models by integrating protein structural data. Drawing from recent advances in graph transformers, our approach refines the self-attention mechanisms of pretrained language transformers by integrating structural information with structure extractor modules. This refined model, termed Protein Structure Transformer (PST), is further pretrained on a small protein structure database, using the same masked language modeling objective as traditional protein language models. Empirical evaluations of PST demonstrate its superior parameter efficiency relative to protein language models, despite being pretrained on a dataset comprising only 542K structures. Notably, PST consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art foundation model for protein sequences, ESM-2, setting a new benchmark in protein function prediction. Our findings underscore the potential of integrating structural information into protein language models, paving the way for more effective and efficient protein modeling Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/BorgwardtLab/PST.

prior_work.title: MULAN: multimodal protein language model for sequence and structure encoding
prior_work.abstract: Abstract Motivation Most protein language models (PLMs) produce high-quality representations using only protein sequences. However, incorporating known protein structures is important for many prediction tasks, leading to increased interest in structure-aware PLMs. Currently, structure-aware PLMs are either trained from scratch or add significant parameter overhead for the structure encoder. Results In this study, we propose MULAN, a MULtimodal PLM for both sequence and ANgle-based structure encoding. MULAN has a pre-trained sequence encoder and an introduced parameter-efficient Structure Adapter, which are then fused and trained together. Based on the evaluation of nine downstream tasks, MULAN models of various sizes show a quality improvement compared to both sequence-only ESM2 and structure-aware SaProt. The main improvements are shown for the protein–protein interaction prediction (up to 0.12 in AUROC). Importantly, unlike other models, MULAN offers a cheap increase in structural awareness of protein representations because of the finetuning of existing PLMs instead of training from scratch. We perform a detailed analysis of the proposed model and demonstrate its awareness of the protein structure. Availability and implementation The implementation, training data, and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/DFrolova/MULAN.

prior_work.title: Coherent Interpretation of Entire Visual Field Test Reports Using a Multimodal Large Language Model (ChatGPT)
prior_work.abstract: This study assesses the accuracy and consistency of a commercially available large language model (LLM) in extracting and interpreting sensitivity and reliability data from entire visual field (VF) test reports for the evaluation of glaucomatous defects. Single-page anonymised VF test reports from 60 eyes of 60 subjects were analysed by an LLM (ChatGPT 4o) across four domains—test reliability, defect type, defect severity and overall diagnosis. prior_work.title: Multimodal detection of hateful memes by applying a vision-language pre-training model
prior_work.abstract: Detrimental to individuals and society, online hateful messages have recently become a major social issue. Among them, one new type of hateful message, “hateful meme”, has emerged and brought difficulties in traditional deep learning-based detection. Because hateful memes were formatted with both text captions and images to express users’ intents, they cannot be accurately identified by singularly analyzing embedded text captions or images. In order to effectively detect a hateful meme, the algorithm must possess strong vision and language fusion capability. In this study, we move closer to this goal by feeding a triplet by stacking the visual features, object tags, and text features of memes generated by the object detection model named Visual features in Vision-Language (VinVl) and the optical character recognition (OCR) technology into a Transformer-based Vision-Language Pre-Training Model (VL-PTM) OSCAR+ to perform the cross-modal learning of memes. After fine-tuning and connecting to a random forest (RF) classifier, our model (OSCAR+RF) achieved an average accuracy and AUROC of 0.684 and 0.768, respectively, on the hateful meme detection task in a public test set, which was higher than the other eleven (11) published baselines. In conclusion, this study has demonstrated that VL-PTMs with the addition of anchor points can improve the performance of deep learning-based detection of hateful memes by involving a more substantial alignment between the text caption and visual information.

S5bbd79075d2e.title: Endowing Protein Language Models with Structural Knowledge
attribution_passages: Understanding the relationships between protein sequence, structure and function is a long-standing biological challenge with manifold implications from drug design to our understanding of evolution. Recently, protein language models have emerged as the preferred method for this challenge, thanks to their ability to harness large sequence databases. Yet, their reliance on expansive sequence data and parameter sets limits their flexibility and practicality in real-world scenarios. Concurrently, the recent surge in computationally predicted protein structures unlocks new opportunities in protein representation learning. While promising, the computational burden carried by such complex data still hinders widely-adopted practical applications. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel framework that enhances protein language models by integrating protein structural data. Drawing from recent advances in graph transformers, our approach refines the self-attention mechanisms of pretrained language transformers by integrating structural information with structure extractor modules. This refined model, termed Protein Structure Transformer (PST), is further pretrained on a small protein structure database, using the same masked language modeling objective as traditional protein language models. Empirical evaluations of PST demonstrate its superior parameter efficiency relative to protein language models, despite being pretrained on a dataset comprising only 542K structures. Notably, PST consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art foundation model for protein sequences, ESM-2, setting a new benchmark in protein function prediction. Our findings underscore the potential of integrating structural information into protein language models, paving the way for more effective and efficient protein modeling Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/BorgwardtLab/PST.

S61de5325f19c.title: MULAN: multimodal protein language model for sequence and structure encoding
attribution_passages: Abstract Motivation Most protein language models (PLMs) produce high-quality representations using only protein sequences. However, incorporating known protein structures is important for many prediction tasks, leading to increased interest in structure-aware PLMs. Currently, structure-aware PLMs are either trained from scratch or add significant parameter overhead for the structure encoder. Results In this study, we propose MULAN, a MULtimodal PLM for both sequence and ANgle-based structure encoding. MULAN has a pre-trained sequence encoder and an introduced parameter-efficient Structure Adapter, which are then fused and trained together. Based on the evaluation of nine downstream tasks, MULAN models of various sizes show a quality improvement compared to both sequence-only ESM2 and structure-aware SaProt. The main improvements are shown for the protein–protein interaction prediction (up to 0.12 in AUROC). Importantly, unlike other models, MULAN offers a cheap increase in structural awareness of protein representations because of the finetuning of existing PLMs instead of training from scratch. We perform a detailed analysis of the proposed model and demonstrate its awareness of the protein structure. Availability and implementation The implementation, training data, and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/DFrolova/MULAN.

S863205b69851.title: Multimodal detection of hateful memes by applying a vision-language pre-training model

draft.title: Structure-Shuffle Controlled Evaluation of Multimodal Protein Language Models on Protein-Protein Interaction Prediction
draft.literature_gap: Structure-aware protein language models such as PST and MULAN report downstream gains over sequence-only ESM2, but the supplied abstracts do not isolate whether those gains are causally due to residue-aligned structural information or to extra parameters, sequence shortcuts, or dataset artifacts. The neighboring vision-language papers expose analogous modality-shortcut risks: hateful-meme detection can exploit text/visual alignment without true cross-modal reasoning, and an LLM reading visual-field reports is strong at text extraction but weak at image-based spatial localization. The gap is a controlled modality-ablation test for protein sequence-structure PLMs: no supplied paper reports whether breaking structure-to-residue alignment removes the reported structural advantage over a sequence-only baseline.
draft.hypothesis: MULAN's reported PPI AUROC gain over ESM2 depends causally on residue-aligned structural input. If the structure-angle tokens are permuted within each protein while keeping the sequence fixed, MULAN's AUROC will drop by a pre-registered margin and become statistically indistinguishable from ESM2. If MULAN retains its full gain under within-protein structure permutation, the gain is not evidence of structural grounding on this task.
draft.method: Use the open-weight MULAN checkpoint and the open-weight ESM2 baseline from the supplied papers, evaluated on a public PPI benchmark released with MULAN (official train/validation/test splits; structures from AlphaFold DB or MULAN-provided structure files). Keep the downstream classifier protocol identical for MULAN and ESM2. Conditions: (A) ESM2 sequence-only; (B) MULAN with native structure-angle tokens; (C) MULAN with within-protein residue-level permutation of structure-angle tokens, preserving token length and marginal angle distribution but destroying residue alignment; repeat permutation 5 times; (D) sanity-check MULAN with structure adapter zeroed/disabled. No retraining is required if released MULAN weights are used; if adapter retraining is needed for the official split, train only the adapter with the released recipe. Report mean test AUROC with bootstrap 95% CIs over test proteins and permutation seeds. This is a modality-shortcut diagnostic adapted from vision-language controlled ablations: the structural channel is mismatched while the sequence channel is held fixed.
draft.minimal_test: 1) Download MULAN code/checkpoints, ESM2 weights, public PPI splits, and public/predicted structures. 2) Reproduce ESM2 and native MULAN PPI AUROC on the official test split. 3) For each test protein, generate 5 within-protein permutations of its structure-angle token sequence. 4) Run MULAN inference under native, permuted, and adapter-zeroed structure inputs. 5) Compute AUROC_native, AUROC_perm_mean, AUROC_ESM2, Δ_native = AUROC_native - AUROC_ESM2, Δ_perm = AUROC_native - AUROC_perm_mean, and residual Δ_res = AUROC_perm_mean - AUROC_ESM2. 6) Pre-register a minimum meaningful structural gain of 0.03 AUROC and equivalence band of 0.01 AUROC.
draft.decisive_metric: Primary metric: PPI test AUROC. Supporting structural grounding requires Δ_native ≥ 0.03 with 95% CI excluding 0, Δ_perm ≥ 0.03 with 95% CI excluding 0, and Δ_res ≤ 0.01. Falsification occurs if Δ_perm < 0.01 or Δ_res ≥ 0.02, meaning permuted-structure MULAN retains a substantial sequence-only gain over ESM2.
draft.supporting_result: Native MULAN beats ESM2 by at least 0.03 AUROC on the public PPI test split; within-protein structure permutation lowers MULAN by at least 0.03 AUROC; permuted MULAN is within 0.01 AUROC of ESM2; adapter-zeroed MULAN approximately matches ESM2. This pattern would support the claim that MULAN's PPI gain is causally tied to residue-aligned structural input rather than sequence-only shortcuts.
draft.falsifying_result: Within-protein structure permutation changes MULAN AUROC by less than 0.01, or permuted MULAN still exceeds ESM2 by at least 0.02 AUROC, or native MULAN does not exceed ESM2 by 0.03 AUROC on the reproduced split. Such a result would falsify the hypothesis that MULAN's PPI advantage is structurally grounded and would indicate a modality-shortcut or parameter-capacity explanation.
draft.related_work: PST (10.48550/arxiv.2401.14819) integrates structural data into a protein language transformer and reports gains over ESM-2, establishing the structure-aware PLM baseline context. MULAN (10.1093/bioadv/vbaf117) proposes a parameter-efficient sequence-plus-angle structure adapter and reports PPI AUROC gains over ESM2 and SaProt, providing the open model and evaluation task targeted here. The hateful-meme vision-language paper (10.1371/journal.pone.0274300) motivates controlled cross-modal alignment tests because multimodal fusion can exploit shortcuts. The visual-field LLM report paper (10.3390/vision9020033) motivates spatial/modality-specific failure diagnostics, since text extraction can succeed while image-based localization fails. No additional prior citations are asserted.
draft.limitations: The test uses one downstream task (PPI) and one structure-aware model family (MULAN), so a negative result would not disprove structural grounding on all tasks. Within-protein permutation creates out-of-distribution structure inputs and may be overly destructive or may preserve global structural statistics. Predicted structures and MULAN's released training data could introduce artifacts. The diagnostic tests reliance on residue-aligned structure, not whether the model learns biophysically correct structural features. ESM2 and MULAN classifier heads must be matched carefully to avoid confounds.
draft.resource_plan: Stay within <=8 A100 GPU-days using public data and open weights only. Data/checkpoint setup: 0.5 day. Reproduce ESM2 and native MULAN PPI AUROC: 1 day. If adapter retraining is required on the official split, train only the lightweight adapter: up to 3 A100-days. Generate and run 5 within-protein structure permutations plus adapter-zeroed diagnostic: 1.5 days. Bootstrap analysis and write-up: 1 day. Reserve 1 day for debugging. No proprietary model weights, no future-paper answer keys, and no hidden test labels are used.

prior_work.title: Analyzing and Improving Optimal-Transport-based Adversarial Networks
prior_work.abstract: Optimal Transport (OT) problem aims to find a transport plan that bridges two distributions while minimizing a given cost function. OT theory has been widely utilized in generative modeling. In the beginning, OT distance has been used as a measure for assessing the distance between data and generated distributions. Recently, OT transport map between data and prior distributions has been utilized as a generative model. These OT-based generative models share a similar adversarial training objective. In this paper, we begin by unifying these OT-based adversarial methods within a single framework. Then, we elucidate the role of each component in training dynamics through a comprehensive analysis of this unified framework. Moreover, we suggest a simple but novel method that improves the previously best-performing OT-based model. Intuitively, our approach conducts a gradual refinement of the generated distribution, progressively aligning it with the data distribution. Our approach achieves a FID score of 2.51 on CIFAR-10 and 5.99 on CelebA-HQ-256, outperforming unified OT-based adversarial approaches.

prior_work.title: Improving Neural Optimal Transport via Displacement Interpolation
prior_work.abstract: Optimal Transport (OT) theory investigates the cost-minimizing transport map that moves a source distribution to a target distribution. Recently, several approaches have emerged for learning the optimal transport map for a given cost function using neural networks. We refer to these approaches as the OT Map. OT Map provides a powerful tool for diverse machine learning tasks, such as generative modeling and unpaired image-to-image translation. However, existing methods that utilize max-min optimization often experience training instability and sensitivity to hyperparameters. In this paper, we propose a novel method to improve stability and achieve a better approximation of the OT Map by exploiting displacement interpolation, dubbed Displacement Interpolation Optimal Transport Model (DIOTM). We derive the dual formulation of displacement interpolation at specific time $t$ and prove how these dual problems are related across time. This result allows us to utilize the entire trajectory of displacement interpolation in learning the OT Map. Our method improves the training stability and achieves superior results in estimating optimal transport maps. We demonstrate that DIOTM outperforms existing OT-based models on image-to-image translation tasks.

prior_work.title: Not-So-Optimal Transport Flows for 3D Point Cloud Generation
prior_work.abstract: Learning generative models of 3D point clouds is one of the fundamental problems in 3D generative learning. One of the key properties of point clouds is their permutation invariance, i.e., changing the order of points in a point cloud does not change the shape they represent. draft.title: Displacement-Interpolation Supervision for Not-So-Optimal Transport Flows on 3D Point Clouds
draft.literature_gap: The supplied cluster contains OT-based adversarial generative models with gradual distribution refinement, displacement-interpolation OT map learning (DIOTM) that improves stability by using the whole interpolation trajectory, and not-so-optimal transport flows (NSOT) that scale permutation-invariant point-cloud generation via offline approximate OT and hybrid coupling. However, the reviews/abstracts expose an untested gap: NSOT addresses permutation invariance and large-cloud scaling but still relies on a flow target whose early trajectory is complex, while DIOTM's multi-time displacement-interpolation supervision has not been tested as a remedy inside permutation-invariant point-cloud OT flows. It is unknown whether multi-time displacement-interpolation supervision plus NSOT-style hybrid coupling reduces early-trajectory complexity and improves sample quality/stability over the NSOT baseline at equal compute.
draft.hypothesis: Adding DIOTM-style multi-time displacement-interpolation supervision to NSOT's offline approximate OT pairs and hybrid coupling will reduce early-trajectory velocity-field complexity and improve point-cloud generation quality/stability over the NSOT baseline at matched compute, without breaking permutation invariance.
draft.method: Use a public ShapeNet subset (e.g., chair and airplane) with 2048-point clouds. Implement a small permutation-invariant flow model trained with NSOT-style offline approximate OT coupling plus hybrid independent coupling. Intervention: add an auxiliary multi-time displacement-interpolation consistency loss at t in {0.1,0.25,0.5,0.75}, using the same offline OT pairs and finite-difference consistency of the learned velocity/map along interpolation paths. Baseline: the supplied NSOT model with offline approximate OT and hybrid coupling but single sampled-time flow-matching supervision. Ablations/diagnostics: (i) remove hybrid independent coupling, (ii) replace multi-time loss with single-time loss, (iii) shuffle point order at test to check permutation invariance, and (iv) measure early-time velocity smoothness on t in [0,0.2]. Train all models from scratch with identical architecture, data, and compute.
draft.minimal_test: Train three seeds per condition on two ShapeNet categories at 2048 points: NSOT baseline, NSOT+multi-time displacement-interpolation supervision, and NSOT without hybrid coupling. Evaluate unconditional generation and shape completion on held-out splits. Log early-time velocity-field smoothness (finite-difference norm/Lipschitz proxy), coupling cost, seed variance, Chamfer distance, Earth Mover's distance, MMD, and 1-NN accuracy. Run within <=8 A100 GPU-days.
draft.decisive_metric: Primary: mean Chamfer distance (CD) and MMD on held-out ShapeNet categories, with seed variance. Diagnostic: early-time (t<0.2) velocity finite-difference smoothness and permutation-invariance error. Decisive comparison is NSOT+multi-time vs NSOT baseline at matched architecture/compute.
draft.supporting_result: The hypothesis is supported if NSOT+multi-time achieves at least 10% lower mean CD and at least 30% lower seed variance than NSOT baseline at equal compute, while early-time velocity smoothness improves and permutation-invariance error remains unchanged or lower. The no-hybrid-coupling ablation should be worse, confirming the diagnostic relevance of coupling mismatch.
draft.falsifying_result: The hypothesis is falsified if NSOT+multi-time gives less than 5% CD improvement or worse seed variance than NSOT baseline, or if it improves CD only by increasing early-time velocity complexity or breaking permutation invariance. prior_work.title: Improving Semantic Understanding in Speech Language Models via Brain-tuning
prior_work.abstract: Speech language models align with human brain responses to natural language to an impressive degree. However, current models rely heavily on low-level speech features, indicating they lack brain-relevant semantics which limits their utility as model organisms of semantic processing in the brain. In this work, we address this limitation by inducing brain-relevant bias directly into the models via fine-tuning with fMRI recordings of people listening to natural stories, a process we name brain-tuning. After testing it on 3 different pretrained model families, we show that brain-tuning not only improves overall alignment with new brain recordings in semantic language regions, but also reduces the reliance on low-level speech features for this alignment. Excitingly, we further show that brain-tuning leads to 1) consistent improvements in performance on a range of downstream tasks and 2) a representational space with increased semantic preference. Our results provide converging evidence, for the first time, that incorporating brain signals into the training of language models improves the models' semantic understanding.

prior_work.title: Speech language models lack important brain-relevant semantics
prior_work.abstract: Despite known differences between reading and listening in the brain, recent work has shown that text-based language models predict both text-evoked and speech-evoked brain activity to an impressive degree. This poses the question of what types of information language models truly predict in the brain. We investigate this question via a direct approach, in which we systematically remove specific low-level stimulus features (textual, speech, and visual) from language model representations to assess their impact on alignment with fMRI brain recordings during reading and listening. Comparing these findings with speech-based language models reveals starkly different effects of low-level features on brain alignment. While text-based models show reduced alignment in early sensory regions post-removal, they retain significant predictive power in late language regions. In contrast, speech-based models maintain strong alignment in early auditory regions even after feature removal but lose all predictive power in late language regions. These results suggest that speech-based models provide insights into additional information processed by early auditory regions, but caution is needed when using them to model processing in late language regions. We make our code publicly available. [https://github.com/subbareddy248/speech-llm-brain]

prior_work.title: A differentiable brain simulator bridging brain simulation and brain-inspired computing
prior_work.abstract: Brain simulation builds dynamical models to mimic the structure and functions of the brain, while brain-inspired computing (BIC) develops intelligent systems by learning from the structure and functions of the brain. The two fields are intertwined and should share a common programming framework to facilitate each other's development. However, none of the existing software in the fields can achieve this goal, because traditional brain simulators lack differentiability for training, while existing deep learning (DL) frameworks fail to capture the biophysical realism and complexity of brain dynamics. In this paper, we introduce BrainPy, a differentiable brain simulator developed using JAX and XLA, with the aim of bridging the gap between brain simulation and BIC. BrainPy expands upon the functionalities of JAX, a powerful AI framework, by introducing complete capabilities for flexible, efficient, and scalable brain simulation. It offers a range of sparse and event-driven operators for efficient and scalable brain simulation, an abstraction for managing the intricacies of synaptic computations, a modular and flexible interface for constructing multi-scale brain models, and an object-oriented just-in-time compilation approach to handle the memory-intensive nature of brain dynamics. We showcase the efficiency and scalability of BrainPy on benchmark tasks, highlight its differentiable simulation for biologically plausible spiking models, and discuss its potential to support research at the intersection of brain simulation and BIC.

Comparing these findings with speech-based language models reveals starkly different effects of low-level features on brain alignment. While text-based models show reduced alignment in early sensory regions post-removal, they retain significant predictive power in late language regions. In contrast, speech-based models maintain strong alignment in early auditory regions even after feature removal but lose all predictive power in late language regions. These results suggest that speech-based models provide insights into additional information processed by early auditory regions, but caution is needed when using them to model processing in late language regions. We make our code publicly available. [https://github.com/subbareddy248/speech-llm-brain]

Sc90bbc899b41.title: A differentiable brain simulator bridging brain simulation and brain-inspired computing
Sc90bbc899b41.fulltext_snippet: Brain simulation builds dynamical models to mimic the structure and functions of the brain, while brain-inspired computing (BIC) develops intelligent systems by learning from the structure and functions of the brain. The two fields are intertwined and should share a common programming framework to facilitate each other's development. However, none of the existing software in the fields can achieve this goal, because traditional brain simulators lack differentiability for training, while existing deep learning (DL) frameworks fail to capture the biophysical realism and complexity of brain dynamics. In this paper, we introduce BrainPy, a differentiable brain simulator developed using JAX and XLA, with the aim of bridging the gap between brain simulation and BIC. BrainPy expands upon the functionalities of JAX, a powerful AI framework, by introducing complete capabilities for flexible, efficient, and scalable brain simulation. It offers a range of sparse and event-driven operators for efficient and scalable brain simulation, an abstraction for managing the intricacies of synaptic computations, a modular and flexible interface for constructing multi-scale brain models, and an object-oriented just-in-time compilation approach to handle the memory-intensive nature of brain dynamics. We showcase the efficiency and scalability of BrainPy on benchmark tasks, highlight its differentiable simulation for biologically plausible spiking models, and discuss its potential to support research at the intersection of brain simulation and BIC.

draft.title: Acoustic-controlled held-out-story test of whether brain-tuning gives speech LMs late-language semantic predictive power

prior_work.title: Can LLMs Understand Time Series Anomalies?
prior_work.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have gained popularity in time series forecasting, but their potential for anomaly detection remains largely unexplored. Our study investigates whether LLMs can understand and detect anomalies in time series data, focusing on zero-shot and few-shot scenarios. Inspired by conjectures about LLMs' behavior from time series forecasting research, we formulate key hypotheses about LLMs' capabilities in time series anomaly detection. We design and conduct principled experiments to test each of these hypotheses. Our investigation reveals several surprising findings about LLMs for time series: (1) LLMs understand time series better as images rather than as text, (2) LLMs do not demonstrate enhanced performance when prompted to engage in explicit reasoning about time series analysis. (3) Contrary to common beliefs, LLMs' understanding of time series does not stem from their repetition biases or arithmetic abilities. (4) LLMs' behaviors and performance in time series analysis vary significantly across different models. This study provides the first comprehensive analysis of contemporary LLM capabilities in time series anomaly detection. Our results suggest that while LLMs can understand trivial time series anomalies, we have no evidence that they can understand more subtle real-world anomalies. Many common conjectures based on their reasoning capabilities do not hold. All synthetic dataset generators, final prompts, and evaluation scripts have been made available in https://github.com/rose-stl-lab/anomllm.

prior_work.title: One-Step Prediction of Financial Time Series
prior_work.abstract: This paper examines the one-step prediction of financial time series from a binary decision theory perspective. Under the assumption that the decision statistic of the binary hypothesis testing problem is a Gaussian random variable, bounds for the forecasting efficiency of the hypothesis testing problem are derived. When the criterion for forecasting performance is the total return over the investment period, an optimisation problem is formulated to compute an optimally weighted decision statistic for the binary hypothesis testing problem. Numerical results are illustrated using weekly time series of excess return between two US dollar bond portfolios having six months duration difference. In particular, it is shown that, on average, a 27 basis point excess return per annum is possible against a given benchmark by carrying out active duration management.

prior_work.title: LLM-ABBA: Understanding Time Series via Symbolic Approximation
prior_work.abstract: The success of large language models (LLMs) for time series has been demonstrated in previous work. Utilizing a symbolic time series representation, one can efficiently bridge the gap between LLMs and time series. However, the remaining challenge is to exploit the semantic information hidden in time series by using symbols or existing tokens of LLMs, while aligning the embedding space of LLMs according to the hidden information of time series. The symbolic time series approximation (STSA) method called adaptive Brownian bridge-based symbolic aggregation (ABBA) shows outstanding efficacy in preserving salient time series features by modeling time series patterns in terms of amplitude and period while using existing tokens of LLMs. In this paper, we introduce a method, called LLM-ABBA, that integrates ABBA into large language models for various downstream time series tasks. By symbolizing time series, LLM-ABBA compares favorably to the recent state-of-the-art (SOTA) in UCR and three medical time series classification tasks. Meanwhile, a fixed-polygonal chain trick in ABBA is introduced to avoid obvious drifting during prediction tasks by significantly mitigating the effects of cumulative error arising from misused symbols during the transition from symbols to numerical values. In time series regression tasks, LLM-ABBA achieves the new SOTA on Time Series Extrinsic Regression (TSER) benchmarks. LLM-ABBA also shows competitive prediction capability compared to recent SOTA time series prediction results. We believe this framework can also seamlessly extend to other time series tasks.

draft.title: Symbolic Bridge or Compression Trap? A Minimal Test of ABBA Symbolic Prompting for Subtle LLM Time-Series Anomaly Detection
draft.literature_gap: The supplied anomaly study shows that open LLMs detect trivial time-series anomalies better when series are rendered as images than as text, and that explicit reasoning prompts do not help; it explicitly finds no evidence for subtle real-world anomaly understanding. LLM-ABBA supplies a symbolic bridge from series to LLM tokens via amplitude/period ABBA symbols, but it has not been tested on subtle anomaly detection, where compression may erase exactly the low-amplitude or short-period deviations that matter. The visible gap is therefore an evaluation gap: no controlled comparison of image prompting, raw numeric text, and ABBA symbolic bridging on subtle anomalies, with an ablation that separates genuine symbolic preservation from token-count or smoothing artifacts.
draft.hypothesis: If ABBA symbolic prompting preserves amplitude/period information relevant to anomalies, then an open-weight LLM given ABBA symbols will achieve higher balanced accuracy on pre-registered subtle anomaly windows than the same LLM given image plots, and this gain will disappear when amplitude symbols are shuffled while token counts and prompt format are held fixed.
draft.method: Use one open-weight instruct model (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct or Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) with vLLM and fixed decoding. Data: public UCR Anomaly Archive labeled windows plus the public synthetic generators/evaluation scripts released with the supplied anomaly paper. Pre-register a subtle subset as labeled anomaly windows whose anomaly-segment robust z-score relative to the preceding 100 normal points is between 1 and 3, or synthetic anomalies injected at 0.5-1.5 sigma amplitude and <=10% period shift. For each window, create four prompts under identical instructions and 8-shot balanced examples: (A) image plot baseline from the supplied anomaly paper, (B) raw numeric text control, (C) ABBA symbolic prompt with amplitude and period tokens, and (D) ablation with amplitude tokens shuffled within the prompt while preserving counts and format. Ask the model to output anomaly yes/no and a segment index; score only the binary label for the primary metric. Run zero-shot and 8-shot; primary analysis is 8-shot. Use bootstrap confidence intervals over windows/datasets. No training, no proprietary weights, no future-paper answer keys.
draft.minimal_test: Train nothing. Evaluate four prompt conditions on a balanced set of 600 windows: 200 subtle anomalies, 200 trivial anomalies, 200 normal windows from UCR plus synthetic controls. Primary comparison is ABBA symbolic vs image baseline on subtle windows; the diagnostic is shuffled-amplitude ABBA vs intact ABBA. The test is minimal because it requires only inference on one 7-8B open-weight model and public labels, with the supplied anomaly paper's image prompt as the required baseline and the shuffled-amplitude ABBA as the required failure-mode ablation.
draft.decisive_metric: Delta balanced accuracy on subtle-anomaly windows: ΔBA = BA_ABBA_subtle - BA_image_subtle. Supporting evidence requires ΔBA >= 0.05 with 95% bootstrap CI lower bound > 0 and the shuffled-amplitude ablation reducing ABBA's subtle BA by at least 0.05. Trivial-anomaly and normal-window balanced accuracy are reported as controls.
draft.supporting_result: ABBA symbolic prompting beats the image baseline on subtle anomalies by at least 5 balanced-accuracy points with a bootstrap CI excluding zero, while both conditions remain high on trivial anomalies; shuffling amplitude tokens drops ABBA's subtle score by at least 5 points and to near the image baseline, indicating the gain comes from preserved amplitude symbols rather than extra tokens or smoothing.
draft.falsifying_result: The hypothesis is falsified if ABBA's subtle-anomaly balanced accuracy is not better than the image baseline by at least 2 points, if the 95% CI includes zero, or if shuffled-amplitude ABBA performs within 2 points of intact ABBA; the latter would indicate that any apparent bridge benefit is a prompt-length or compression artifact rather than symbolic preservation of anomaly-relevant amplitude/period information.

The subtle subset uses a pre-registered robust-z threshold and synthetic injection levels, which may not match all real-world subtle anomalies. ABBA has implementation choices such as fixed-polygonal-chain settings and symbol vocabulary that could affect results. The test measures window-level detection, not precise anomaly localization. prior_work.title: AQUATIC-Diff: Additive Quantization for Truly Tiny Compressed Diffusion Models
prior_work.abstract: Significant investments have been made towards the commodification of diffusion models for generation of diverse media. Their mass-market adoption is however still hobbled by the intense hardware resource requirements of diffusion model inference. Model quantization strategies tailored specifically towards diffusion models have been useful in easing this burden, yet have generally explored the Uniform Scalar Quantization (USQ) family of quantization methods. In contrast, Vector Quantization (VQ) methods, which operate on groups of multiple related weights as the basic unit of compression, have seen substantial success in Large Language Model (LLM) quantization. In this work, we apply codebook-based additive vector quantization to the problem of diffusion model compression. Our resulting approach achieves a new Pareto frontier for the extremely low-bit weight quantization on the standard class-conditional benchmark of LDM-4 on ImageNet at 20 inference time steps. Notably, we report sFID 1.92 points lower than the full-precision model at W4A8 and the best-reported results for FID, sFID and ISC at W2A8. We are also able to demonstrate FLOPs savings on arbitrary hardware via an efficient inference kernel, as opposed to savings resulting from small integer operations which may lack broad hardware support.

prior_work.title: EfficientDM: Efficient Quantization-Aware Fine-Tuning of Low-Bit Diffusion Models
prior_work.abstract: Diffusion models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in image synthesis and related generative tasks. Nevertheless, their practicality for real-world applications is constrained by substantial computational costs and latency issues. Quantization is a dominant way to compress and accelerate diffusion models, where post-training quantization (PTQ) and quantization-aware training (QAT) are two main approaches, each bearing its own properties. While PTQ exhibits efficiency in terms of both time and data usage, it may lead to diminished performance in low bit-width. On the other hand, QAT can alleviate performance degradation but comes with substantial demands on computational and data resources. In this paper, we introduce a data-free and parameter-efficient fine-tuning framework for low-bit diffusion models, dubbed EfficientDM, to achieve QAT-level performance with PTQ-like efficiency. Specifically, we propose a quantization-aware variant of the low-rank adapter (QALoRA) that can be merged with model weights and jointly quantized to low bit-width. The fine-tuning process distills the denoising capabilities of the full-precision model into its quantized counterpart, eliminating the requirement for training data. We also introduce scale-aware optimization and temporal learned step-size quantization to further enhance performance. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms previous PTQ-based diffusion models while maintaining similar time and data efficiency. Specifically, there is only a 0.05 sFID increase when quantizing both weights and activations of LDM-4 to 4-bit on ImageNet 256x256. Compared to QAT-based methods, our EfficientDM also boasts a 16.2x faster quantization speed with comparable generation quality. Code is available at \href{https://github.com/ThisisBillhe/EfficientDM}{this hrl}.

prior_work.title: L4Q: Parameter Efficient Quantization-Aware Fine-Tuning on Large Language Models
prior_work.abstract: Due to the high memory and computational costs associated with large language models (LLMs), model compression techniques such as quantization, which reduces inference costs, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods like Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), which reduce training costs, have gained significant popularity. This trend has spurred active research into quantization-aware PEFT techniques, aimed at maintaining model accuracy while minimizing memory overhead during both inference and training. Previous quantization-aware PEFT methods typically apply post-training quantization (PTQ) to pre-trained LLMs, followed by PEFT to recover accuracy loss. Meanwhile, this approach has limitations in recovering the accuracy loss. In this paper, we propose L4Q, a method that integrates Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) with LoRA. By employing a memory-optimized layer design, L4Q significantly reduces QAT's memory overhead, making its training cost comparable to LoRA, while preserving the advantage of QAT in producing fully quantized LLMs with high accuracy. Our experiments demonstrate that this combined approach to quantization and fine-tuning achieves superior accuracy compared to decoupled fine-tuning schemes, particularly in 4-bit and 3-bit quantization, positioning L4Q as an efficient QAT solution. Using the LLaMA and Mistral models with instructional datasets, we showcase L4Q's capabilities in language tasks and few-shot learning.

draft.title: QALoRA Recovery of Additive Vector-Quantized Diffusion Weights: A Minimal Falsifiable Test
draft.literature_gap: The supplied cluster separates two advances that have not been crossed: AQUATIC-Diff shows additive vector quantization (VQ) gives a strong low-bit Pareto frontier for LDM-4 diffusion but evaluates only post-quantization weights, without a quantization-aware fine-tuning recovery stage. EfficientDM provides a data-free, parameter-efficient QALoRA recovery recipe for low-bit diffusion models, but its quantization target is the uniform scalar quantization family, not codebook-based additive VQ. L4Q shows that integrating QAT with LoRA can beat decoupled PTQ-then-PEFT recovery for LLMs, but not for diffusion models or VQ codebooks. Thus the visible gap is whether the residual error of additive VQ diffusion weights is recoverable by a lightweight QAT/LoRA stage, or whether codebook quantization errors are structurally harder to recover than scalar-quantization errors.
draft.hypothesis: Applying an EfficientDM-style data-free QALoRA recovery stage to AQUATIC-Diff's additive vector-quantized LDM-4 weights at W2A8 will recover at least 50% of the full-precision-to-W2A8 sFID gap, while preserving codebook utilization; if recovery is negligible or a matched-bit uniform-scalar-quantization QALoRA ablation matches it, then additive-VQ diffusion errors are not meaningfully recoverable by low-rank QAT and the apparent VQ advantage is not QAT-compatible.
draft.method: Use the public LDM-4 class-conditional ImageNet 256x256 checkpoint and a public ImageNet validation subset. Recreate the AQUATIC-Diff W2A8 additive-VQ weight quantizer for LDM-4 (codebook-based additive VQ on weights, 8-bit activations), keeping the same 20-step sampling protocol. Baseline arm B0 is the AQUATIC-Diff W2A8 model without fine-tuning. Intervention arm B1 adds an EfficientDM-style data-free QALoRA recovery: low-rank adapters on denoising network linear layers, merged and jointly quantized into the additive-VQ format, trained only by distilling the full-precision LDM-4 denoiser on synthetic/noise inputs with scale-aware optimization and temporal learned step sizes where applicable. Ablation diagnostic B2 repeats B1 at matched bit-width and matched adapter/training budget but replaces additive VQ with uniform scalar quantization, to test whether any gain is VQ-specific rather than generic QAT recovery. Record per-codebook usage and weight residual norms. Evaluate FID, sFID, and IS on the same public validation subset and sampling steps. No proprietary weights or future-paper answer keys are used.
draft.minimal_test: Three-arm test on LDM-4/ImageNet 256x256 at W2A8 and 20 sampling steps: B0 = AQUATIC-Diff additive-VQ without recovery (supplied-paper baseline); B1 = B0 + EfficientDM-style data-free QALoRA recovery; B2 = matched-budget uniform-scalar-quantization + QALoRA ablation. Train B1/B2 for a fixed small budget (e.g., <=3 A100-days each), then evaluate identical image batches. Success requires B1 to improve sFID over B0 by at least half the B0-to-full-precision sFID gap and to beat B2 on sFID at matched bits. Failure is B1 recovery below 10% of that gap, B1 worse than B0, or B2 matching/beating B1 while codebook utilization in B1 collapses relative to B0.
draft.decisive_metric: Relative sFID-gap recovery R = (sFID_B0 - sFID_B1) / (sFID_B0 - sFID_FP), where sFID_FP is the full-precision LDM-4 sFID. Secondary decisive checks: FID_B1 <= FID_B0 and sFID_B1 < sFID_B2 at matched bits; codebook utilization in B1 must remain within 20% of B0. The hypothesis is supported if R >= 0.5 with stable codebook utilization; falsified if R < 0.1, sFID_B1 >= sFID_B0, or sFID_B2 <= sFID_B1.
draft.supporting_result: B1 achieves R >= 0.5 at W2A8, i.e., the additive-VQ QALoRA model closes at least half the sFID gap to full precision, improves FID over B0, preserves codebook usage within 20% of B0, and outperforms the matched-bit uniform-scalar QALoRA ablation B2 on sFID. This would indicate that additive-VQ weight errors in diffusion models are partially recoverable by lightweight data-free QAT and that the AQUATIC-Diff frontier is compatible with EfficientDM-style recovery.
draft.falsifying_result: B1 yields R < 0.1 or sFID_B1 >= sFID_B0, meaning QALoRA cannot recover additive-VQ diffusion errors; or B1 improves sFID only by dropping codebook utilization below 80% of B0, indicating adapter compensation rather than codebook recovery; or B2 matches/beats B1 at matched bits, indicating the recovery is not specific to additive VQ and the proposed VQ+QAT synthesis is not supported.
draft.related_work[1]: AQUATIC-Diff: Additive Quantization for Truly Tiny Compressed Diffusion Models (arXiv:2506.05960) provides the additive vector-quantization LDM-4 baseline and W2A8/W4A8 evaluation protocol.
draft.related_work[2]: EfficientDM: Efficient Quantization-Aware Fine-Tuning of Low-Bit Diffusion Models (arXiv:2310.03270) provides the data-free QALoRA recovery recipe, scale-aware optimization, and LDM-4 W4 evaluation precedent used for the intervention arm.
draft.related_work[3]: L4Q: Parameter Efficient Quantization-Aware Fine-Tuning on Large Language Models (arXiv:2402.04902) motivates integrating QAT with LoRA rather than decoupled PTQ-then-PEFT, but is limited to LLMs and does not test diffusion or codebook VQ.
draft.limitations: Only LDM-4 class-conditional ImageNet 256x256 at 20 steps is tested, so conclusions may not transfer to text-to-image diffusion or other step counts. Additive-VQ quantizer details may need reimplementation from the paper; if exact AQUATIC-Diff code is unavailable, the baseline is an approximate reproduction, which weakens direct comparison. QALoRA training is data-free but still requires full-precision teacher access. The matched-bit scalar ablation controls bit-width but cannot perfectly match all quantizer design choices. Evaluation uses a public validation subset, not the full test server.

Use only public LDM-4 checkpoint, public ImageNet validation data, and open-source quantization/LoRA code; no proprietary model weights and no future-paper answer keys.

Research Background & Open Challenges:
# Towards Reasoning in Large Language Models: A Survey

## 1. Verified Paper Identity & Links
- **Title**: Towards Reasoning in Large Language Models: A Survey
- **Authors**: Jie Huang, Kevin Chen-Chuan Chang
- **arXiv Entry**: [https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10403](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10403)
- **Full PDF**: [https://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.10403.pdf](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.10403.pdf)
- **Field**: llm_and_reasoning

## 2. Official Paper Abstract
Reasoning is a fundamental aspect of human intelligence that plays a crucial role in activities such as problem solving, decision making, and critical thinking. In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have made significant progress in natural language processing, and there is observation that these models may exhibit reasoning abilities when they are sufficiently large. However, it is not yet clear to what extent LLMs are capable of reasoning. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge on reasoning in LLMs, including techniques for improving and eliciting reasoning in these models, methods and benchmarks for evaluating reasoning abilities, findings and implications of previous research in this field, and suggestions on future directions. Our aim is to provide a detailed and up-to-date review of this topic and stimulate meaningful discussion and future work.

## 3. Explicit Research Gaps & Open Challenges
The following core challenges and research gaps are extracted and synthesized directly from the survey's *Open Problems / Challenges / Future Work* sections:

- **Challenge 1 (Spurious Reasoning Paths & Unfaithful Rationales)**: Generated reasoning steps often deviate from internal computations, producing correct final answers through flawed intermediate logical steps.

- **Challenge 2 (Catastrophic Error Accumulation in Multi-Step Chains)**: In long deductive chains (>10 steps), the probability of generating at least one faulty deduction approaches 1.0 without step-level verification.

- **Challenge 3 (Inherent Limits of Autoregressive Search without Backtracking)**: Standard next-token generation cannot backtrack when entering dead ends during complex proof searches.

- **Challenge 4 (Generalization to Out-of-Distribution Problem Geometries)**: CoT methods fail when problem premises are perturbed or framed with counter-intuitive symbolic variables.

## 4. Evaluation Scope & Constraints
Auto Research Agents must formulate an innovative, testable research proposal aimed at resolving at least one of the explicit challenges above. The proposed methodology and experiments must fit within standard academic computing budgets (e.g. 4x A100 GPU cluster, 200 GPU-hours) using publicly accessible datasets and models.

prior_work.title: Autonomous Agents and Policy Compliance: A Framework for Reasoning About Penalties
prior_work.abstract: This paper presents a logic programming-based framework for policy-aware autonomous agents that can reason about potential penalties for non-compliance and act accordingly. While prior work has primarily focused on ensuring compliance, our approach considers scenarios where deviating from policies may be necessary to achieve high-stakes goals. Additionally, modeling non-compliant behavior can assist policymakers by simulating realistic human decision-making. Our framework extends Gelfond and Lobo's Authorization and Obligation Policy Language (AOPL) to incorporate penalties and integrates Answer Set Programming (ASP) for reasoning. Compared to previous approaches, our method ensures well-formed policies, accounts for policy priorities, and enhances explainability by explicitly identifying rule violations and their consequences. Building on the work of Harders and Inclezan, we introduce penalty-based reasoning to distinguish between non-compliant plans, prioritizing those with minimal repercussions. To support this, we develop an automated translation from the extended AOPL into ASP and refine ASP-based planning algorithms to account for incurred penalties. Experiments in two domains demonstrate that our framework generates higher-quality plans that avoid harmful actions while, in some cases, also improving computational efficiency. These findings underscore its potential for enhancing autonomous decision-making and informing policy refinement. Under consideration in Theory and Practice of Logic Programming (TPLP).

prior_work.title: Neural-Symbolic Reasoning: Towards the Integration of Logical Reasoning with Large Language Models
prior_work.abstract: Neural-symbolic reasoning aims to deeply integrate logical automated reasoning with the flexibility of large language model (LLM) reasoning. This survey provides a comprehensive review and position on the state of the art in neural-symbolic integration, covering foundational concepts, key methodologies, existing frameworks, and open research challenges. We examine how classical symbolic techniques (e.g., theorem proving, model checking, knowledge representation) can be combined with neural networks and LLMs to achieve robust reasoning systems that leverage the strengths of both paradigms. Prior work spans diverse domains including program verification, explainable AI, robotics, security, and blockchain, reflecting the broad impact of neural-symbolic approaches. We provide rigorous technical details on representative integration architectures, inference algorithms, symbolic encodings, and training strategies proposed in the literature. We also discuss evaluation methodologies for neural-symbolic systems, comparing their performance, soundness, and interpretability. Finally, we outline future directions with concrete proposals for advancing neural-symbolic reasoning, such as enhanced neural theorem provers, neurosymbolic knowledge bases, and trustworthy AI agents, with implementation-level considerations and theoretical motivation. This paper positions neural-symbolic reasoning as a crucial research area for achieving explainable and verifiable AI in the era of powerful LLMs.

prior_work.title: Towards Structured Reasoning: A Comprehensive Survey of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Large Language Models
prior_work.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning has emerged as a transformative paradigm for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). This survey provides a comprehensive analysis of CoT reasoning, spanning from foundational prompting techniques to the recent emergence of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) such as OpenAI o1 and DeepSeek-R1. We present a unified taxonomy that categorizes CoT methods into four dimensions: (1) prompting strategies including zero-shot, few-shot, and self-consistency approaches; (2) structural extensions such as Tree-of-Thought, Graph-of-Thought, and Forestof-Thought; (3) training paradigms encompassing supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and preference optimization; and (4) emerging paradigms including latent reasoning and multi-modal CoT. Through extensive analysis of over 150 papers, we identify key characteristics that distinguish Long CoT reasoning, including deep multi-step inference, heuristicguided search, and self-verification mechanisms. We systematically compare performance across 25+ benchmarks spanning mathematical, commonsense, symbolic, logical, and multi-modal reasoning tasks. Our analysis reveals critical challenges including reasoning faithfulness, computational efficiency, and the "illusion of thinking" phenomenon. We conclude by outlining promising research directions including efficient reasoning, multi-modal integration, and the development of more robust evaluation frameworks. This survey serves as a comprehensive resource for researchers and practitioners seeking to understand and advance the frontier of reasoning in LLMs.

prior_work.title: Reasoning in Large Language Models: A Survey
prior_work.abstract: With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities in problem-solving. While LLMs have revolutionized natural language processing (NLP), their inherent limitations in structured reasoning impede performance on complex AI tasks that demand multi-step logic, contextual comprehension, and knowledge synthesis. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of approaches to bridge this gap, categorizing reasoning techniques into basic and advanced paradigms. We analyze cutting-edge strategies—including prompt engineering, retrieval-augmented reasoning, and neural-symbolic architectures—which offer diverse perspectives on reasoning across the phases of query formulation, information retrieval (IR), and answer generation. By establishing a taxonomy of reasoning-enhanced IR models and exploring their reasoning applications, we illustrate measurable improvements in the accuracy and interpretability of contemporary LLMs, particularly IR-related models. Nevertheless, persistent challenges in multi-hop reasoning, output consistency, and domain adaptation call for future efforts focused on modular systems, dynamic knowledge integration, and reasoning-aware training frameworks. Our findings and syntheses emphasize that the next evolution of LLMs—and certain IR models alike—resides not merely in retrieving information, but in the true ability to understand, retain, and reason with information, mirroring human cognition.

draft.title: VERICHAIN: Step-Level Verification and Bounded Backtracking for Faithful Long-Chain Reasoning in Open LLMs
draft.literature_gap: The survey identifies two linked open challenges: catastrophic error accumulation in multi-step chains and the inability of standard autoregressive CoT search to backtrack from dead ends. Existing work on CoT, self-consistency, and tree search mostly samples or votes over whole chains and optimizes final-answer accuracy, not step-level validity under controlled chain depth. Neural-symbolic approaches can enforce soundness but usually require formalization and do not provide a cheap, model-agnostic verifier-plus-backtracking procedure for open 7-8B LLMs. The gap is a controlled, compute-matched test of whether a compact counterfactually trained step verifier, used online to gate generation and trigger bounded backtracking, reduces depth-dependent error accumulation and improves faithful reasoning on both in-distribution and premise-perturbed deductive tasks.
draft.hypothesis: If a compact step verifier trained on counterfactually perturbed deduction steps is used to accept, reject, and trigger bounded backtracking during generation by open 7-8B LLMs, then the accuracy-vs-depth decay and faithful final-answer rate on multi-step deductive reasoning will improve over CoT, self-consistency, and self-verification at matched token/compute budgets, and these gains will persist under out-of-distribution premise perturbations.
draft.method: Target Challenges 2 and 3. Use open models Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with 4-bit inference on 4x A100 40GB. Train a compact step verifier (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct with LoRA, plus DeBERTa-v3-large as a cheap ablation) on automatically labeled step triples: premises + prior valid steps + candidate next step. Positive labels come from gold derivations; negatives are generated by controlled corruptions (negation flip, entity/relation swap, rule misapplication, arithmetic slip, unsupported leap, contradiction with a premise). Use ProofWriter and ProntoQA plus a synthetic DEPTH-DED generator with controlled depths 3, 6, 10, 15, and 20. At inference, VERICHAIN samples k=4 candidate next steps per step, scores each with the verifier, accepts the highest-scoring step above a calibrated threshold, and if no candidate passes, backtracks up to B=2 previous steps and resamples. Match total generated tokens to self-consistency with k=4 and k=8. Official baselines: standard CoT, zero-shot CoT, self-consistency k=4/8, least-to-most prompting, Tree-of-Thoughts with a small budget, and self-verification. Ablations: verifier gating without backtracking; random verifier with backtracking; verifier trained without counterfactual corruptions; oracle gold-step verifier as an upper bound; no step gate. Add API baseline GPT-4o-mini CoT and self-consistency within the $200 API budget. Use 40 annotator hours to validate 600 held-out step labels, build an error taxonomy, and spot-check OOD perturbations.
draft.minimal_test: Using Qwen2.5-7B and the 1.5B verifier on ProntoQA/DEPTH-DED at depths 3, 6, 10, 15, and 20 (500 examples per depth), compare CoT, self-consistency k=4, self-verification, and VERICHAIN k=4 at matched generated-token budgets. Train the verifier on 20k synthetic step triples from disjoint generator templates, then evaluate final accuracy, step validity, faithful success, verifier AUROC, and the slope of accuracy vs depth. This minimal test fits in about 60 GPU-hours and is falsifiable before full ablations.
draft.decisive_metric: Primary decisive metric: depth-conditional faithful accuracy at depth >=12 under matched token budget, where faithful means final answer correct and all accepted steps pass a held-out gold verifier. Success requires VERICHAIN to beat the best baseline by at least 8 absolute points at depth >=12 and reduce the accuracy-vs-depth slope by at least 50%, with step-verifier AUROC at least 0.80. Secondary: invalid-step rate and OOD premise-perturbation accuracy.
draft.supporting_result: VERICHAIN improves faithful accuracy at depth >=12 by at least 8 absolute points over self-consistency k=4 at matched token budget, reduces invalid-step rate by at least 30% relative, achieves verifier AUROC at least 0.80 on held-out corrupted steps, and retains at least a 5-point gain on premise-perturbed OOD examples. Research Background & Open Challenges:
# A Survey on Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models

## 1. Verified Paper Identity & Links
- **Title**: A Survey on Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models
- **Authors**: Hanchao Liu, Wenyuan Xue, Yifei Chen et al.
- **arXiv Entry**: [https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.00253](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.00253)
- **Full PDF**: [https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.00253.pdf](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.00253.pdf)
- **Field**: multimodal_and_cv

## 2. Official Paper Abstract
Recent development of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) has attracted growing attention within the AI landscape for its practical implementation potential. However, ``hallucination'', or more specifically, the misalignment between factual visual content and corresponding textual generation, poses a significant challenge of utilizing LVLMs. In this comprehensive survey, we dissect LVLM-related hallucinations in an attempt to establish an overview and facilitate future mitigation. Our scrutiny starts with a clarification of the concept of hallucinations in LVLMs, presenting a variety of hallucination symptoms and highlighting the unique challenges inherent in LVLM hallucinations. Subsequently, we outline the benchmarks and methodologies tailored specifically for evaluating hallucinations unique to LVLMs. Additionally, we delve into an investigation of the root causes of these hallucinations, encompassing insights from the training data and model components. We also critically review existing methods for mitigating hallucinations. The open questions and future directions pertaining to hallucinations within LVLMs are discussed to conclude this survey.

## 3. Explicit Research Gaps & Open Challenges
The following core challenges and research gaps are extracted and synthesized directly from the survey's *Open Problems / Challenges / Future Work* sections:

- **Challenge 1 (Statistical Language Prior Dominance)**: Decoders over-rely on unimodal text co-occurrence statistics, predicting common visual patterns regardless of actual image pixel content.

- **Challenge 2 (Visual Token Dilution & Resolution Bottlenecks)**: Downsampling high-resolution images strips dense fine-grained spatial and text details, causing misattribution in cluttered scenes.

- **Challenge 3 (Fine-Grained Attribute-Object Misbinding)**: Inability of shallow cross-attention layers to correctly associate colors, materials, and relative positions with respective instances.

- **Challenge 4 (Evaluation Gaming via Output Length & Yes/No Biases)**: Binary classification benchmarks (POPE) fail to detect nuanced multi-sentence descriptive hallucinations.

## 4. Evaluation Scope & Constraints
Auto Research Agents must formulate an innovative, testable research proposal aimed at resolving at least one of the explicit challenges above. The proposed methodology and experiments must fit within standard academic computing budgets (e.g. 4x A100 GPU cluster, 200 GPU-hours) using publicly accessible datasets and models.

prior_work.title: A Survey on Hallucination in Large Language and Foundation Models
prior_work.abstract: Generative text models, particularly large language models (LLMs) and foundation models, have influenced numerous fields, including high-quality text generation, reasoning, and multimodal synthesis. These models have been widely applied in healthcare, legal analysis, and scientific research. However, where accuracy and reliability are critical, generative text models pose a significant risk due to hallucination, where generated outputs include incorrect factuality, fabricated, or misleading information. In this survey, we present a review of hallucination in generative AI, covering its taxonomy, detection methods, mitigation strategies, and evaluation benchmarks. We first establish a structured taxonomy, distinguishing between intrinsic vs. extrinsic hallucination and factual vs. semantic hallucination, also discussing task-specific variations in areas such as summarization, machine translation, and dialogue generation. Next, we examine state-of-the-art hallucination detection techniques, including uncertainty estimation, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), self-consistency validation, and internal state monitoring. We further explore mitigation strategies, such as fine-tuning, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), knowledge injection, adversarial training, and contrastive learning. Additionally, we review key evaluation metrics and benchmarks, including FEVER, TruthfulQA, HALL-E, and Entity-Relationship-Based Hallucination Benchmarks (ERBench), which serve as standardized measures for assessing hallucination severity. Despite notable efforts, hallucination remains an open challenge, necessitating further improvements in real-time detection, multimodal hallucination evaluation, and trustworthiness frameworks. We show critical research gaps including the need for standardized hallucination taxonomies, scalable mitigation techniques, and human-AI hybrid verification methods. Our survey aims to serve as a foundational resource for researchers and practitioners, providing insights into current methodologies and guiding future advancements in trustworthy and explainable generative AI.

prior_work.title: Beyond Tokens: A Survey on Decoding Methods for Large Language Models and Large Vision-Language Models
prior_work.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and large vision-language models (LVLMs) have demonstrated impressive generative capabilities, yet ensuring their outputs align with user intent is still challenging. While most existing approaches address this issue at the training stage, inference-time approaches like decoding methods offer a more efficient and scalable solution. Decoding methods control model generation by guiding token-level selection, performing sequence-level generation, or generating tokens in parallel to accelerate the process. In this survey, we identify three emerging paradigms from recent works on decoding methods for LLMs and LVLMs, provide a systematic review of these methods, highlight ongoing challenges, and discuss potential future research directions. Our goal is to underscore the efficiency and effectiveness of decoding methods and offer a practical view of how these methods could be used for diverse tasks. Paper lists and more resources on decoding methods for LLMs and LVLMs can be found at https://github.com/wang2226/Awesome-LLM-Decoding.

prior_work.title: A Survey of Hallucination Problems Based on Large Language Models
prior_work.abstract: Large language models (LLM) have made significant achievements in the field of natural language processing, but the generated text often contains content that is inconsistent with the real world or user input, known as hallucinations. This article investigates the current situation of hallucinations in LLM, including the definition, types, causes, and solutions of hallucinations. Illusions are divided into different types such as factual and faithful, mainly caused by factors such as training data defects, low utilization of facts, and randomness in the decoding process. The phenomenon of hallucinations poses a threat to the reliability of LLM, especially in fields such as healthcare, finance, and law, which may lead to serious consequences. To address this issue, this article investigates methods such as managing training datasets, knowledge editing, and enhancing retrieval generation. Future research should classify and evaluate illusions more finely, explore multimodal strategies, enhance model stability, and integrate human intelligence and artificial intelligence to jointly address challenges, promoting the continuous progress of LLM.
