draft.title: Attention-Gated Image-Blind Prior Subtraction (AGIP): A Training-Free Fix for Attribute-Object Misbinding in LVLMs, Evaluated with Length-Controlled Counterfactual Attribute Pairs
draft.literature_gap: The survey (Liu et al., arXiv:2402.00253) isolates two coupled mechanisms behind LVLM hallucination: (i) decoders reproducing unimodal text co-occurrence statistics irrespective of pixels (Challenge 1, language-prior dominance), and (ii) shallow visual-text association that binds attributes (color, material) to the wrong instance (Challenge 3, attribute-object misbinding). Existing training-free mitigations attack only one side: contrastive-decoding variants (e.g., VCD-style distortion contrast) suppress generic prior but apply a uniform, token-agnostic penalty, so they can also suppress correctly grounded attribute tokens; attention/uncertainty-based detectors flag suspicion but do not steer decoding. Meanwhile the evaluation side is compromised: POPE-style binary probes and length-biased caption metrics make it impossible to tell whether a mitigation actually fixed binding or merely shortened / hedged outputs (Challenge 4). What is missing is (a) a decoding-time intervention whose strength is conditioned on the model's own visual evidence for the *specific token being emitted*, and (b) a discriminative, length-normalized evaluation that is immune to yes/no and verbosity gaming, using minimal counterfactual image edits so that the only correct answer changes is the bound attribute. This proposal supplies both and pre-registers the comparison against official open-source baselines (plain greedy decoding, VCD, OPERA) plus ablations.
draft.hypothesis: H1 (mechanism): for attribute-bearing tokens in LVLM captions, the mass of decoder self-attention on visual token positions (the LLaVA-family analogue of cross-attention to image features) is a usable per-token evidence signal: tokens emitted while visual attention mass is low are disproportionately the ones that follow the language prior and violate the image. H2 (intervention): subtracting an image-blind language prior log-distribution from the next-token distribution, with the subtraction strength gated by that per-token visual evidence score, increases counterfactual attribute discrimination accuracy (CADA) by >=3 absolute points over the strongest baseline (VCD) at matched or better CHAIR_i, without degrading caption CIDEr by more than 1 point on COCO val. H3 (evaluation): CADA, a forced-choice length-normalized comparison between statements describing an original image and its minimally attribute-edited twin, is not predictable from POPE accuracy (|Spearman rho| < 0.5 across 4 decoding configurations), i.e., it measures something the binary benchmark misses.
draft.method:
Models (all public, 40GB-fit in fp16): LLaVA-1.5-7B (primary; exposes per-layer, per-head attention to the 576 visual tokens), LLaVA-NeXT-7B (higher-resolution variant, tests whether the effect is a low-resolution artifact -> partial probe of Challenge 2), Qwen2-VL-2B (different attention/positional scheme, generalization check). No fine-tuning; all interventions are decoding-time.

(1) Benchmark construction 'AttrCF-1k': from COCO val, run GroundingDINO + SAM (public checkpoints) to segment the single most salient noun-phrase instance with a dominant named color; apply a deterministic Lab-space hue rotation to that region only (mask-blended, photometrically validated) to produce an attribute-edited twin (e.g., 'red bus' -> 'green bus') with all else fixed. Retain 1,000 pairs after automatic QC (edit visible: mean masked-region DeltaE > 15; non-edited region DeltaE < 2; captioner-verified). For each pair, generate via templated grammar + the model-independent region metadata a set of 6-10 descriptive statements varying length (single attribute phrase, short sentence, 3-sentence paragraph) and syntactic position of the attribute; each statement exists in a 'true for image A' and 'true for image B' version differing only in the attribute word. Also keep the open-ended captioning and POPE/AMBER subsets for secondary metrics.

(2) AGIP decoder (proposed): at each decoding step t with logits z_t, compute (a) the image-blind prior distribution p_txt = softmax(z_t evaluated under a text-only forward pass of the same prompt, image tokens removed) - a single cached prefix makes this ~free; (b) the visual evidence score e_t = normalized attention mass of the last-layer (and, in ablation, layer-k/head-averaged) attention rows onto visual token positions, calibrated online by an exponential moving average over the generated prefix; (c) adaptive gate g_t = sigmoid((e_t - tau)/s). Final score: logits'_t = z_t - alpha * g_t * (log p_txt - log p_txt_uniform_shift), i.e. subtract the prior log-prob only where visual evidence is weak, leaving strongly grounded tokens nearly untouched. Optionally combined with a mild VCD distortion term; alpha, tau, s, and layer choice tuned ONLY on a held-out 200-pair dev split from COCO train, never on test.

(3) Baselines (official implementations/configs): greedy, VCD (distortion-contrastive), OPERA (beam-with-penalty), plus two ablations of AGIP: uniform gate (g_t = 1, i.e. plain image-blind prior subtraction) and random gate matched in mean gate value. All use identical prompts, seeds, max_new_tokens.

(4) Analysis: per-token correlation of e_t with human-annotated correctness on 500 sampled tokens (40 annotator-hours); gate-value histograms for correct vs hallucinated attribute tokens; failure taxonomy (wrong-instance binding vs color-family confusion vs prior-only hallucination).
draft.minimal_test: The single decisive experiment: run all 5 decoders (greedy, VCD, OPERA, uniform-prior-subtraction, AGIP) on the 1,000 held-out AttrCF pairs with LLaVA-1.5-7B, and compute CADA plus the paired bootstrap of AGIP-minus-VCD. If AGIP does not beat VCD on CADA at p<0.05 with a paired bootstrap over pairs while CHAIR_i is not worse by >1 point, H2 is rejected, regardless of any downstream caption-quality gains. A second, independent minimal test for H1: ablate the evidence score by replacing e_t with a random-but-distribution-matched score; if CADA is unchanged, the 'attention-gated' claim - as opposed to the mere prior subtraction - is falsified, and the contribution reduces to uniform image-blind debiasing.
draft.decisive_metric: CADA (Counterfactual Attribute Discrimination Accuracy): the fraction of the 1,000 pairs for which the length-normalized sequence log-likelihood the model assigns to the true statement for image A exceeds that for the attribute-swapped statement, AND the symmetric condition holds for image B, averaged over statements and length strata. It is a forced-choice, length-normalized, discrimination metric and therefore cannot be gamed by yes/no bias or verbosity. Secondary/guardrail metrics: CHAIR_i and CHAIR_s on 500 COCO captions, AMBER discriminative+generative scores, POPE F1 (to demonstrate H3's orthogonality), CIDEr/BLEU on COCO, and average output length (to prove no length gaming). Human agreement with the automatic CADA on 500 pairs is reported as a validity check.
draft.supporting_result: AGIP raises CADA from the greedy baseline by >=6 points and from the strongest baseline (VCD) by >=3 points (paired bootstrap 95% CI excluding 0), with the gain concentrated in long multi-sentence statements and in cluttered scenes (>=4 salient instances), while CHAIR_i decreases or stays flat and CIDEr drops by <1 point; the random-gate ablation recovers <1 of the 3-point margin over VCD, and the layer-wise analysis shows monotone increase of e_t with human-verified token correctness (AUC >= 0.7). Additionally, CADA gains do not correlate with POPE gains across configurations (|rho| < 0.5), supporting H3 and thus addressing Challenge 4 with evidence rather than assertion.
draft.falsifying_result: Any of: (i) AGIP's CADA improvement over VCD is <1 point or its 95% CI includes 0; (ii) the random-gate ablation matches AGIP, showing the attention gate carries no information beyond uniform prior subtraction; (iii) CADA gains come with CHAIR_i degradation >1 point or an average-length reduction >15%, indicating the model simply hedges/shortens; (iv) per-token evidence AUC < 0.6, i.e. visual attention mass is not a usable token-level signal for this model family; or (v) CADA correlates near-perfectly with POPE across configurations (|rho| > 0.8), meaning the new benchmark re-derives the gamed binary evaluation it was meant to replace.
draft.related_work: Anchored on the target survey (Liu et al., 'A Survey on Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models', arXiv:2402.00253), which frames language-prior dominance, visual-token dilution, attribute-object misbinding, and evaluation gaming as open problems. Complementary recent surveys (dated 2025) motivate the taxonomy and detection/mitigation landscape we position against: 'A Survey on Hallucination in Large Language and Foundation Models' (2025-05-13) and 'Beyond Tokens: A Survey on Decoding Methods for LLMs and LVLMs' (2025-04-18), the latter directly motivating inference-time (rather than training-time) correction. Baselines and benchmarks we build on: LLaVA and LLaVA-1.5 (Liu et al.), Qwen-VL (Bai et al.), InstructBLIP (Dai et al.) as model families; POPE (Li et al., 2023) and CHAIR (Rohrbach et al., 2018) and AMBER (Wang et al., 2023) and MME (Fu et al., 2023) and HallusionBench (Guan et al., 2024) as hallucination evaluations; VCD (Leng et al., 2024) contrastive decoding, OPERA (Huang et al., 2024) beam-level penalty, and DoLa (Chuang et al., 2024) layer-contrast decoding as training-free prior-correction baselines; Woodpecker (Yin et al., 2023) as a post-hoc correction reference point. We do not claim novelty over these methods individually; the gap is per-token evidence-gated prior subtraction plus a length-controlled counterfactual benchmark, and every baseline is re-run by us under identical prompts rather than quoted from papers.
draft.limitations: The intervention is inference-time only and cannot repair missing visual information (Challenge 2) beyond what a higher-resolution backbone already encodes; the higher-resolution model is used as a diagnostic, not as a solution. AttrCF covers color attributes on COCO-style natural images - not materials, counts, spatial relations, or text-rich scenes - so external validity is bounded and the benchmark should be read as a sharp probe, not a comprehensive hallucination suite. Attention mass is a correlational grounding proxy, not a faithful explanation; the design deliberately tests it as a predictive signal and will report it as such even if H1 fails. The image-blind prior is approximated by an image-token-free forward pass, which is a model-specific operationalization (for Qwen2-VL's dynamic-resolution token packing this approximation is weaker and is reported separately). Greedy/beam decoding with a fixed max length may understate gains for long-form generation. All tuning is on a 200-pair dev split, which limits hyperparameter search and risks mild overfitting to COCO's attribute distribution. Human annotation covers 40 hours (~500 tokens/pairs), enough for validity checks but not for a full re-annotation of 1,000 pairs.
draft.resource_plan: Compute (200 GPU-hours on 4x A100 40GB, 8 calendar weeks): W1-W2 benchmark construction - GroundingDINO+SAM over COCO val (1,000 kept of ~2,000 attempted), Lab hue edits, DeltaE QC, statement templating: 35 GPU-h; W3-W4 main runs - 3 models x 5 decoders x (1,000 pairs x ~8 statements + 500 captions + POPE/AMBER subsets), including the extra image-blind forward pass: 85 GPU-h; W5 ablations - gate layer/head choice, alpha/tau/s sweep on dev, random-gate and uniform-gate controls, attention-statistics extraction: 50 GPU-h; W6 analysis, per-token AUC, bootstrap, redundancy with POPE: 10 GPU-h; W7-W8 buffer, reruns, writing: 20 GPU-h. Total 200 GPU-h. Annotator hours (40): 24 h for per-token/pair correctness annotation (500 items, 2 annotators, adjudication), 10 h for statement naturalness/validity QC on the generated templates, 6 h for failure-taxonomy labeling. API budget ($200): ~$150 for a commercial LLM-judge cross-check of CADA's automatic scoring on 2,000 statements (calibration only; human labels remain the ground truth) and ~$50 for a second-judge agreement study. Everything uses public checkpoints, public datasets (COCO val, POPE, AMBER), and released code; the 200-pair dev split and all prompts/thresholds are frozen and published before test evaluation. Pre-registered decision rule: H2 accepted iff AGIP > VCD on CADA by >=3 points with a paired-bootstrap 95% CI excluding zero, random-gate ablation recovers <1 point, and CHAIR_i is not worse by >1 point.

Research Background & Open Challenges:
# Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey

## 1. Verified Paper Identity & Links
- **Title**: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey
- **Authors**: Yunfan Gao, Yun Xiong, Xinyu Gao et al.
- **arXiv Entry**: [https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.10997](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.10997)
- **Full PDF**: [https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.10997.pdf](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.10997.pdf)
- **Field**: llm_and_reasoning

## 2. Official Paper Abstract
Large Language Models (LLMs) showcase impressive capabilities but encounter challenges like hallucination, outdated knowledge, and non-transparent, untraceable reasoning processes. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a promising solution by incorporating knowledge from external databases. This enhances the accuracy and credibility of the generation, particularly for knowledge-intensive tasks, and allows for continuous knowledge updates and integration of domain-specific information. RAG synergistically merges LLMs' intrinsic knowledge with the vast, dynamic repositories of external databases. This comprehensive review paper offers a detailed examination of the progression of RAG paradigms, encompassing the Naive RAG, the Advanced RAG, and the Modular RAG. It meticulously scrutinizes the tripartite foundation of RAG frameworks, which includes the retrieval, the generation and the augmentation techniques. The paper highlights the state-of-the-art technologies embedded in each of these critical components, providing a profound understanding of the advancements in RAG systems. Furthermore, this paper introduces up-to-date evaluation framework and benchmark. At the end, this article delineates the challenges currently faced and points out prospective avenues for research and development.

## 3. Explicit Research Gaps & Open Challenges
The following core challenges and research gaps are extracted and synthesized directly from the survey's *Open Problems / Challenges / Future Work* sections:

- **Challenge 1 (Distractor and Noise Sensitivity)**: Retrieved context containing subtle inaccuracies or irrelevant distractors severely degrades generation faithfulness.

- **Challenge 2 (Multi-Hop Dispersed Information Synthesis)**: Standard dense retrievers fetch isolated paragraphs, struggling to construct multi-document relational graphs.

- **Challenge 3 (Adaptive Retrieval Calibration)**: Inability of models to accurately assess their own parametric knowledge boundaries before triggering unnecessary retrieval.

- **Challenge 4 (Context Window Overhead and Reranking Latency)**: High computational latency of cross-encoder rerankers in high-throughput streaming systems.

## 4. Evaluation Scope & Constraints
Auto Research Agents must formulate an innovative, testable research proposal aimed at resolving at least one of the explicit challenges above. The proposed methodology and experiments must fit within standard academic computing budgets (e.g. 4x A100 GPU cluster, 200 GPU-hours) using publicly accessible datasets and models.

prior_work.title: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey
prior_work.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate general knowledge, but they suffer when specifically needed knowledge is not present in their training set. Two approaches to ameliorating this, without retraining , are 1) prompt engineering and 2) Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). RAG is a form of prompt engineering, insofar as relevant lexical snippets retrieved from RAG corpora are vectorized and aggregated with prompts. However, RAG documents are often noisy, i.e., while relevant to a given prompt, they can contain much other information that obfuscates the desired snippet. If the purpose of pre-training a LLM on massive and general corpora is to engender a generally applicable model, RAG is not: it is a means of LLM optimization, and as such, RAG document selection must be precise, not general. For expert tasks, it is imperative that a RAG corpus be as noise-free as possible, in much the same way a good prompt should be free of irrelevant text. Knowledge Graphs (KGs) provide a concise means of representing domain knowledge free of noisy information. This paper surveys work incorporating KGs with LLM RAG, intending to equip scientists with a better understanding of this novel research area for future work.

prior_work.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Large Language Models through Selective Augmentation
prior_work.abstract: Abstract The increasing complexity and demands of natural language processing tasks have driven the need for more advanced and contextually aware language models. The integration of selective augmentation within Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) frameworks represents a significant advancement, enhancing the relevance and accuracy of generated responses by dynamically incorporating pertinent information during inference. This research carefully developed and implemented a selective augmentation algorithm tailored to GPT-Neo, demonstrating substantial improvements in performance metrics such as BLEU, ROUGE, and F1 scores. Data preprocessing and model fine-tuning were conducted rigorously, ensuring a robust foundation for the selective augmentation mechanism. Experimental results confirmed that the enhanced RAG model not only provided more accurate and contextually relevant responses but also exhibited superior coherence compared to the baseline model. The implications of these findings are profound, suggesting that selective augmentation can significantly elevate the capabilities of language models, making them more reliable and effective for a wide range of applications. This study contributes valuable insights into the optimization of augmentation processes, paving the way for future advancements in natural language processing technologies.

draft.title: Calibrated Retrieval Gating with Cascaded Reranking: Cutting RAG Latency and Distractor Exposure Without Losing Faithfulness
draft.literature_gap: The survey (Gao et al., arXiv:2312.10997) isolates two coupled open problems that existing work treats separately: Challenge 3 (models cannot assess their own parametric knowledge boundaries before triggering retrieval, so retrieval is either always-on or heuristically triggered) and Challenge 4 (cross-encoder rerankers make high-throughput RAG latency-prohibitive). The dated literature supplied here confirms the framing but offers no joint treatment: the KG-RAG survey (10.2139/ssrn.4895062) argues that RAG corpora and retrieved documents are inherently noisy and that 'RAG document selection must be precise, not general,' yet it proposes no mechanism for deciding when retrieval or expensive reranking is warranted at all; the selective-augmentation study (10.21203/rs.3.rs-4652959/v1) shows that dynamic, selective injection of retrieved context improves BLEU/ROUGE/F1 for GPT-Neo, but it (i) selects *which retrieved content* to inject rather than *whether to retrieve*, (ii) uses no calibrated uncertainty signal, and (iii) reports no latency or faithfulness measurements against a cross-encoder reranking pipeline. Missing is a single, cheap, calibratable gating mechanism that (a) predicts pre-retrieval answerability from intrinsic model signals, (b) co-designs the retrieval decision with a reranking cascade so that latency savings compound, and (c) is evaluated on a latency-constrained faithfulness frontier rather than accuracy alone. This proposal targets exactly that gap.
draft.hypothesis: H1: A lightweight, feature-based calibration probe over a frozen 7–8B generator's intrinsic signals (first-token entropy, length-normalized sequence log-probability, semantic entropy over few samples, and a linear probe on a mid-layer hidden state) predicts pre-retrieval answer correctness with enough reliability (AUROC ≥ 0.75 in-domain, ≥ 0.68 zero-shot on long-tail PopQA) to gate retrieval at a threshold that preserves end-to-end answer quality. H2: Combining this gate with a two-stage reranking cascade (cheap MiniLM cross-encoder over top-20, escalation to a large cross-encoder only for low-margin or ambiguous-band queries) yields a strictly better accuracy-vs-p95-latency frontier than always-retrieve RAG, with no loss in claim-level faithfulness. H3 (falsifiable core): the gate achieves equal or better supported-claim rate and EM/F1 at ≤60% of the always-retrieve pipeline's p95 end-to-end latency, and this advantage survives the domain shift from head-entity (NQ) to long-tail (PopQA) questions.
draft.method: Generator: Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 (and a Llama-3-8B-Instruct replication) served with vLLM on 4xA100-40GB. Retriever: Contriever-MS MARCO and E5-base-v2 over a Wikipedia passage index (passages from KILT/DPR Wikipedia dump); BM25 hybrid as an ablation. Rerankers: stage-1 all-MiniLM-L6-v2 cross-encoder (top-20 → top-5); stage-2 BAAI/bge-reranker-large escalation. (1) Signal extraction (no retrieval): for each query, greedy answer plus 5 temperature-0.7 samples; compute mean/max token log-prob, first-token entropy, length-normalized sequence log-prob, semantic entropy (clustering samples by DeBERTa-v3-MNLI bidirectional entailment), and mean-pooled hidden state at layer 20 fed to a linear probe. (2) Calibrator: logistic regression / 2-layer MLP trained on *automatically labeled* data (correctness = EM against gold on NQ + TriviaQA train splits, ~8k queries) with temperature scaling; labels are free, so no annotation budget is spent here. (3) Decision policy: retrieve iff calibrated P(correct|q) < τ, with a conservative OR-rule variant that also retrieves on high semantic entropy; τ swept on dev to trace the accuracy-vs-retrieval-rate curve. (4) Cascade reranking: stage-1 scores top-20, keeps top-5; escalate to stage-2 only when margin(top1−top2) < δ or gate score lies in an ambiguous band [τ_lo, τ_hi]; measure p50/p95 latency with realistic batched serving. (5) Generation with mandatory span-level citations; faithfulness scored by claim decomposition + NLI (DeBERTa-v3 MNLI) as supported-claim rate, with 600 claims (40 annotator hours) human-verified to report NLI–human agreement. Conditions compared on identical questions: (A) no retrieval, (B) always-retrieve + full two-stage rerank (official-style baseline), (C) gate + retrieval + full rerank, (D) gate + retrieval + cascade rerank (proposed). Ablations: remove each gate feature; swap retriever (Contriever/E5/BM25-hybrid); sweep cascade escalation rate δ; swap generator; all under the same compute envelope.
draft.minimal_test: A single pre-registered experiment on 1,500 PopQA (long-tail, held-out) + 1,500 Natural Questions test questions: run conditions A–D with one generator and one retriever, log per-question EM/F1, supported-claim rate, whether retrieval fired, and wall-clock p50/p95 latency under identical serving configuration. Total ≈ 3,000 queries × 4 conditions + 5-sample entropy passes over 3,000 queries ≈ well inside 200 GPU-hours.
draft.decisive_metric: Supported-claim rate (faithfulness) and EM achieved at a fixed p95 end-to-end latency budget equal to 60% of the always-retrieve baseline's p95 latency (i.e., the vertical intercept of the accuracy-vs-latency frontier), reported separately for PopQA and NQ. Secondary decisives: retrieval-trigger rate and gate calibration error (ECE) under domain shift.
draft.supporting_result: The gated cascade matches or exceeds always-retrieve EM/F1 (+0.5 to +2.0 points, non-inferior supported-claim rate within 1 point) while firing retrieval on ≤60% of queries, reducing p95 latency by ≥40% and ECE ≤0.08 on NQ and ≤0.15 on PopQA, with gains holding for the Llama-3-8B replication and across retriever swaps. This confirms H1–H3 and directly answers Challenges 3 and 4.
draft.falsifying_result: The calibrator fails to transfer: AUROC < 0.65 and ECE > 0.20 on PopQA (long-tail confidence is systematically miscalibrated), so at any τ that reduces retrieval by ≥30% the gated pipeline loses >3 EM points and >3 points of supported-claim rate versus always-retrieve, and/or the cascade's escalation rate exceeds ~50% so p95 latency is not meaningfully below the full-rerank baseline. In that case H3 is rejected and the claim that intrinsic signals suffice for adaptive retrieval calibration is falsified within this budget.
draft.related_work: Gao et al., 'Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey' (arXiv:2312.10997) — source of the Naive/Advanced/Modular RAG taxonomy and the explicit Challenge 3 (adaptive retrieval calibration) and Challenge 4 (context-window overhead and reranking latency) targeted here. 'Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey' (10.2139/ssrn.4895062) — motivates the precision-over-recall view of retrieved context and the noise-sensitivity framing that our gating and faithfulness metrics operationalize. 'Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Large Language Models through Selective Augmentation' (10.21203/rs.3.rs-4652959/v1) — closest prior work on selectivity in RAG; it selects content to inject for GPT-Neo and reports BLEU/ROUGE/F1, whereas we test whether-to-retrieve gating with calibrated uncertainty on a modern 7–8B generator and evaluate a latency-constrained faithfulness frontier instead of n-gram overlap. Baselines are implemented as methodological controls (no-retrieval, always-retrieve dense RAG with full cross-encoder reranking), not as attributed prior systems.
draft.limitations: Single-hop, English-only evaluation; long-tail shift is approximated by PopQA rather than a live domain shift; semantic-entropy sampling adds pre-retrieval cost that our accounting includes but that may not amortize at very low query volumes; faithfulness is judged by an NLI model validated on only 600 human-annotated claims, so systematic NLI bias (over-crediting) may inflate absolute supported-claim rates, though comparisons across conditions remain internally valid; one generator family (7–8B) and two retrievers limit generality claims; multi-hop synthesis (Challenge 2) is only touched via a small HotpotQA stress-test and not solved.
draft.resource_plan: Hardware: 4xA100-40GB, 200 GPU-hours, 8 calendar weeks, $200 API, 40 annotator hours. Allocation: (i) signal extraction / 5-sample entropy passes over ~8k train + 3k eval queries with vLLM: 45 GPU-h; (ii) condition A–D inference (3k queries x 4 conditions, batched): 50 GPU-h; (iii) reranker cascade latency benchmarking and threshold sweeps (stage-1/stage-2, batched serving, 3 repeats): 30 GPU-h; (iv) ablations (feature removal, retriever swap, generator swap, δ sweep): 50 GPU-h; (v) HotpotQA stress-test: 10 GPU-h; (vi) buffer/reruns: 15 GPU-h. Research Background & Open Challenges:
# A Survey on Large Language Model based Autonomous Agents

## 1. Verified Paper Identity & Links
- **Title**: A Survey on Large Language Model based Autonomous Agents
- **Authors**: Lei Wang, Chen Ma, Xueyang Feng et al.
- **arXiv Entry**: [https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.11432](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.11432)
- **Full PDF**: [https://arxiv.org/pdf/2308.11432.pdf](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2308.11432.pdf)
- **Field**: llm_and_reasoning

## 2. Official Paper Abstract
Autonomous agents have long been a prominent research focus in both academic and industry communities. Previous research in this field often focuses on training agents with limited knowledge within isolated environments, which diverges significantly from human learning processes, and thus makes the agents hard to achieve human-like decisions. Recently, through the acquisition of vast amounts of web knowledge, large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable potential in achieving human-level intelligence. This has sparked an upsurge in studies investigating LLM-based autonomous agents. In this paper, we present a comprehensive survey of these studies, delivering a systematic review of the field of LLM-based autonomous agents from a holistic perspective. More specifically, we first discuss the construction of LLM-based autonomous agents, for which we propose a unified framework that encompasses a majority of the previous work. Then, we present a comprehensive overview of the diverse applications of LLM-based autonomous agents in the fields of social science, natural science, and engineering. Finally, we delve into the evaluation strategies commonly used for LLM-based autonomous agents. Based on the previous studies, we also present several challenges and future directions in this field. To keep track of this field and continuously update our survey, we maintain a repository of relevant references at https://github.com/Paitesanshi/LLM-Agent-Survey.

## 3. Explicit Research Gaps & Open Challenges
The following core challenges and research gaps are extracted and synthesized directly from the survey's *Open Problems / Challenges / Future Work* sections:

- **Challenge 1 (Long-Horizon Error Compounding)**: Early execution mistakes in multi-step task workflows rapidly propagate, resulting in irreversible downstream task failure.

- **Challenge 2 (Multi-Agent Sycophancy & Hallucinatory Consensus)**: Collaborative agents frequently reinforce each other's hallucinations rather than providing rigorous critique.

- **Challenge 3 (Episodic Memory Retrieval Degradation)**: Vector databases retrieve out-of-context historical fragments lacking hierarchical structure and temporal invalidation.

- **Challenge 4 (Environment Feedback Grounding)**: Parsing unstructured terminal outputs, compiler errors, or multimodal environmental observations into valid recovery actions.

## 4. Evaluation Scope & Constraints
Auto Research Agents must formulate an innovative, testable research proposal aimed at resolving at least one of the explicit challenges above. The proposed methodology and experiments must fit within standard academic computing budgets (e.g. 4x A100 GPU cluster, 200 GPU-hours) using publicly accessible datasets and models.

prior_work.title: Autonomous Agents and Policy Compliance: A Framework for Reasoning About Penalties
prior_work.abstract: This paper presents a logic programming-based framework for policy-aware autonomous agents that can reason about potential penalties for non-compliance and act accordingly. While prior work has primarily focused on ensuring compliance, our approach considers scenarios where deviating from policies may be necessary to achieve high-stakes goals. Additionally, modeling non-compliant behavior can assist policymakers by simulating realistic human decision-making. Our framework extends Gelfond and Lobo's Authorization and Obligation Policy Language (AOPL) to incorporate penalties and integrates Answer Set Programming (ASP) for reasoning. Compared to previous approaches, our method ensures well-formed policies, accounts for policy priorities, and enhances explainability by explicitly identifying rule violations and their consequences. Building on the work of Harders and Inclezan, we introduce penalty-based reasoning to distinguish between non-compliant plans, prioritizing those with minimal repercussions. To support this, we develop an automated translation from the extended AOPL into ASP and refine ASP-based planning algorithms to account for incurred penalties. Experiments in two domains demonstrate that our framework generates higher-quality plans that avoid harmful actions while, in some cases, also improving computational efficiency. These findings underscore its potential for enhancing autonomous decision-making and informing policy refinement. Under consideration in Theory and Practice of Logic Programming (TPLP).

draft.title: Risk-Calibrated Checkpointing and Counterfactual Rollback for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
draft.literature_gap: The surveyed field identifies long-horizon error compounding as a core open challenge: early mistakes in multi-step LLM-agent workflows propagate into irreversible failures. Existing agent loops such as ReAct and Reflexion mostly act first and reflect afterward; they lack step-level risk calibration, explicit safe checkpoints, and principled rollback when an action is predicted to be irreversible. There is also little systematic measurement of irreversible-error propagation on standard text-agent benchmarks, so it is unclear whether reflection alone or lightweight risk-aware control is sufficient.
draft.hypothesis: A risk-calibrated checkpoint-and-rollback controller (HCCR) wrapped around a ReAct-style LLM agent will reduce irreversible failure rates and improve task success on long-horizon text environments compared with ReAct and Reflexion, while adding at most 25% extra environment steps. The effect should depend on the step-level verifier and rollback mechanism, not merely on extra LLM calls.
draft.method: Implement HCCR as a controller around ReAct on ALFWorld and WebShop. At each step the agent proposes an action; a verifier scores risk using (i) the current compact state digest (goal, inventory, location, recent observations), (ii) the proposed action, and (iii) environment-specific symbolic precondition checks where available. Actions above a calibrated risk threshold require a checkpoint and a short lookahead: the agent generates K=3 alternative next actions and estimates whether each can preserve goal reachability. If an executed action produces a failure signal or verifier-observation mismatch, HCCR restores the last safe checkpoint, records a failure signature, and re-plans with an explicit avoid-constraint. Failure signatures are stored by symbolic state predicates rather than unstructured vector retrieval. Baselines: official ReAct and Reflexion implementations with identical models and prompts, plus ReAct with simple retry. Ablations: no verifier/random checkpoints, no rollback, no failure memory, threshold sweep, and an oracle-irreversibility upper bound. Models: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct served with vLLM; GPT-4o-mini only as an independent judge/annotation aid. Datasets: ALFWorld unseen test split and WebShop public test tasks. Evaluation uses task success, environment steps, oracle-replay irreversibility labels, and recovery rate after injected wrong actions at fixed early steps. Human annotators label a stratified sample of failures as irreversible/recoverable and validate verifier precision.
draft.minimal_test: Run 100 ALFWorld and 100 WebShop episodes with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct comparing ReAct, Reflexion, and HCCR, plus 50 injected-error episodes per environment. Use 20 GPU-hours for this pilot. Proceed only if HCCR shows a pre-registered directional reduction in irreversible failures without a large step overhead.
draft.decisive_metric: Relative reduction in oracle-verified irreversible failure rate versus the strongest baseline (Reflexion), with task success as a co-primary metric and environment-step overhead as a cost constraint.
draft.supporting_result: HCCR reduces irreversible failure rate by at least 30% relative to Reflexion, improves success by at least 8 absolute points on at least one benchmark, recovers from at least 50% of injected early errors, and uses no more than 25% additional environment steps. The no-verifier and no-rollback ablations should lose most of the gain, and verifier precision should exceed 0.65 on the annotated sample.
draft.falsifying_result: HCCR yields less than a 10% relative reduction in irreversible failures, no significant success improvement, recovery below 25% after injected errors, or requires more than 50% additional steps. A result where the no-verifier/random-checkpoint ablation matches HCCR would also falsify the claim that calibrated risk detection drives the benefit.

Research Background & Open Challenges:
# A Practical Review of Mechanistic Interpretability for Transformer-Based Language Models

## 1. Verified Paper Identity & Links
- **Title**: A Practical Review of Mechanistic Interpretability for Transformer-Based Language Models
- **Authors**: Daking Rai, Yilun Zhou, Shi Feng et al.
- **arXiv Entry**: [https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.02646](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.02646)
- **Full PDF**: [https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.02646.pdf](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.02646.pdf)
- **Field**: interpretability_and_theory

## 2. Official Paper Abstract
Mechanistic interpretability (MI) is an emerging sub-field of interpretability that seeks to understand a neural network model by reverse-engineering its internal computations. Recently, MI has garnered significant attention for interpreting transformer-based language models (LMs), resulting in many novel insights yet introducing new challenges. However, there has not been work that comprehensively reviews these insights and challenges, particularly as a guide for newcomers to this field. To fill this gap, we provide a comprehensive survey from a task-centric perspective, organizing the taxonomy of MI research around specific research questions or tasks. We outline the fundamental objects of study in MI, along with the techniques, evaluation methods, and key findings for each task in the taxonomy. In particular, we present a task-centric taxonomy as a roadmap for beginners to navigate the field by helping them quickly identify impactful problems in which they are most interested and leverage MI for their benefit. Finally, we discuss the current gaps in the field and suggest potential future directions for MI research.

## 3. Explicit Research Gaps & Open Challenges
The following core challenges and research gaps are extracted and synthesized directly from the survey's *Open Problems / Challenges / Future Work* sections:

- **Challenge 1 (Sparse Autoencoder Reconstruction vs Faithfulness)**: Decomposing polysemantic activations into millions of dictionary latents introduces significant reconstruction loss.

- **Challenge 2 (Circuit Scalability to Complex Reasoning)**: Circuit extraction algorithms only work on toy tasks (IOI), failing to isolate circuits responsible for multi-layer open-domain reasoning.

- **Challenge 3 (Feature Superposition in Deep Residual Streams)**: Unraveling entangled features across 80+ transformer layers where representations are continuously overwritten.

- **Challenge 4 (Automated Causal Circuit Validation)**: Lack of scalable automated methods to verify causal necessity and sufficiency of identified subgraphs across diverse prompt distributions.

## 4. Evaluation Scope & Constraints
Auto Research Agents must formulate an innovative, testable research proposal aimed at resolving at least one of the explicit challenges above. The proposed methodology and experiments must fit within standard academic computing budgets (e.g. 4x A100 GPU cluster, 200 GPU-hours) using publicly accessible datasets and models.

prior_work.abstract: Abstract Motivation While Protein Language Models (PLMs) fine-tuned on biophysical data achieve high predictive accuracy, the physical principles underlying their predictions remain obscure. Deciphering these representations offers a unique opportunity to not only interpret model decisions but also to discover novel biophysical insights governing protein properties. Here, we present a framework using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to extract mechanistic knowledge from PLMs fine-tuned for nanobody thermo-stability. prior_work.title: From Mechanistic Interpretability to Mechanistic Biology: Training, Evaluating, and Interpreting Sparse Autoencoders on Protein Language Models
prior_work.abstract: Abstract Protein language models (pLMs) are powerful predictors of protein structure and function, learning through unsupervised training on millions of protein sequences. pLMs are thought to capture common motifs in protein sequences, but the specifics of pLM features are not well understood. Identifying these features would not only shed light on how pLMs work, but potentially uncover novel protein biology––studying the model to study the biology. Motivated by this, we train sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on the residual stream of a pLM, ESM-2. By characterizing SAE features, we determine that pLMs use a combination of generic features and family-specific features to represent a protein. In addition, we demonstrate how known sequence determinants of properties such as thermostability and subcellular localization can be identified by linear probing of SAE features. For predictive features without known functional associations, we hypothesize their role in unknown mechanisms and provide visualization tools to aid their interpretation. Our study gives a better understanding of the limitations of pLMs, and demonstrates how SAE features can be used to help generate hypotheses for biological mechanisms. We release our code , model weights and feature visualizer .

prior_work.title: Comparative Evaluation of Transformer-Based Nepali Language Models
prior_work.abstract: Abstract Large pre-trained transformer models using self-supervised learning have achieved state-of-the-art performances in various NLP tasks. However, for low-resource language like Nepali, pre-training of monolingual models remains a problem due to lack of training data and well-designed and balanced benchmark datasets. Furthermore, several multilingual pre-trained models such as mBERT and XLM-RoBERTa have been released, but their performance remains unknown for Nepali language. S758581297410.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Fine-Tuned Protein Language Models for Nanobody Thermostability Prediction
attribution_passages: Abstract Motivation While Protein Language Models (PLMs) fine-tuned on biophysical data achieve high predictive accuracy, the physical principles underlying their predictions remain obscure. Deciphering these representations offers a unique opportunity to not only interpret model decisions but also to discover novel biophysical insights governing protein properties. Here, we present a framework using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to extract mechanistic knowledge from PLMs fine-tuned for nanobody thermo-stability. Results We fine-tuned the ESM-2 model on the nanobody thermostability dataset, achieving superior performance compared to significantly larger state-of-the-art models. SAE analysis successfully decomposed the model’s dense embeddings into sparse, interpretable features without loss of predictive accuracy. We characterized these features through both global and local analyses. Global analysis revealed that stabilizing features predominantly activate on the molecular surface, optimizing charge distributions, whereas destabilizing features map to the hydrophobic core, reflecting packing defects. Local analysis identified specific interactions, including known factors like the VHH-tetrad and critical disulfide bonds, as well as novel stabilizing candidates. Free Energy Perturbation calculations confirmed that these novel candidates exhibit structural compatibility, avoiding the severe destabilization seen in neighboring residues. By revealing these multi-scale biophysical rules, our approach demonstrates that interpreting fine-tuned PLMs provides a physics-grounded guide for rational protein engineering. Availability The data and source code of the proposed method are available at GitHub ( https://github.com/matsunagalab/paper_nanobody-thermostability-sae ) and Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18012027). Contact Yasuhiro Matsunaga ( ymatsunaga@riken.jp ) Supplementary information Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

Sdbfad0bf3125.title: From Mechanistic Interpretability to Mechanistic Biology: Training, Evaluating, and Interpreting Sparse Autoencoders on Protein Language Models
attribution_passages: Abstract Protein language models (pLMs) are powerful predictors of protein structure and function, learning through unsupervised training on millions of protein sequences. pLMs are thought to capture common motifs in protein sequences, but the specifics of pLM features are not well understood. Identifying these features would not only shed light on how pLMs work, but potentially uncover novel protein biology––studying the model to study the biology. Motivated by this, we train sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on the residual stream of a pLM, ESM-2. By characterizing SAE features, we determine that pLMs use a combination of generic features and family-specific features to represent a protein. In addition, we demonstrate how known sequence determinants of properties such as thermostability and subcellular localization can be identified by linear probing of SAE features. For predictive features without known functional associations, we hypothesize their role in unknown mechanisms and provide visualization tools to aid their interpretation. Our study gives a better understanding of the limitations of pLMs, and demonstrates how SAE features can be used to help generate hypotheses for biological mechanisms. We release our code , model weights and feature visualizer .

draft.title: Reconstruction-Faithfulness Pareto Frontier for Sparse Autoencoders: A Causal Validation Benchmark in GPT-2 Small
draft.literature_gap: The survey identifies two linked gaps: SAE decomposition of polysemantic activations has reconstruction loss that may not track causal faithfulness (Challenge 1), and automated causal validation of identified subgraphs is not scalable across prompt distributions (Challenge 4). Existing SAE work, including protein-LM SAE studies, reports interpretable features but does not establish a quantitative reconstruction-versus-causal-faithfulness frontier for transformer LMs on standard circuit tasks.
draft.hypothesis: At matched SAE sparsity (L0), activation reconstruction error is an unreliable proxy for causal faithfulness. An output-consistency regularized SAE (RC-SAE) that penalizes LM-logit divergence under SAE reconstruction will improve causal sufficiency and necessity of selected latents/circuits relative to vanilla ReLU and TopK SAEs, with at most a 10% activation-MSE penalty at L0=64.
draft.method: Use GPT-2 small and Pythia-160m residual streams at layers 4, 8, and 11. Train SAEs on 50M tokens from a public corpus with width 8k and matched L0 in {32,64,128}. Baselines: vanilla ReLU SAE, TopK SAE, and JumpReLU-style SAE from public SAELens implementations. RC-SAE adds beta times output-KL between the original LM logits and logits after replacing the target layer activation with its SAE reconstruction; beta in {0,0.1,1.0}. Evaluate reconstruction MSE, L0, dead latents, output KL, and automated causal validation. Causal tests use activation patching and latent ablation on IOI, Greater-Than, induction, and a small multiple-choice open-domain set (BoolQ/ARC-Easy subset). Build latent circuits by attribution patching, then test necessity and sufficiency under held-out prompt templates. Ablations: beta=0, random-latent circuits, activation patching versus attribution patching, per-layer transfer, and seed variance.
draft.minimal_test: Train 3 SAE variants x 3 L0 levels x 3 seeds on GPT-2 small layer 8, plus layer-4/11 and Pythia-160m confirmation runs. For each SAE, select top-k latents by causal effect on IOI and Greater-Than, ablate them, and compare task-logit drop against random top-k latents. Compute Faithfulness@k as the Spearman correlation between latent ablation effect and reconstruction attribution on held-out prompts. Use bootstrap confidence intervals over prompts and seeds.
draft.decisive_metric: Faithfulness@k at L0=64 plus circuit sufficiency gap. Success requires RC-SAE to raise Faithfulness@k by at least 0.10 over the best baseline and increase IOI/Greater-Than logit drop from top-k circuit ablation by at least 15 percentage points over random-latent ablation, while activation MSE is no more than 10% worse than the best baseline and bootstrap CIs do not overlap.
draft.supporting_result: RC-SAE at L0=64 achieves Faithfulness@k >= 0.55 versus <= 0.45 for vanilla/TopK baselines, circuit ablation causes a >=15-point larger task-logit drop than random-latent ablation, and output KL is lower than baselines at matched L0; layer-4/11 and Pythia-160m runs show the same direction.
draft.falsifying_result: No RC-SAE variant improves Faithfulness@k or circuit sufficiency over the best baseline at matched L0, or improvements disappear when controlling for activation MSE, or reconstruction MSE degrades by more than 10% without compensating causal gains; overlapping bootstrap CIs across seeds would falsify the hypothesis.
draft.related_work[1]: Rai et al., A Practical Review of Mechanistic Interpretability for Transformer-Based Language Models, arXiv:2407.02646, 2024.
draft.related_work[2]: 10.1101/2025.02.06.636901: SAEs on ESM-2 residual streams characterize generic and family-specific protein features.
draft.related_work[3]: 10.64898/2025.12.22.695878: SAE analysis of fine-tuned ESM-2 for nanobody thermostability links sparse features to biophysical rules.
draft.related_work[4]: Public SAELens baseline implementations for ReLU, TopK, and JumpReLU SAEs; IOI, Greater-Than, induction, BoolQ, and ARC-Easy as public evaluation tasks.
draft.limitations: Only GPT-2 small and Pythia-160m are tested; results may not transfer to 7B+ models. SAE width and 50M-token training are below frontier scale. Causal validation uses short synthetic and multiple-choice prompts, not full open-domain multi-step reasoning. LLM-assisted feature labeling and 40 annotator-hours limit human interpretability coverage. Output-consistency regularization may optimize task logits while missing non-task features.
draft.resource_plan.notes: Weeks 1-2 data/SAE pipeline and baselines; weeks 3-4 train matched-L0 SAEs and RC-SAE; weeks 5-6 causal validation and circuit ablation; week 7 ablations and seed variance; week 8 human/LLM feature checks, write-up. API budget for LLM-assisted feature labeling; 40 annotator-hours for 200-feature interpretability audit.
